paragraphs: This paper offers a common explanation for several ways neural networks fail to generalize. Its argument is that learning can introduce random information into a network beyond the information supplied by the training examples. In the authors' complexity-based account, this extra information makes the learned function more complex and harms its expected behavior on new cases.

The paper studies replication as a response to that problem. Multiple networks with the same architecture are trained independently on the same data, and their results are averaged. Although their training examples match, the independently trained networks can incorporate different random information during learning.

The analysis concludes that replication almost always reduces expected complexity and therefore improves expected generalization within the proposed framework. Simulations are reported as supporting this effect. The emphasis on expectation matters: the claim concerns the anticipated effect of averaging independently trained replicas. The contribution links that averaging procedure to a theory of how randomness entering the learning process can increase unnecessary complexity.
summary.tldr: A complexity-based analysis argues that averaging independently trained replicas reduces random information and improves expected generalization.

title: Chaitin-Kolmogorov Complexity and Generalization in Neural Networks

abstract: We have produced a VLSI circuit capable of learning to approximate ar(cid:173) bitrary smooth of a single variable using a technique closely related to splines. The circuit effectively has 512 knots space on a uniform grid and has full support for learning. The circuit also can be used to approximate multi-variable functions as sum of splines. An interesting, and as of yet, nearly untapped set of applications for VLSI imple(cid:173) mentation of neural network learning systems can be found in adaptive control and non-linear signal processing. In most such applications, the learning task consists of approximating a real function of a small number of continuous variables from discrete data points. Special purpose hardware is especially interesting for applica(cid:173) tions of this type since they generally require real time on-line learning and there can be stiff constraints on the power budget and size of the hardware. Frequently, the already difficult learning problem is made more complex by the non-stationary nature of the underlying process. Conventional feed-forward networks with sigmoidal units are clearly inappropriate for applications of this type. Although they have exhibited remarkable performance in some types of time series prediction problems (for example, Wiegend, 1990 and Atlas, 1990), their learning rates in general are too slow for on-line learning. On-line performance can be improved most easily by using networks with more constrained architecture, effectively making the learning problem easier by giving the network a hint about the learning task. Networks that build local representations of the data, such as radial basis functions, are excellent candidates for these type of problems. paragraphs: The authors built an analog VLSI circuit that learns smooth functions of one variable using an approach closely related to splines. Splines organize an approximation around locations called knots; this circuit effectively supplies 512 knots on a uniform grid. It includes support for learning and can also represent multivariable functions as sums of splines.

The motivation comes from adaptive control and nonlinear signal processing, where a system must learn a continuous relationship from discrete observations. Such applications may require learning during operation, within tight limits on hardware size and power. The relationship being learned may also change over time, making slow adaptation particularly problematic.

The paper argues that a more constrained architecture can simplify this learning task. It points to local representations and notes that fixing unit positions and widths makes the learning problem linear. The circuit embodies this emphasis on giving the learner useful structure. Its contribution is a hardware implementation tailored to function approximation, with learning built into the device.
summary.tldr: An analog VLSI circuit learns smooth functions using a spline-like representation with 512 uniformly spaced knots.

title: An Analog VLSI Splining Network

abstract: We present a distribution-free model for incremental learning when concepts vary with time. Concepts are caused to change by an adversary while an incremental learning algorithm attempts to track the changing concepts by minimizing the error between the current target concept and the hypothesis. For a single half(cid:173) plane and the intersection of two half-planes, we show that the average mistake rate depends on the maximum rate at which an adversary can modify the concept. These theoretical predictions are verified with simulations of several learning algorithms including back propagation.
originalAbstract: We present a distribution-free model for incremental learning when concepts vary with time. Concepts are caused to change by an adversary while an incremental learning algorithm attempts to track the changing concepts by minimizing the error between the current target concept and the hypothesis. For a single half(cid:173) plane and the intersection of two half-planes, we show that the average mistake rate depends on the maximum rate at which an adversary can modify the concept. These theoretical predictions are verified with simulations of several learning algorithms including back propagation.

paragraphs: This paper studies incremental learning when the rule being learned changes over time. A learner continually updates its hypothesis while an adversary modifies the target concept. The objective is to keep the learner’s predictions close to the current target, making ongoing tracking accuracy the central issue rather than eventual convergence to one fixed rule.

The framework is distribution-free and examines two geometric concept classes: a single half-plane and the intersection of two half-planes. A half-plane describes the region on one side of a straight boundary. The analysis connects the learner’s average mistake rate to the maximum rate at which the adversary can change the target concept.

Simulations of several learning algorithms, including backpropagation, verify the theoretical predictions. The important implication is that learning performance depends on how quickly the target is allowed to move. The work provides a way to reason about this dependence explicitly, tying the difficulty of tracking a changing rule to a constraint on the source of that change.
summary.tldr: A theory of incremental learning links mistakes on changing half-plane concepts to the maximum speed of adversarial change.

title: Incrementally Learning Time-varying Half-planes

abstract: Experiments were performed to reveal some of the computational properties of the human motor memory system. We show that as humans practice reaching movements while interacting with a novel mechanical environment, they learn an internal model of the inverse dynamics of that environment. Subjects show recall of this model at testing sessions 24 hours after the initial practice. The representation of the internal model in memory is such that there is interference when there is an attempt to learn a new inverse dynamics map immediately after an anticorrelated mapping was learned. We suggest that this interference is an indication that the same computational elements used to encode the first inverse dynamics map are being used to learn the second mapping. We predict that this leads to a forgetting of the initially learned skill.

The representation of the internal model in memory is such that there is interference when there is an attempt to learn a new inverse dynamics map immediately after an anticorrelated mapping was learned. paragraphs: The paper investigates what people learn when practicing reaching movements in an unfamiliar mechanical environment. The experiments indicate that practice builds an internal model of inverse dynamics: a mapping that connects a desired movement to the commands needed under the environment's mechanical conditions. This frames motor learning as acquiring a usable computational model.

Participants recalled the learned model when tested 24 hours after initial practice. The experiments also examined what happens when another mapping is learned immediately afterward. When the new mapping was anticorrelated with the first, learning showed interference. The relationship between the two mappings therefore mattered for how successfully the second could be acquired.

The authors interpret this interference as evidence that the two mappings draw on the same computational elements in memory. Reusing those elements to encode the second mapping could disrupt what they previously represented. They consequently predict forgetting of the initially learned skill. The observed recall and interference establish the behavioral findings, while shared computational elements and resulting forgetting form the proposed explanation and prediction.
summary.tldr: Reaching experiments show retained inverse-dynamics learning and interference between opposing mappings, suggesting shared motor-memory resources.

title: Interference in Learning Internal Models of Inverse Dynamics in Humans

abstract: Filial imprinting in domestic chicks is of interest in psychology, biology, and computational modeling because it exemplifies simple, rapid, in(cid:173) nately programmed learning which is biased toward learning about some objects. Hom et al. have recently discovered a naive visual preference for heads and necks which develops over the course of the first three days of life. The neurological basis of this predisposition is almost en(cid:173) tirely unknown; that of imprinting-related learning is fairly clear. This project is the first model of the predisposition consistent with what is known about learning in imprinting. The model develops the predisposi(cid:173) tion appropriately, learns to "approach" a training object, and replicates one interaction between the two processes. Future work will replicate more interactions between imprinting and the predisposition in chicks, and analyze why the system works.

paragraphs: Filial imprinting provides a way to study how rapid learning interacts with an animal's built-in preferences. Domestic chicks do not approach learning with entirely neutral interests: the abstract describes a visual preference for heads and necks that develops during their first three days. The paper models how this predisposition can coexist with learning about a particular object.

The authors construct a neural network model designed to remain consistent with existing knowledge about imprinting-related learning. This is a meaningful constraint because the neurological basis of imprinting is described as relatively clear, while the basis of the visual predisposition is largely unknown. The model connects these two processes within one computational account.

The network develops the preference, learns to approach a training object, and reproduces one interaction between predisposition and imprinting. These results show that the two forms of behavior can be represented together. The authors identify reproducing additional interactions and explaining why the system works as future work, so the demonstrated account covers a specific part of their relationship.
summary.tldr: A neural network models how chicks develop an early visual preference while learning to approach an imprinted object.

title: A Neural Network Model of Naive Preference and Filial Imprinting in the Domestic Chick

abstract: We present the CEM (Conditional Expectation Maximi::ation) al(cid:173) gorithm as an extension of the EM (Expectation M aximi::ation) algorithm to conditional density estimation under missing data. A bounding and maximization process is given to specifically optimize conditional likelihood instead of the usual joint likelihood. We ap(cid:173) ply the method to conditioned mixture models and use bounding techniques to derive the model's update rules . Monotonic conver(cid:173) gence, computational efficiency and regression results superior to EM are demonstrated.
originalAbstract: We present the CEM (Conditional Expectation Maximi::ation) al(cid:173) gorithm as an extension of the EM (Expectation M aximi::ation) algorithm to conditional density estimation under missing data. A bounding and maximization process is given to specifically optimize conditional likelihood instead of the usual joint likelihood. We ap(cid:173) ply the method to conditioned mixture models and use bounding techniques to derive the model's update rules . Monotonic conver(cid:173) gence, computational efficiency and regression results superior to EM are demonstrated.

paragraphs: This paper extends expectation maximization to conditional density estimation when data are missing. The distinction concerns the objective being optimized. Ordinary EM targets joint likelihood, while the proposed Conditional Expectation Maximization algorithm targets conditional likelihood: the probability of the quantities to be predicted given the quantities available as conditions.

The authors construct a bounding-and-maximization procedure specifically for that conditional objective. They apply it to conditioned mixture models and derive parameter update rules using the bounds. This supplies an optimization method aligned with conditional prediction while retaining the iterative structure of improving a bound and updating the model.

The paper demonstrates monotonic convergence, computational efficiency, and regression results superior to EM in the comparisons reported. Monotonic convergence describes the behavior of the optimization procedure; the regression comparison describes the observed predictive results. Together, these findings support adapting the fitting objective to the conditional task. The contribution is both an extension of EM for missing-data settings and a concrete set of updates for conditioned mixture models.
summary.tldr: Conditional EM optimizes conditional likelihood through bound maximization and demonstrates monotonic convergence and improved regression results over EM.

title: Maximum Conditional Likelihood via Bound Maximization and the CEM Algorithm

abstract: Learning Real-Time A* (LRTA*) is a popular control method that interleaves plan(cid:173) ning and plan execution and has been shown to solve search problems in known environments efficiently. In this paper, we apply LRTA * to the problem of getting to a given goal location in an initially unknown environment. Uninformed LRTA * with maximal lookahead always moves on a shortest path to the closest unvisited state, that is, to the closest potential goal state. This was believed to be a good exploration heuristic, but we show that it does not minimize the worst-case plan-execution time compared to other uninformed exploration methods. This result is also of interest to reinforcement-learning researchers since many reinforcement learning methods use asynchronous dynamic programming, interleave planning and plan execution, and exhibit optimism in the face of uncertainty, just like LRTA *.

paragraphs: Learning Real-Time A*, or LRTA*, alternates planning with taking actions. Although it had been shown to solve search problems efficiently in known environments, this paper examines reaching a specified goal in an initially unknown environment. Here, movement also serves exploration: an unvisited location remains a possible place to discover the goal.

The authors establish that uninformed LRTA* with maximal lookahead follows a shortest path to the nearest unvisited state. This gives a precise account of the exploration behavior induced by the algorithm under those conditions. Choosing the nearest unexplored possibility appears attractive because each immediate exploration decision minimizes the distance to a new state.

The paper nevertheless shows that this behavior does not minimize worst-case plan-execution time among uninformed exploration methods. Locally short trips to unexplored locations do not establish the strongest worst-case guarantee for the overall search. The result also matters to reinforcement learning because many methods share LRTA*'s combination of asynchronous dynamic programming, interleaved planning and action, and optimism about unknown possibilities.
summary.tldr: Uninformed LRTA* with maximal lookahead explores the nearest unvisited state, but this strategy does not minimize worst-case execution time.

title: Exploring Unknown Environments with Real-Time Search or Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The information bottleneck method is an unsupervised model independent data organization technique. Given a joint distribution peA, B), this method con(cid:173) structs a new variable T that extracts partitions, or clusters, over the values of A that are informative about B. In a recent paper, we introduced a general princi(cid:173) pled framework for multivariate extensions of the information bottleneck method that allows us to consider multiple systems of data partitions that are inter-related. In this paper, we present a new family of simple agglomerative algorithms to construct such systems of inter-related clusters. We analyze the behavior of these algorithms and apply them to several real-life datasets.

paragraphs: The information bottleneck method organizes data by grouping values of one variable while retaining information about another. Given a joint distribution over A and B, it constructs a variable T representing clusters of A that remain informative about B. This makes relevance to another variable part of the clustering problem.

The paper builds on a multivariate framework that allows several systems of partitions to be related to one another. Such a formulation concerns more than a single grouping considered in isolation: the relationships among multiple cluster systems become part of what the method must construct.

The authors introduce a family of simple agglomerative algorithms for this task. Agglomerative construction forms groups through merging, providing an algorithmic route to the interrelated partitions described by the framework. They analyze the algorithms' behavior and apply them to several real datasets. The contribution is a practical family of procedures for multivariate information-bottleneck organization, with analysis and applications rather than a stated universal performance advantage.
summary.tldr: The paper develops agglomerative algorithms that construct interrelated cluster systems within the multivariate information bottleneck framework.

title: Agglomerative Multivariate Information Bottleneck

abstract: We formulate the regression problem as one of maximizing the mini- mum probability, symbolized by (cid:10), that future predicted outputs of the regression model will be within some (cid:6)" bound of the true regression function. Our formulation is unique in that we obtain a direct estimate of this lower probability bound (cid:10). The proposed framework, minimax probability machine regression (MPMR), is based on the recently de- scribed minimax probability machine classiﬁcation algorithm [Lanckriet et al.] and uses Mercer Kernels to obtain nonlinear regression models. MPMR is tested on both toy and real world data, verifying the accuracy of the (cid:10) bound, and the efﬁcacy of the regression models.

Our formulation is unique in that we obtain a direct estimate of this lower probability bound (cid:10). The proposed framework, minimax probability machine regression (MPMR), is based on the recently de- scribed minimax probability machine classiﬁcation algorithm [Lanckriet et al.] and uses Mercer Kernels to obtain nonlinear regression models. MPMR is tested on both toy and real world data, verifying the accuracy of the (cid:10) bound, and the efﬁcacy of the regression models.

paragraphs: Regression predicts a numerical output, but a prediction alone does not say how reliably it will stay close to the underlying function. This paper formulates regression around that reliability question. Its objective is to maximize a lower bound on the probability that future predictions fall within a specified error tolerance of the true regression function.

The resulting method, minimax probability machine regression, directly estimates this lower probability bound. The tolerance describes how much error is acceptable, while the bound expresses a conservative probability of meeting that tolerance. These quantities give the regression objective an explicit interpretation in terms of prediction accuracy and reliability.

The framework extends an existing minimax probability classification approach and uses Mercer kernels to construct nonlinear regression models. Tests on synthetic and real-world data support both the accuracy of the estimated probability bound and the effectiveness of the predictors. The bound concerns a probability of staying within tolerance, so it should not be read as a promise that every future prediction satisfies the tolerance.
summary.tldr: Minimax probability machine regression learns nonlinear predictors while directly estimating a lower bound on their probability of meeting an error tolerance.

title: A Formulation for Minimax Probability Machine Regression

abstract: Machine learning is often used to automatically solve human tasks. In this paper, we look for tasks where machine learning algorithms are not as good as humans with the hope of gaining insight into their current limitations. We studied various Human Interactive Proofs (HIPs) on the market, because they are systems designed to tell computers and humans apart by posing challenges presumably too hard for computers. We found that most HIPs are pure recognition tasks which can easily be broken using machine learning. The harder HIPs use a combination of segmentation and recognition tasks. From this observation, we found that building segmentation tasks is the most effective way to confuse machine learning algorithms. This has enabled us to build effective HIPs (which we deployed in MSN Passport), as well as design challenging segmentation tasks for machine learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Human Interactive Proofs are challenges intended to distinguish people from computers by presenting tasks that computers supposedly find difficult. This paper studies such systems to identify weaknesses in machine learning through tasks where humans retain an advantage. The authors examine several available visual challenges.

They find that most of the studied systems rely on recognition alone and can be defeated easily with machine learning. Harder systems combine recognition with segmentation: the computer must work out which image portions form separate items as well as identify them. Within their investigation, constructing segmentation challenges proves the most effective way to confuse the learning algorithms.

The authors use this observation to build effective challenges deployed in MSN Passport and to design difficult segmentation tasks for machine learning research. The findings connect practical challenge design with an analysis of what makes a visual task hard for the studied algorithms. The reported lesson concerns those systems and methods, rather than establishing that segmentation will remain a permanent barrier to automated recognition.
summary.tldr: The study finds segmentation more challenging than recognition alone for the examined machine-learning systems and uses that insight to design deployed human-verification challenges.

title: Using Machine Learning to Break Visual Human Interaction Proofs (HIPs)

abstract: We propose to selectively remove examples from the training set using probabilistic estimates related to editing algorithms (Devijver and Kittler, 1982). This heuristic procedure aims at creating a separable distribution of training examples with minimal impact on the position of the decision boundary. It breaks the linear dependency between the number of SVs and the number of training examples, and sharply reduces the complexity of SVMs during both the training and prediction stages.
originalAbstract: We propose to selectively remove examples from the training set using probabilistic estimates related to editing algorithms (Devijver and Kittler, 1982). This heuristic procedure aims at creating a separable distribution of training examples with minimal impact on the position of the decision boundary. It breaks the linear dependency between the number of SVs and the number of training examples, and sharply reduces the complexity of SVMs during both the training and prediction stages.

paragraphs: The paper targets the computational cost of support vector machines during both learning and prediction. Its focus is the relationship between training-set size and the number of support vectors retained by the model. If that number grows linearly with the training data, adding examples also increases the complexity of the resulting classifier.

The proposed procedure selectively removes training examples using probabilistic estimates related to data-editing algorithms. The aim is to produce a separable distribution of retained examples while changing the decision boundary as little as possible. Selection therefore serves a geometric purpose: the method attempts to simplify the data supporting the classifier without substantially moving the separation it learns.

The authors report that this procedure breaks the linear dependence between support-vector count and training-set size and sharply reduces training and prediction complexity. The boundary-preservation objective is explicitly heuristic, however. The contribution is a practical strategy for reducing the examples that drive SVM complexity, with minimal boundary movement presented as its aim rather than an exact guarantee.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic editing removes selected training examples to reduce SVM complexity while aiming to preserve the decision boundary.

title: Breaking SVM Complexity with Cross-Training

abstract: When training and test samples follow different input distributions (i.e., the situation called \emph{covariate shift}), the maximum likelihood estimator is known to lose its consistency. For regaining consistency, the log-likelihood terms need to be weighted according to the \emph{importance} (i.e., the ratio of test and training input densities). Thus, accurately estimating the importance is one of the key tasks in covariate shift adaptation. A naive approach is to first estimate training and test input densities and then estimate the importance by the ratio of the density estimates. However, since density estimation is a hard problem, this approach tends to perform poorly especially in high dimensional cases. In this paper, we propose a direct importance estimation method that does not require the input density estimates. Our method is equipped with a natural model selection procedure so tuning parameters such as the kernel width can be objectively optimized. This is an advantage over a recently developed method of direct importance estimation. Simulations illustrate the usefulness of our approach.

paragraphs: Covariate shift occurs when training and test inputs follow different distributions. The paper considers correcting likelihood-based learning by weighting training contributions according to their importance for the test distribution. The required importance is the ratio of the test input density to the training input density, making accurate ratio estimation a central task.

One approach estimates both densities separately and then divides them. The authors argue that this can perform poorly, especially in high dimensions, because estimating the densities is itself difficult. They propose estimating importance directly, avoiding the need to solve those two density-estimation problems as intermediate steps.

The method also includes a model-selection procedure for choosing tuning parameters such as kernel width. This provides an objective way to tune the estimator, which the abstract identifies as an advantage over another direct importance-estimation method. Simulations illustrate the approach’s usefulness. The contribution combines a more targeted estimation problem with a way to select its settings, addressing both how importance weights are obtained and how the estimator is configured.
summary.tldr: Direct density-ratio estimation with built-in model selection supports adaptation when training and test input distributions differ.

title: Direct Importance Estimation with Model Selection and Its Application to Covariate Shift Adaptation

abstract: Discriminative tasks, including object categorization and detection, are central components of high-level computer vision. Sometimes, however, we are interested in more refined aspects of the object in an image, such as pose or particular regions. In this paper we develop a method (LOOPS) for learning a shape and image feature model that can be trained on a particular object class, and used to outline instances of the class in novel images. Furthermore, while the training data consists of uncorresponded outlines, the resulting LOOPS model contains a set of landmark points that appear consistently across instances, and can be accurately localized in an image. Our model achieves state-of-the-art results in precisely outlining objects that exhibit large deformations and articulations in cluttered natural images. These localizations can then be used to address a range of tasks, including descriptive classification, search, and clustering.
originalAbstract: Discriminative tasks, including object categorization and detection, are central components of high-level computer vision. Sometimes, however, we are interested in more refined aspects of the object in an image, such as pose or particular regions. In this paper we develop a method (LOOPS) for learning a shape and image feature model that can be trained on a particular object class, and used to outline instances of the class in novel images. Furthermore, while the training data consists of uncorresponded outlines, the resulting LOOPS model contains a set of landmark points that appear consistently across instances, and can be accurately localized in an image. Our model achieves state-of-the-art results in precisely outlining objects that exhibit large deformations and articulations in cluttered natural images. These localizations can then be used to address a range of tasks, including descriptive classification, search, and clustering.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object's category does not necessarily reveal its pose or the locations of its particular regions. The paper develops LOOPS to provide this more detailed description. Trained for an object class, the method learns a model combining shape and image features and uses it to outline new instances in images.

A notable feature is the relationship between its training annotations and learned representation. Training provides outlines without correspondences across instances, yet the model develops landmark points that recur consistently across objects. These landmarks can be accurately localized in an image, giving the resulting outline an internal structure useful for comparing instances.

The authors report state-of-the-art outlining results for objects with large deformations and articulations in cluttered natural images. This supports the model's ability to handle substantial shape variation in the evaluated setting. The resulting localizations can support descriptive classification, search, and clustering: tasks that benefit from knowing how an object is arranged and where its regions lie, in addition to knowing its class.
summary.tldr: LOOPS learns consistent landmarks from uncorresponded outlines and precisely localizes deformable objects in cluttered images.

title: Shape-Based Object Localization for Descriptive Classification

abstract: Kernel supervised learning methods can be unified by utilizing the tools from regularization theory. The duality between regularization and prior leads to interpreting regularization methods in terms of maximum a posteriori estimation and has motivated Bayesian interpretations of kernel methods. In this paper we pursue a Bayesian interpretation of sparsity in the kernel setting by making use of a mixture of a point-mass distribution and prior that we refer to as ``Silverman's g-prior.'' We provide a theoretical analysis of the posterior consistency of a Bayesian model choice procedure based on this prior. We also establish the asymptotic relationship between this procedure and the Bayesian information criterion.

The duality between regularization and prior leads to interpreting regularization methods in terms of maximum a posteriori estimation and has motivated Bayesian interpretations of kernel methods. In this paper we pursue a Bayesian interpretation of sparsity in the kernel setting by making use of a mixture of a point-mass distribution and prior that we refer to as ``Silverman's g-prior.'' We also establish the asymptotic relationship between this procedure and the Bayesian information criterion.

paragraphs: Regularization provides a common way to understand kernel-based supervised learning. A penalty on a fitted function can also be interpreted through a Bayesian prior, connecting regularized solutions to maximum a posteriori estimation. The paper uses this relationship to investigate a Bayesian account of sparsity in kernel methods.

The proposed construction mixes a point-mass distribution with a distribution the authors call Silverman's g-prior. The point-mass component provides a way to express exact sparsity within the prior formulation. This turns sparsity into a model-choice question handled by Bayesian inference, connecting the selection of a sparse representation to assumptions encoded in the prior.

The paper's main contribution is theoretical: it analyzes posterior consistency for the resulting Bayesian model-choice procedure. This concerns the procedure's behavior as evidence accumulates, rather than simply its fit to a fixed dataset. The authors also establish an asymptotic relationship with the Bayesian information criterion. Together, these results connect the proposed sparse Bayesian formulation to both large-sample model-choice behavior and an established criterion for comparing models.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes posterior consistency and the asymptotic connection to BIC for sparse Bayesian kernel model choice using Silverman's g-prior.

title: Posterior Consistency of the Silverman g-prior in Bayesian Model Choice

abstract: Score functions induced by generative models extract fixed-dimension feature vectors from different-length data observations by subsuming the process of data generation, projecting them in highly informative spaces called score spaces. In this way, standard discriminative classifiers are proved to achieve higher performances than a solely generative or discriminative approach. In this paper, we present a novel score space that exploits the free energy associated to a generative model through a score function. This function aims at capturing both the uncertainty of the model learning and ``local compliance of data observations with respect to the generative process. Theoretical justifications and convincing comparative classification results on various generative models prove the goodness of the proposed strategy.

In this way, standard discriminative classifiers are proved to achieve higher performances than a solely generative or discriminative approach. In this paper, we present a novel score space that exploits the free energy associated to a generative model through a score function. This function aims at capturing both the uncertainty of the model learning and ``local compliance of data observations with respect to the generative process. Theoretical justifications and convincing comparative classification results on various generative models prove the goodness of the proposed strategy.

paragraphs: The paper considers how to combine generative models with discriminative classification. A generative model describes how observations arise, while a discriminative classifier uses features to distinguish classes. Score spaces connect these roles by converting observations, including observations of different lengths, into feature vectors with a fixed number of dimensions.

The authors introduce a score space based on the free energy associated with a generative model. Its score function aims to capture two kinds of information: uncertainty in learning the model and how individual observations locally agree with the modeled generation process. Those signals become features that a standard discriminative classifier can use.

This approach matters because the representation incorporates information from modeling the data before classification begins. The paper provides theoretical justification and comparative classification results across several generative models in support of the strategy. Its contribution is therefore a particular way to construct informative features from generative modeling, backed by classification evidence. The stated aim of representing uncertainty and local agreement explains what distinguishes this score function within the broader score-space approach.
summary.tldr: A free-energy score function converts generative-model information into fixed-size features for discriminative classification.

title: Free energy score space

abstract: A common approach for handling the complexity and inherent ambiguities of 3D human pose estimation is to use pose priors learned from training data. Existing approaches however, are either too simplistic (linear), too complex to learn, or can only learn latent spaces from "simple data", i.e., single activities such as walking or running. In this paper, we present an efficient stochastic gradient descent algorithm that is able to learn probabilistic non-linear latent spaces composed of multiple activities. Furthermore, we derive an incremental algorithm for the online setting which can update the latent space without extensive relearning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the task of monocular and multi-view tracking and show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art.

Existing approaches however, are either too simplistic (linear), too complex to learn, or can only learn latent spaces from "simple data", i.e., single activities such as walking or running. In this paper, we present an efficient stochastic gradient descent algorithm that is able to learn probabilistic non-linear latent spaces composed of multiple activities. paragraphs: Estimating a person’s three-dimensional pose from images is ambiguous, so tracking systems often use learned pose priors to guide their estimates. The paper targets a difficulty in learning these priors: existing approaches can be overly simple, difficult to train, or restricted to latent representations of a single activity such as walking.

The authors introduce an efficient stochastic gradient descent algorithm for learning probabilistic nonlinear latent spaces containing multiple activities. Such a space provides a learned representation of pose variation that can accommodate more than one kind of movement. The contribution addresses both the flexibility of the representation and the computational problem of fitting it.

They also derive an incremental algorithm that updates the latent space in an online setting without extensive relearning. This extends the approach beyond a representation that must remain fixed after initial training. Experiments on monocular and multiple-view tracking demonstrate the method’s effectiveness and report performance above the state of the art. The results support using these richer learned pose representations for the tracking tasks examined.
summary.tldr: Efficient training and incremental updates make probabilistic nonlinear pose representations spanning multiple activities useful for improved human tracking.

title: Learning Probabilistic Non-Linear Latent Variable Models for Tracking Complex Activities

abstract: We consider infinite-horizon stationary $\gamma$-discounted Markov Decision Processes, for which it is known that there exists a stationary optimal policy. Using Value and Policy Iteration with some error $\epsilon$ at each iteration, it is well-known that one can compute stationary policies that are $\frac{2\gamma{(1-\gamma)^2}\epsilon$-optimal. After arguing that this guarantee is tight, we develop variations of Value and Policy Iteration for computing non-stationary policies that can be up to $\frac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma}\epsilon$-optimal, which constitutes a significant improvement in the usual situation when $\gamma$ is close to $1$. Surprisingly, this shows that the problem of ``computing near-optimal non-stationary policies'' is much simpler than that of ``computing near-optimal stationary policies''.
originalAbstract: We consider infinite-horizon stationary $\gamma$-discounted Markov Decision Processes, for which it is known that there exists a stationary optimal policy. Using Value and Policy Iteration with some error $\epsilon$ at each iteration, it is well-known that one can compute stationary policies that are $\frac{2\gamma{(1-\gamma)^2}\epsilon$-optimal. After arguing that this guarantee is tight, we develop variations of Value and Policy Iteration for computing non-stationary policies that can be up to $\frac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma}\epsilon$-optimal, which constitutes a significant improvement in the usual situation when $\gamma$ is close to $1$. Surprisingly, this shows that the problem of ``computing near-optimal non-stationary policies'' is much simpler than that of ``computing near-optimal stationary policies''.

paragraphs: In a stationary discounted Markov decision process, the decision problem itself does not change over time, and an optimal stationary policy exists. Such a policy uses the same decision rule whenever a state is encountered. The paper asks what happens when policies must be computed approximately, with error introduced at every iteration.

The authors examine value iteration and policy iteration and argue that their familiar guarantees for approximate stationary policies are tight. They then develop variants that produce non-stationary policies, whose decision rules can change over time. These variants can attain substantially better near-optimality guarantees, particularly when the discount factor is close to one.

The distinction is between the existence of an optimal solution and the difficulty of computing a good approximate solution within a restricted policy class. Even though a stationary optimum exists, allowing time-dependent decisions can make approximate computation easier. The result concerns infinite-horizon discounted problems with per-iteration error and shows why a richer output policy can improve the consequences of imperfect planning.
summary.tldr: With per-iteration approximation error, non-stationary policies can offer better near-optimality guarantees even for stationary discounted decision problems.

title: On the Use of Non-Stationary Policies for Stationary Infinite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes

abstract: We present the first result for kernel regression where the procedure adapts locally at a point $x$ to both the unknown local dimension of the metric and the unknown H\{o}lder-continuity of the regression function at $x$. The result holds with high probability simultaneously at all points $x$ in a metric space of unknown structure."
originalAbstract: We present the first result for kernel regression where the procedure adapts locally at a point $x$ to both the unknown local dimension of the metric and the unknown H\{o}lder-continuity of the regression function at $x$. The result holds with high probability simultaneously at all points $x$ in a metric space of unknown structure."

paragraphs: The paper studies kernel regression when the relevant structure of the input space is unknown. Its central concern is local adaptation: the procedure should respond to the properties of the space and the regression function around the particular point where a prediction is needed.

Two unknown quantities matter together. Local metric dimension describes the dimensional structure near a point, while local Hölder continuity describes how smoothly the regression function varies there. The result establishes adaptation to both quantities at once. This matters because adapting to the geometry alone would leave the function's local behavior unaddressed, and adapting only to smoothness would leave the geometry unaddressed.

The guarantee holds with high probability simultaneously across all points in the metric space. That simultaneous statement gives the result broader scope than a guarantee established only for one preselected location. The authors identify this as the first kernel-regression result combining both forms of local adaptation, without requiring the metric space's structure to be known.
summary.tldr: Kernel regression can adapt simultaneously to unknown local dimension and local smoothness, with a high-probability guarantee across the metric space.

title: Adaptivity to Local Smoothness and Dimension in Kernel Regression

abstract: Many powerful Monte Carlo techniques for estimating partition functions, such as annealed importance sampling (AIS), are based on sampling from a sequence of intermediate distributions which interpolate between a tractable initial distribution and an intractable target distribution. The near-universal practice is to use geometric averages of the initial and target distributions, but alternative paths can perform substantially better. We present a novel sequence of intermediate distributions for exponential families: averaging the moments of the initial and target distributions. We derive an asymptotically optimal piecewise linear schedule for the moments path and show that it performs at least as well as geometric averages with a linear schedule. Moment averaging performs well empirically at estimating partition functions of restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs), which form the building blocks of many deep learning models, including Deep Belief Networks and Deep Boltzmann Machines.
originalAbstract: Many powerful Monte Carlo techniques for estimating partition functions, such as annealed importance sampling (AIS), are based on sampling from a sequence of intermediate distributions which interpolate between a tractable initial distribution and an intractable target distribution. The near-universal practice is to use geometric averages of the initial and target distributions, but alternative paths can perform substantially better. We present a novel sequence of intermediate distributions for exponential families: averaging the moments of the initial and target distributions. We derive an asymptotically optimal piecewise linear schedule for the moments path and show that it performs at least as well as geometric averages with a linear schedule. Moment averaging performs well empirically at estimating partition functions of restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs), which form the building blocks of many deep learning models, including Deep Belief Networks and Deep Boltzmann Machines.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo methods such as annealed importance sampling estimate partition functions by moving through intermediate probability distributions. These distributions connect an easy starting point to a difficult target. The usual construction uses geometric averages, but the choice of connecting path can substantially affect how well estimation works.

For exponential families, this paper proposes a path built by averaging moments of the starting and target distributions. Moments summarize distributional properties through expected quantities. The authors also derive an asymptotically optimal piecewise linear schedule for progressing along this moments path. Their comparison shows performance at least as good as geometric averaging with a linear schedule.

The paper evaluates moment averaging on partition-function estimation for restricted Boltzmann machines and reports favorable empirical performance. These models also serve as components of deeper probabilistic architectures, making their normalization problem relevant beyond a single model. The contribution joins two design choices: which intermediate distributions to use and how to schedule movement between them. The stated comparison is specifically against the linear geometric schedule.
summary.tldr: For exponential families, moment-based annealing with an asymptotically optimal schedule improves the design of intermediate distributions for partition-function estimation.

title: Annealing between distributions by averaging moments

abstract: We analyze new online gradient descent algorithms for distributed systems with large delays between gradient computations and the corresponding updates. Using insights from adaptive gradient methods, we develop algorithms that adapt not only to the sequence of gradients, but also to the precise update delays that occur. We first give an impractical algorithm that achieves a regret bound that precisely quantifies the impact of the delays. We then analyze AdaptiveRevision, an algorithm that is efficiently implementable and achieves comparable guarantees. The key algorithmic technique is appropriately and efficiently revising the learning rate used for previous gradient steps. Experimental results show when the delays grow large (1000 updates or more), our new algorithms perform significantly better than standard adaptive gradient methods.
originalAbstract: We analyze new online gradient descent algorithms for distributed systems with large delays between gradient computations and the corresponding updates. Using insights from adaptive gradient methods, we develop algorithms that adapt not only to the sequence of gradients, but also to the precise update delays that occur. We first give an impractical algorithm that achieves a regret bound that precisely quantifies the impact of the delays. We then analyze AdaptiveRevision, an algorithm that is efficiently implementable and achieves comparable guarantees. The key algorithmic technique is appropriately and efficiently revising the learning rate used for previous gradient steps. Experimental results show when the delays grow large (1000 updates or more), our new algorithms perform significantly better than standard adaptive gradient methods.

paragraphs: In distributed online learning, a gradient may be computed long before its corresponding update is applied. The learner can change substantially during that delay, so the timing of updates becomes part of the optimization problem. This paper develops gradient descent algorithms that adapt both to the gradients received and to the particular delays that occur.

The authors first present an impractical algorithm whose regret bound explicitly quantifies the effect of delays. That construction establishes a theoretical reference point. They then analyze AdaptiveRevision, an efficiently implementable algorithm with comparable guarantees, connecting the delay-sensitive analysis to a method intended to be usable.

AdaptiveRevision's central technique is to revise the learning rates associated with earlier gradient steps efficiently and appropriately. This extends adaptation beyond responding only to gradient values. Experiments show significantly better performance than standard adaptive gradient methods when delays reach 1,000 updates or more. The reported advantage is therefore tied to a concrete large-delay regime, where accounting for update timing becomes especially consequential.
summary.tldr: AdaptiveRevision adjusts earlier learning rates to account for delayed gradients, with regret guarantees and empirical gains under large update delays.

title: Delay-Tolerant Algorithms for Asynchronous Distributed Online Learning

abstract: We introduce a model-based excessive gap technique to analyze first-order primal- dual methods for constrained convex minimization. As a result, we construct first- order primal-dual methods with optimal convergence rates on the primal objec- tive residual and the primal feasibility gap of their iterates separately. Through a dual smoothing and prox-center selection strategy, our framework subsumes the augmented Lagrangian, alternating direction, and dual fast-gradient methods as special cases, where our rates apply.
originalAbstract: We introduce a model-based excessive gap technique to analyze first-order primal- dual methods for constrained convex minimization. As a result, we construct first- order primal-dual methods with optimal convergence rates on the primal objec- tive residual and the primal feasibility gap of their iterates separately. Through a dual smoothing and prox-center selection strategy, our framework subsumes the augmented Lagrangian, alternating direction, and dual fast-gradient methods as special cases, where our rates apply.

paragraphs: Constrained convex optimization requires progress on two fronts: improving the objective and satisfying the constraints. An intermediate solution can perform well on one measure while still needing improvement on the other. This paper introduces a model-based excessive gap technique for analyzing first-order primal-dual methods with these two goals explicitly separated.

Using the technique, the authors construct methods with optimal convergence rates for both the primal objective residual and the primal feasibility gap. The objective residual measures distance from the optimal objective value, while the feasibility gap measures constraint violation. Separate rate guarantees describe how each quantity improves along the generated iterates, making the nature of convergence more explicit.

The framework uses dual smoothing and a strategy for choosing prox-centers. With these choices, it includes augmented Lagrangian, alternating direction, and dual fast-gradient methods as special cases. The stated rates apply within those cases. The contribution therefore provides both optimization methods and a common analytical framework connecting several established approaches to constrained convex minimization.
summary.tldr: A unified primal-dual framework gives optimal convergence rates separately for objective error and constraint violation.

title: Constrained convex minimization via model-based excessive gap

abstract: A determinantal point process (DPP) is a probabilistic model of set diversity compactly parameterized by a positive semi-definite kernel matrix. To fit a DPP to a given task, we would like to learn the entries of its kernel matrix by maximizing the log-likelihood of the available data. However, log-likelihood is non-convex in the entries of the kernel matrix, and this learning problem is conjectured to be NP-hard. Thus, previous work has instead focused on more restricted convex learning settings: learning only a single weight for each row of the kernel matrix, or learning weights for a linear combination of DPPs with fixed kernel matrices. In this work we propose a novel algorithm for learning the full kernel matrix. By changing the kernel parameterization from matrix entries to eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and then lower-bounding the likelihood in the manner of expectation-maximization algorithms, we obtain an effective optimization procedure. We test our method on a real-world product recommendation task, and achieve relative gains of up to 16.5% in test log-likelihood compared to the naive approach of maximizing likelihood by projected gradient ascent on the entries of the kernel matrix.
originalAbstract: A determinantal point process (DPP) is a probabilistic model of set diversity compactly parameterized by a positive semi-definite kernel matrix. To fit a DPP to a given task, we would like to learn the entries of its kernel matrix by maximizing the log-likelihood of the available data. However, log-likelihood is non-convex in the entries of the kernel matrix, and this learning problem is conjectured to be NP-hard. Thus, previous work has instead focused on more restricted convex learning settings: learning only a single weight for each row of the kernel matrix, or learning weights for a linear combination of DPPs with fixed kernel matrices. In this work we propose a novel algorithm for learning the full kernel matrix. By changing the kernel parameterization from matrix entries to eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and then lower-bounding the likelihood in the manner of expectation-maximization algorithms, we obtain an effective optimization procedure. We test our method on a real-world product recommendation task, and achieve relative gains of up to 16.5% in test log-likelihood compared to the naive approach of maximizing likelihood by projected gradient ascent on the entries of the kernel matrix.

paragraphs: A determinantal point process models diversity within a set through a positive semidefinite kernel matrix. Learning that matrix would let the model adapt its notion of diversity to a task. However, likelihood maximization over the matrix entries is nonconvex, and the learning problem is conjectured to be NP-hard.

Earlier approaches therefore concentrated on restricted convex settings, such as adjusting one weight per kernel row or mixing models with fixed kernels. This paper instead proposes learning the full kernel. It changes the representation from individual matrix entries to eigenvalues and eigenvectors, then constructs a lower bound on likelihood in the style of expectation-maximization to guide optimization.

The authors evaluate the procedure on a real-world product recommendation task. They report relative improvements of up to 16.5% in test log-likelihood over directly optimizing kernel entries with projected gradient ascent. This is evidence for more effective full-kernel fitting in the tested application; the reported metric measures probabilistic fit and does not itself establish a corresponding percentage improvement in recommendation outcomes.
summary.tldr: An expectation-maximization-style procedure learns a full DPP kernel and improves test log-likelihood on a product recommendation task.

title: Expectation-Maximization for Learning Determinantal Point Processes

abstract: This work presents novel algorithms for learning Bayesian networks of bounded treewidth. Both exact and approximate methods are developed. The exact method combines mixed integer linear programming formulations for structure learning and treewidth computation. The approximate method consists in sampling k-trees (maximal graphs of treewidth k), and subsequently selecting, exactly or approximately, the best structure whose moral graph is a subgraph of that k-tree. The approaches are empirically compared to each other and to state-of-the-art methods on a collection of public data sets with up to 100 variables.
originalAbstract: This work presents novel algorithms for learning Bayesian networks of bounded treewidth. Both exact and approximate methods are developed. The exact method combines mixed integer linear programming formulations for structure learning and treewidth computation. The approximate method consists in sampling k-trees (maximal graphs of treewidth k), and subsequently selecting, exactly or approximately, the best structure whose moral graph is a subgraph of that k-tree. The approaches are empirically compared to each other and to state-of-the-art methods on a collection of public data sets with up to 100 variables.

paragraphs: This paper develops methods for learning Bayesian network structures subject to a bound on treewidth. The task involves choosing dependencies among variables while satisfying a structural constraint on the resulting network. The authors provide both exact and approximate approaches, addressing the same constrained learning problem through different ways of organizing the search.

The exact approach combines mixed integer linear programming formulations for two tasks: learning the network structure and computing treewidth. Incorporating both formulations makes the treewidth constraint part of the optimization. The approximate approach instead samples k-trees, which are maximal graphs with treewidth k. Each sampled graph supplies a structural envelope within which a Bayesian network can be selected.

Within that envelope, the method searches for the best network whose associated moral graph is a subgraph of the sampled k-tree; this inner selection can itself be exact or approximate. The paper empirically compares these alternatives with one another and with existing methods on public datasets containing up to 100 variables. The abstract establishes the scope of this comparison without claiming that one approach consistently wins.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces exact and approximate algorithms for learning Bayesian networks while explicitly bounding their treewidth.

title: Advances in Learning Bayesian Networks of Bounded Treewidth

abstract: We propose a simple, scalable, and fast gradient descent algorithm to optimize a nonconvex objective for the rank minimization problem and a closely related family of semidefinite programs. With $O(r^3 \kappa^2 n \log n)$ random measurements of a positive semidefinite $n\times n$ matrix of rank $r$ and condition number $\kappa$, our method is guaranteed to converge linearly to the global optimum.
originalAbstract: We propose a simple, scalable, and fast gradient descent algorithm to optimize a nonconvex objective for the rank minimization problem and a closely related family of semidefinite programs. With $O(r^3 \kappa^2 n \log n)$ random measurements of a positive semidefinite $n\times n$ matrix of rank $r$ and condition number $\kappa$, our method is guaranteed to converge linearly to the global optimum.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a gradient descent method for recovering a low-rank matrix from random linear measurements. Its target is a positive semidefinite matrix, and the method addresses both rank minimization and a closely related family of semidefinite programs. The authors describe the algorithm as simple, scalable, and fast.

The central theoretical result concerns optimization of a nonconvex objective. For an n-by-n matrix with rank r and condition number κ, the method is guaranteed to reach the global optimum with O(r³κ²n log n) random measurements. This measurement requirement explicitly connects the guarantee to matrix size, rank, and conditioning; the result is not an unconditional claim about arbitrary matrix problems.

The convergence guarantee is linear, meaning that optimization error decreases geometrically as the method progresses. The significance is that a comparatively simple iterative procedure has a global guarantee in the specified random-measurement setting. The paper therefore supplies a principled route to these matrix problems through nonconvex gradient descent.
summary.tldr: A gradient descent method provably converges linearly to the global optimum for specified low-rank matrix problems given sufficiently many random measurements.

title: A Convergent Gradient Descent Algorithm for Rank Minimization and Semidefinite Programming from Random Linear Measurements

abstract: We initiate the study of the classical Submodular Cover (SC) problem in the data streaming model which we refer to as the Streaming Submodular Cover (SSC). We show that any single pass streaming algorithm using sublinear memory in the size of the stream will fail to provide any non-trivial approximation guarantees for SSC. Hence, we consider a relaxed version of SSC, where we only seek to find a partial cover. We design the first Efficient bicriteria Submodular Cover Streaming (ESC-Streaming) algorithm for this problem, and provide theoretical guarantees for its performance supported by numerical evidence. Our algorithm finds solutions that are competitive with the near-optimal offline greedy algorithm despite requiring only a single pass over the data stream. In our numerical experiments, we evaluate the performance of ESC-Streaming on active set selection and large-scale graph cover problems.
originalAbstract: We initiate the study of the classical Submodular Cover (SC) problem in the data streaming model which we refer to as the Streaming Submodular Cover (SSC). We show that any single pass streaming algorithm using sublinear memory in the size of the stream will fail to provide any non-trivial approximation guarantees for SSC. Hence, we consider a relaxed version of SSC, where we only seek to find a partial cover. We design the first Efficient bicriteria Submodular Cover Streaming (ESC-Streaming) algorithm for this problem, and provide theoretical guarantees for its performance supported by numerical evidence. Our algorithm finds solutions that are competitive with the near-optimal offline greedy algorithm despite requiring only a single pass over the data stream. In our numerical experiments, we evaluate the performance of ESC-Streaming on active set selection and large-scale graph cover problems.

paragraphs: The submodular cover problem seeks a collection whose combined value meets a coverage requirement. The paper asks what remains possible when data arrive as a stream and memory is smaller than the stream itself. It proves that a single-pass algorithm with sublinear memory cannot obtain any nontrivial approximation guarantee for the original streaming problem.

The authors therefore relax the objective to partial coverage and introduce ESC-Streaming, an efficient bicriteria algorithm. This changes the requirements in a way that permits theoretical performance guarantees while keeping the operational advantage of processing the stream only once.

Numerical evaluations consider active-set selection and large-scale graph cover. The resulting solutions are competitive with a near-optimal offline greedy algorithm. The distinction between full and partial cover is essential: the constructive result addresses the relaxed problem and does not overturn the impossibility theorem for the original formulation.
summary.tldr: Partial coverage makes streaming submodular cover feasible despite a full-cover impossibility result.

title: An Efficient Streaming Algorithm for the Submodular Cover Problem

abstract: Two-stream Convolutional Networks (ConvNets) have shown strong performance for human action recognition in videos. Recently, Residual Networks (ResNets) have arisen as a new technique to train extremely deep architectures. In this paper, we introduce spatiotemporal ResNets as a combination of these two approaches. Our novel architecture generalizes ResNets for the spatiotemporal domain by introducing residual connections in two ways. First, we inject residual connections between the appearance and motion pathways of a two-stream architecture to allow spatiotemporal interaction between the two streams. Second, we transform pretrained image ConvNets into spatiotemporal networks by equipping these with learnable convolutional filters that are initialized as temporal residual connections and operate on adjacent feature maps in time. This approach slowly increases the spatiotemporal receptive field as the depth of the model increases and naturally integrates image ConvNet design principles. The whole model is trained end-to-end to allow hierarchical learning of complex spatiotemporal features. We evaluate our novel spatiotemporal ResNet using two widely used action recognition benchmarks where it exceeds the previous state-of-the-art.

Recently, Residual Networks (ResNets) have arisen as a new technique to train extremely deep architectures. In this paper, we introduce spatiotemporal ResNets as a combination of these two approaches. First, we inject residual connections between the appearance and motion pathways of a two-stream architecture to allow spatiotemporal interaction between the two streams. Second, we transform pretrained image ConvNets into spatiotemporal networks by equipping these with learnable convolutional filters that are initialized as temporal residual connections and operate on adjacent feature maps in time. paragraphs: Recognizing actions in video requires learning about both appearance and motion across time. This paper combines two-stream convolutional networks with residual networks to build a spatiotemporal architecture. Residual connections are introduced in two complementary ways, allowing the design to integrate information between streams and across neighboring moments.

First, residual connections link the appearance and motion pathways, enabling interactions between their representations. Second, pretrained image networks receive learnable convolutional filters operating on adjacent feature maps in time. Those filters are initialized as temporal residual connections. As the network becomes deeper, the span of space and time available to its features gradually increases.

The complete model is trained end to end so that it can learn increasingly complex spatiotemporal features across its hierarchy. Evaluation on two widely used action-recognition benchmarks exceeds the previous state of the art. The contribution shows how residual connections can support both cross-stream interaction and temporal processing, while bringing pretrained image-network designs into video recognition. The performance finding applies to the two evaluated benchmarks.
summary.tldr: Spatiotemporal residual networks connect appearance, motion, and neighboring time steps to improve video action recognition.

title: Spatiotemporal Residual Networks for Video Action Recognition

abstract: We develop methods for rapidly identifying important components of a convex optimization problem for the purpose of achieving fast convergence times. By considering a novel problem formulation—the minimization of a sum of piecewise functions—we describe a principled and general mechanism for exploiting piecewise linear structure in convex optimization. This result leads to a theoretically justified working set algorithm and a novel screening test, which generalize and improve upon many prior results on exploiting structure in convex optimization. In empirical comparisons, we study the scalability of our methods. paragraphs: Large convex optimization problems may contain components whose importance differs over the course of solving them. Identifying the important components quickly can help an algorithm converge faster. This paper develops a general approach to doing so by exploiting piecewise linear structure in the optimization problem.

The authors formulate the task as minimizing a sum of piecewise functions. From this formulation, they derive a principled mechanism for using the structure, leading to a theoretically justified working-set algorithm and a new screening test. These results generalize and improve on earlier methods for exploiting structure. The working-set approach concentrates computation on a selected collection of components.

title: Unified Methods for Exploiting Piecewise Linear Structure in Convex Optimization

abstract: We show that given an estimate $\widehat{\mat A}$ that is close to a general high-rank positive semi-definite (PSD) matrix $\mat A$ in spectral norm (i.e., $\|\widehat{\mat A}-\mat A\|_2 \leq \delta$), the simple truncated Singular Value Decomposition of $\widehat{\mat A}$ produces a multiplicative approximation of $\mat A$ in Frobenius norm. This observation leads to many interesting results on general high-rank matrix estimation problems: 1.High-rank matrix completion: we show that it is possible to recover a {general high-rank matrix} $\mat A$ up to $(1+\varepsilon)$ relative error in Frobenius norm from partial observations, with sample complexity independent of the spectral gap of $\mat A$. 2.High-rank matrix denoising: we design algorithms that recovers a matrix $\mat A$ with relative error in Frobenius norm from its noise-perturbed observations, without assuming $\mat A$ is exactly low-rank. 3.Low-dimensional estimation of high-dimensional covariance: given $N$ i.i.d.~samples of dimension $n$ from $\mathcal N_n(\mat 0,\mat A)$, we show that it is possible to estimate the covariance matrix $\mat A$ with relative error in Frobenius norm with $N\approx n$,improving over classical covariance estimation results which requires $N\approx n^2$.

paragraphs: This paper examines how truncated singular value decomposition can help estimate matrices that are not exactly low rank. Its starting point is a high-rank positive semidefinite matrix and an initial estimate that is close in spectral norm. The authors show that truncating the estimate's singular value decomposition yields a multiplicative approximation in Frobenius norm.

The distinction between these error measures drives the applications: a spectral-norm guarantee on an initial estimate can be turned into a relative Frobenius-norm approximation. For high-rank matrix completion, the authors obtain a 1+epsilon relative-error result from partial observations with sample complexity independent of the spectral gap. They also develop denoising algorithms without requiring an exactly low-rank target.

The authors show that relative Frobenius error can be achieved with approximately n samples, compared with the approximately n-squared requirement of the classical results they discuss. The Gaussian sampling setting is part of this covariance claim.
summary.tldr: Truncated SVD converts spectral-norm accuracy into relative Frobenius-norm guarantees, enabling results for high-rank completion, denoising, and covariance estimation.

title: On the Power of Truncated SVD for General High-rank Matrix Estimation Problems

abstract: Attention mechanism is effective in both focusing the deep learning models on relevant features and interpreting them. However, attentions may be unreliable since the networks that generate them are often trained in a weakly-supervised manner. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the notion of input-dependent uncertainty to the attention mechanism, such that it generates attention for each feature with varying degrees of noise based on the given input, to learn larger variance on instances it is uncertain about. We learn this Uncertainty-aware Attention (UA) mechanism using variational inference, and validate it on various risk prediction tasks from electronic health records on which our model significantly outperforms existing attention models. The analysis of the learned attentions shows that our model generates attentions that comply with clinicians' interpretation, and provide richer interpretation via learned variance. Further evaluation of both the accuracy of the uncertainty calibration and the prediction performance with "I don't know'' decision show that UA yields networks with high reliability as well.

paragraphs: Attention mechanisms help a model emphasize relevant features and can be used to interpret its predictions. However, the networks producing attention are often only weakly supervised, so their apparent emphasis may be unreliable. This paper introduces uncertainty into attention itself, allowing an explanation to express how confidently the model assigns importance.

The proposed Uncertainty-aware Attention mechanism generates feature attention with input-dependent noise. It learns larger variance for instances about which it is uncertain, and the authors train it using variational inference. The result associates attention with both a learned emphasis and a measure of variability, providing more information than attention values alone.

On risk-prediction tasks using electronic health records, the model significantly outperforms existing attention models. Analysis finds attention patterns consistent with clinicians' interpretations and richer explanations through the learned variance. Further evaluations examine uncertainty calibration and prediction when the model can decline to decide. These results support the reported reliability of the approach across prediction, interpretation, and uncertainty assessment in the studied tasks.
summary.tldr: Input-dependent uncertainty in attention improves clinical risk prediction and adds information about the reliability of feature emphasis.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Attention for Reliable Interpretation and Prediction

abstract: We consider the problem of learning a multi-class classifier from labels as well as simple explanations that we call "discriminative features". We show that such explanations can be provided whenever the target concept is a decision tree, or more generally belongs to a particular subclass of DNF formulas. We present an efficient online algorithm for learning from such feedback and we give tight bounds on the number of mistakes made during the learning process. These bounds depend only on the size of the target concept and not on the overall number of available features, which could be infinite. We also demonstrate the learning procedure experimentally.

These bounds depend only on the size of the target concept and not on the overall number of available features, which could be infinite. We also demonstrate the learning procedure experimentally.

paragraphs: A classifier can learn from more than a label: a teacher may also explain which feature distinguishes the correct category from an incorrect one. This paper formalizes such explanations as discriminative features and studies how to use them in an online multiclass learning process.

The authors show that the required explanations are available when the target is a decision tree or belongs to a specified subclass of disjunctive normal form formulas. They develop an efficient online algorithm that learns from this combination of labels and feature feedback.

The theoretical mistake bounds are tight and depend on the size of the target concept, rather than the total number of available features, which may even be infinite. Experiments demonstrate the procedure. The guarantee relies on the specified target classes and feedback model; it does not assert that arbitrary natural-language explanations automatically have these properties.
summary.tldr: Simple feature explanations can support efficient online classification with bounded mistakes.

title: Learning from discriminative feature feedback

abstract: Motivated by the problem of automated repair of software vulnerabilities, we propose an adversarial learning approach that maps from one discrete source domain to another target domain without requiring paired labeled examples or source and target domains to be bijections. We demonstrate that the proposed adversarial learning approach is an effective technique for repairing software vulnerabilities, performing close to seq2seq approaches that require labeled pairs. The proposed Generative Adversarial Network approach is application-agnostic in that it can be applied to other problems similar to code repair, such as grammar correction or sentiment translation.
originalAbstract: Motivated by the problem of automated repair of software vulnerabilities, we propose an adversarial learning approach that maps from one discrete source domain to another target domain without requiring paired labeled examples or source and target domains to be bijections.
