The proposed Generative Adversarial Network approach is application-agnostic in that it can be applied to other problems similar to code repair, such as grammar correction or sentiment translation.

paragraphs: This paper approaches software-vulnerability repair as learning a transformation between discrete domains. The central question is whether a useful repair mapping can be learned without labeled examples pairing each source item with its desired target. Removing that requirement changes the kind of training data the method needs.

The proposed approach uses adversarial learning to learn the mapping. It also does not require a bijection between the source and target domains, meaning it does not impose an exact one-to-one correspondence. Together, these properties allow the formulation to address transformations where paired supervision and a one-to-one domain relationship are unavailable.

For software repair, the authors report performance close to sequence-to-sequence approaches that do require labeled pairs. The claim is competitive performance despite different supervision requirements, rather than superiority over those approaches. They also describe the method as application-agnostic and identify grammar correction and sentiment translation as possible uses. Those examples indicate the broader scope of the formulation; the stated demonstration concerns vulnerability repair.
summary.tldr: An adversarial approach learns software-vulnerability repairs without paired labels and performs close to sequence-to-sequence methods that require them.

title: Learning to Repair Software Vulnerabilities with Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: In this paper we consider the problem of computing an $\epsilon$-optimal policy of a discounted Markov Decision Process (DMDP) provided we can only access its transition function through a generative sampling model that given any state-action pair samples from the transition function in $O(1)$ time. Given such a DMDP with states $\states$, actions $\actions$, discount factor $\gamma\in(0,1)$, and rewards in range $[0, 1]$ we provide an algorithm which computes an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with probability $1 - \delta$ where {\it both} the run time spent and number of sample taken is upper bounded by \[ O\left[\frac{|\cS||\cA|}{(1-\gamma)^3 \epsilon^2} \log \left(\frac{|\cS||\cA|}{(1-\gamma)\delta \epsilon} \right) \log\left(\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)\epsilon}\right)\right] ~. \] For fixed values of $\epsilon$, this improves upon the previous best known bounds by a factor of $(1 - \gamma)^{-1}$ and matches the sample complexity lower bounds proved in \cite{azar2013minimax} up to logarithmic factors. We also extend our method to computing $\epsilon$-optimal policies for finite-horizon MDP with a generative model and provide a nearly matching sample complexity lower bound.

paragraphs: The paper studies planning in a discounted Markov decision process when transitions are accessible through a generative sampling model. This model must return a transition sample for any requested state-action pair in constant time. With rewards between zero and one, the objective is to compute a policy within a chosen accuracy tolerance with high probability.

The proposed algorithm bounds both runtime and sample use. Apart from logarithmic factors, the bound scales with the number of state-action pairs, the inverse square of the accuracy tolerance, and the inverse cube of one minus the discount factor. Thus, the guarantee accounts for computation as well as the amount of sampled transition information.

For fixed accuracy, the authors improve the previous best bounds by a factor of one divided by one minus the discount factor. The sample bound matches known lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. They also extend the method to finite-horizon problems and provide a nearly matching sample lower bound, supporting near-optimal efficiency within the stated sampling setting.
summary.tldr: With constant-time access to transition samples, a planning algorithm achieves nearly optimal sample use alongside a matching runtime upper bound.

title: Near-Optimal Time and Sample Complexities for Solving Markov Decision Processes with a Generative Model

abstract: While great progress has been made recently in automatic image manipulation, it has been limited to object centric images like faces or structured scene datasets. In this work, we take a step towards general scene-level image editing by developing an automatic interaction-free object removal model. Our model learns to find and remove objects from general scene images using image-level labels and unpaired data in a generative adversarial network (GAN) framework. We achieve this with two key contributions: a two-stage editor architecture consisting of a mask generator and image in-painter that co-operate to remove objects, and a novel GAN based prior for the mask generator that allows us to flexibly incorporate knowledge about object shapes. We experimentally show on two datasets that our method effectively removes a wide variety of objects using weak supervision only.

paragraphs: Removing an object from an image involves both locating it and replacing its pixels with plausible scene content. This paper develops an automatic object removal system for general scenes. It aims to extend image editing beyond object-centered images, such as faces, and datasets whose scenes have a more regular structure.

The system learns using labels attached to whole images and unpaired data. Its editor has two cooperating stages: a mask generator identifies the region to remove, and an image in-painter fills that region. This division connects the decision about where an object is with the task of producing the edited image.

A further contribution is an adversarially learned prior for the mask generator, which provides a flexible way to incorporate knowledge about object shapes. The authors report effective removal of a wide variety of objects across two datasets using only weak supervision. These results support learning automatic scene editing without requiring detailed object annotations or paired editing examples.
summary.tldr: A cooperating mask generator and image in-painter learn automatic object removal from image-level labels and unpaired data.

title: Adversarial Scene Editing: Automatic Object Removal from Weak Supervision

abstract: We consider a least squares regression problem where the data has been generated from a linear model, and we are interested to learn the unknown regression parameters. We consider "sketch-and-solve" methods that randomly project the data first, and do regression after. Previous works have analyzed the statistical and computational performance of such methods. However, the existing analysis is not fine-grained enough to show the fundamental differences between various methods, such as the Subsampled Randomized Hadamard Transform (SRHT) and Gaussian projections. In this paper, we make progress on this problem, working in an asymptotic framework where the number of datapoints and dimension of features goes to infinity. We find the limits of the accuracy loss (for estimation and test error) incurred by popular sketching methods. We show separation between different methods, so that SRHT is better than Gaussian projections. Our theoretical results are verified on both real and synthetic data. The analysis of SRHT relies on novel methods from random matrix theory that may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Sketch-and-solve regression first compresses data through a random projection, then fits a regression model to the compressed version. This paper studies the statistical accuracy lost through that compression when data come from a linear model. Its goal is to distinguish projection methods more precisely than earlier statistical and computational analyses allowed.

The authors use an asymptotic setting in which both the number of observations and the number of features grow without bound. Within that framework, they derive limiting accuracy losses for estimating regression parameters and predicting test data. Considering both quantities separates recovering the underlying model from using it to make predictions.

The analysis distinguishes popular sketching methods and shows an advantage for the Subsampled Randomized Hadamard Transform over Gaussian projections in the studied setting. Experiments on real and synthetic data verify the theoretical results. The work also develops random matrix techniques for analyzing the Hadamard-based method. Its central contribution is a finer account of how the choice of compression affects regression accuracy.
summary.tldr: An asymptotic analysis distinguishes regression sketching methods and shows lower accuracy loss for SRHT than Gaussian projections.

title: Asymptotics for Sketching in Least Squares Regression

abstract: Understanding and reasoning about physics is an important ability of intelligent agents. We develop the PHYRE benchmark for physical reasoning that contains a set of simple classical mechanics puzzles in a 2D physical environment. The benchmark is designed to encourage the development of learning algorithms that are sample-efficient and generalize well across puzzles. We test several modern learning algorithms on PHYRE and find that these algorithms fall short in solving the puzzles efficiently. We expect that PHYRE will encourage the development of novel sample-efficient agents that learn efficient but useful models of physics. For code and to play PHYRE for yourself, please visit https://player.phyre.ai.

paragraphs: PHYRE is a benchmark for studying whether learning agents can reason about physical situations. It consists of simple classical-mechanics puzzles in a two-dimensional environment. The purpose is to provide a shared task setting in which researchers can examine how agents learn to solve physical problems, with particular attention to the efficiency of that learning.

The benchmark is designed around two goals: sample efficiency and generalization across puzzles. Sample efficiency concerns how much experience an agent needs, while generalization concerns whether what it learns helps on other puzzles. Together, these goals focus evaluation on acquiring useful physical knowledge that carries beyond a single problem, rather than judging success on an isolated puzzle alone.

The authors test several modern learning algorithms and find that they do not solve the puzzles efficiently. This result identifies a challenge for the evaluated methods and motivates further work on useful, efficient models of physics. The paper’s main contribution is the benchmark and its initial evaluation; the development of more sample-efficient agents is an intended consequence of making that challenge available.
summary.tldr: PHYRE introduces two-dimensional physics puzzles that expose difficulties in efficient learning and encourage generalization across physical reasoning tasks.

title: PHYRE: A New Benchmark for Physical Reasoning

abstract: This paper studies the estimation of large-scale optimal transport maps (OTM), which is a well known challenging problem owing to the curse of dimensionality. Existing literature approximates the large-scale OTM by a series of one-dimensional OTM problems through iterative random projection. Such methods, however, suffer from slow or none convergence in practice due to the nature of randomly selected projection directions. Instead, we propose an estimation method of large-scale OTM by combining the idea of projection pursuit regression and sufficient dimension reduction. The proposed method, named projection pursuit Monge map (PPMM), adaptively selects the most informative'' projection direction in each iteration. We theoretically show the proposed dimension reduction method can consistently estimate the most informative'' projection direction in each iteration. Furthermore, the PPMM algorithm weakly convergences to the target large-scale OTM in a reasonable number of steps. Empirically, PPMM is computationally easy and converges fast. We assess its finite sample performance through the applications of Wasserstein distance estimation and generative models.

paragraphs: Estimating an optimal transport map becomes difficult in high dimensions. One existing approach breaks the problem into successive one-dimensional transport problems along random projection directions. The paper identifies a weakness of that strategy: randomly chosen directions can lead to slow convergence or failure to converge in practice.

Projection pursuit Monge map, or PPMM, selects projection directions adaptively. It combines projection pursuit regression with sufficient dimension reduction to identify the most informative direction at each iteration. The authors theoretically show that the dimension-reduction procedure consistently estimates that direction, giving the selection rule a statistical justification.

The paper also establishes weak convergence of PPMM to the target transport map in a reasonable number of steps. Empirical results describe the procedure as computationally easy and fast to converge, with finite-sample evaluations involving Wasserstein distance estimation and generative models. Its central contribution is a principled way to choose useful one-dimensional problems, supported by both convergence analysis and application results.
summary.tldr: PPMM adaptively chooses informative projection directions to estimate large-scale optimal transport maps, with theoretical and empirical convergence support.

title: Large-scale optimal transport map estimation using projection pursuit

abstract: Motivated by pricing in ad exchange markets, we consider the problem of robust learning of reserve prices against strategic buyers in repeated contextual second-price auctions. Buyers' valuations \new{for} an item depend on the context that describes the item. However, the seller is not aware of the relationship between the context and buyers' valuations, i.e., buyers' preferences. The seller's goal is to design a learning policy to set reserve prices via observing the past sales data, and her objective is to minimize her regret for revenue, where the regret is computed against a clairvoyant policy that knows buyers' heterogeneous preferences. Given the seller's goal, utility-maximizing buyers have the incentive to bid untruthfully in order to manipulate the seller's learning policy. We propose two learning policies that are robust to such strategic behavior. These policies use the outcomes of the auctions, rather than the submitted bids, to estimate the preferences while controlling the long-term effect of the outcome of each auction on the future reserve prices. The first policy called Contextual Robust Pricing (CORP) is designed for the setting where the market noise distribution is known to the seller and achieves a T-period regret of $O(d\log(Td) \log (T))$, where $d$ is the dimension of {the} contextual information. The second policy, which is a variant of the first policy, is called Stable CORP (SCORP). This policy is tailored to the setting where the market noise distribution is unknown to the seller and belongs to an ambiguity set. We show that the SCORP policy has a T-period regret of $O(\sqrt{d\log(Td)}\;T^{2/3})$.

paragraphs: A seller repeatedly running auctions must learn how item characteristics affect buyers’ values. Buyers can exploit this learning process by bidding strategically to influence future reserve prices. The paper studies how to learn prices despite that incentive, measuring lost revenue against a seller who already knows buyers’ differing preferences.

The proposed policies estimate preferences from auction outcomes instead of submitted bids. They also control how much each auction outcome can affect reserve prices over the longer term. These choices address the connection between current buyer behavior and future pricing, which makes ordinary learning from sales data vulnerable to manipulation.

Stable CORP handles an unknown distribution within an ambiguity set, with regret O(√(d log(Td)) T^(2/3)). Here d counts contextual dimensions and T counts auction periods. Both bounds describe sublinear growth in cumulative regret for fixed d, under their respective settings.
summary.tldr: CORP and SCORP learn reserve prices from auction outcomes while limiting strategic buyers’ influence on future prices.

title: Dynamic Incentive-Aware Learning: Robust Pricing in Contextual Auctions

abstract: Fairness-aware learning involves designing algorithms that do not discriminate with respect to some sensitive feature (e.g., race or gender). Existing work on the problem operates under the assumption that the sensitive feature available in one's training sample is perfectly reliable. This assumption may be violated in many real-world cases: for example, respondents to a survey may choose to conceal or obfuscate their group identity out of fear of potential discrimination. This poses the question of whether one can still learn fair classifiers given noisy sensitive features. In this paper, we answer the question in the affirmative: we show that if one measures fairness using the mean-difference score, and sensitive features are subject to noise from the mutually contaminated learning model, then owing to a simple identity we only need to change the desired fairness-tolerance. The requisite tolerance can be estimated by leveraging existing noise-rate estimators from the label noise literature. We finally show that our procedure is empirically effective on two case-studies involving sensitive feature censoring.

paragraphs: Fairness-aware learning often assumes that the sensitive group information in training data is reliable. That can fail when people conceal or obscure their identities, including out of concern about discrimination. This paper asks whether classifiers can still be learned fairly when the sensitive features themselves are noisy.

The answer is positive under two specific conditions: fairness is measured by the mean-difference score, and noise follows the mutually contaminated learning model. Under that setup, a mathematical identity shows that the required correction is a change to the desired fairness tolerance. The needed tolerance can be estimated using existing noise-rate estimators from research on noisy labels.

The authors evaluate the procedure in two case studies involving censoring of sensitive features and report that it is empirically effective. The result provides a concrete way to adapt a fairness constraint to unreliable group information. Its scope is tied to the stated fairness measure and noise model, which make the tolerance adjustment mathematically justified.
summary.tldr: Under a specified noise model and mean-difference fairness measure, noisy sensitive features can be handled by adjusting fairness tolerance.

title: Noise-tolerant fair classification

abstract: Gaussian processes are the leading class of distributions on random functions, but they suffer from well known issues including difficulty scaling and inflexibility with respect to certain shape constraints (such as nonnegativity). Here we propose Deep Random Splines, a flexible class of random functions obtained by transforming Gaussian noise through a deep neural network whose output are the parameters of a spline. Unlike Gaussian processes, Deep Random Splines allow us to readily enforce shape constraints while inheriting the richness and tractability of deep generative models. We also present an observational model for point process data which uses Deep Random Splines to model the intensity function of each point process and apply it to neural population data to obtain a low-dimensional representation of spiking activity. Inference is performed via a variational autoencoder that uses a novel recurrent encoder architecture that can handle multiple point processes as input. We use a newly collected dataset where a primate completes a pedaling task, and observe better dimensionality reduction with our model than with competing alternatives.

Modeling these functions requires flexibility while respecting constraints such as nonnegativity. The paper proposes Deep Random Splines as an alternative to Gaussian processes, which can be difficult to scale and adapt to certain shape constraints.

A Deep Random Spline is produced by passing Gaussian noise through a deep network that outputs spline parameters. title: Deep Random Splines for Point Process Intensity Estimation of Neural Population Data

abstract: To operate effectively in the real world, agents should be able to act from high-dimensional raw sensory input such as images and achieve diverse goals across long time-horizons. Current deep reinforcement and imitation learning methods can learn directly from high-dimensional inputs but do not scale well to long-horizon tasks. In contrast, classical graphical methods like A* search are able to solve long-horizon tasks, but assume that the state space is abstracted away from raw sensory input. Recent works have attempted to combine the strengths of deep learning and classical planning; however, dominant methods in this domain are still quite brittle and scale poorly with the size of the environment. We introduce Sparse Graphical Memory (SGM), a new data structure that stores states and feasible transitions in a sparse memory. SGM aggregates states according to a novel two-way consistency objective, adapting classic state aggregation criteria to goal-conditioned RL: two states are redundant when they are interchangeable both as goals and as starting states. Theoretically, we prove that merging nodes according to two-way consistency leads to an increase in shortest path lengths that scales only linearly with the merging threshold. Experimentally, we show that SGM significantly outperforms current state of the art methods on long horizon, sparse-reward visual navigation tasks. Project video and code are available at https://sites.google.com/view/sparse-graphical-memory.

paragraphs: Long-horizon visual navigation needs both an understanding of sensory input and a way to plan over many steps. Deep learning can handle images, while graphical search can organize long routes through abstract states. This paper introduces Sparse Graphical Memory, or SGM, to combine these capabilities while addressing brittleness and poor scaling in existing combinations.

SGM stores states and feasible transitions in a sparse graph. Its key compression rule is two-way consistency: two states count as redundant when they are interchangeable both as destinations and as starting points. This criterion adapts state aggregation to goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, ensuring that merging considers both roles a state can play in a navigation problem.

The theoretical analysis shows that merging according to this rule increases shortest-path lengths by an amount that scales only linearly with the merging threshold. Experiments report significant improvements over current state-of-the-art methods on long-horizon visual navigation with sparse rewards. The contribution connects a compact planning memory with an explicit bound on the path-length consequences of its compression.
summary.tldr: Sparse Graphical Memory compresses navigation states using two-way consistency, bounding path-length increases and improving long-horizon visual planning.

title: Sparse Graphical Memory for Robust Planning

abstract: We give methods for Bayesian inference of directed acyclic graphs, DAGs, and the induced causal effects from passively observed complete data. Our methods build on a recent Markov chain Monte Carlo scheme for learning Bayesian networks, which enables efﬁcient approximate sampling from the graph posterior, provided that each node is assigned a small number K of candidate parents. We present algorithmic techniques to signiﬁcantly reduce the space and time requirements, which make the use of substantially larger values of K feasible. Furthermore, we investigate the problem of selecting the candidate parents per node so as to maximize the covered posterior mass. Finally, we combine our sampling method with a novel Bayesian approach for estimating causal effects in linear Gaussian DAG models. Numerical experiments demonstrate the performance of our methods in detecting ancestor–descendant relations, and in causal effect estimation our Bayesian method is shown to outperform previous approaches.

paragraphs: This paper develops Bayesian methods for learning directed acyclic graphs and their implied causal effects from complete, passively observed data. It builds on a Markov chain Monte Carlo approach that approximately samples graph structures from their posterior distribution. That approach is efficient when each node has a small set of candidate parents.

The authors reduce the method's time and memory requirements, making substantially larger candidate-parent sets feasible. They also study how to choose those candidates so that the allowed graph structures cover as much posterior probability as possible. This addresses both the cost of searching possible structures and the consequences of restricting the search.

The graph sampler is then combined with a new Bayesian method for estimating causal effects in linear Gaussian DAG models. Numerical experiments demonstrate performance in detecting ancestor-descendant relations, and the causal-effect method outperforms previous approaches in the reported evaluations. The work therefore links more scalable uncertainty over graph structure with causal-effect estimation under the specified model family.
summary.tldr: More efficient Bayesian graph sampling supports larger candidate-parent sets and improves reported causal-effect estimation in linear Gaussian DAG models.

title: Towards Scalable Bayesian Learning of Causal DAGs

abstract: Learning with the \textit{instance-dependent} label noise is challenging, because it is hard to model such real-world noise. Note that there are psychological and physiological evidences showing that we humans perceive instances by decomposing them into parts. Annotators are therefore more likely to annotate instances based on the parts rather than the whole instances, where a wrong mapping from parts to classes may cause the instance-dependent label noise. Motivated by this human cognition, in this paper, we approximate the instance-dependent label noise by exploiting \textit{part-dependent} label noise. Specifically, since instances can be approximately reconstructed by a combination of parts, we approximate the instance-dependent \textit{transition matrix} for an instance by a combination of the transition matrices for the parts of the instance. The transition matrices for parts can be learned by exploiting anchor points (i.e., data points that belong to a specific class almost surely). Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate our method is superior to the state-of-the-art approaches for learning from the instance-dependent label noise.

paragraphs: Label errors can depend on the particular example being annotated, making them difficult to describe with a single noise pattern. This paper draws motivation from evidence that people perceive examples through their constituent parts. If annotators associate a part with the wrong class, that association may help explain why some examples receive incorrect labels.

The method approximates instance-dependent noise using part-dependent noise. Just as an example can be approximately reconstructed from a combination of parts, its label transition matrix is approximated by combining transition matrices for those parts. These matrices describe how true classes can be mapped to observed labels, giving the noise model a reusable structure across examples.

The part-level matrices are learned using anchor points: examples belonging to a particular class with near certainty. This provides a concrete source of information for estimating the component noise patterns. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets show performance superior to state-of-the-art approaches considered for instance-dependent label noise. The findings support the part-based approximation as a useful way to tackle otherwise difficult example-specific annotation errors.
summary.tldr: The method approximates example-specific label noise by combining part-level noise models learned with nearly certain class examples.

title: Part-dependent Label Noise: Towards Instance-dependent Label Noise

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a prominent approach to optimizing expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions. The massive computational capability of edge devices such as mobile phones, coupled with privacy concerns, has led to a surging interest in federated learning (FL) which focuses on collaborative training of deep neural networks (DNNs) via first-order optimization techniques. However, some common machine learning tasks such as hyperparameter tuning of DNNs lack access to gradients and thus require zeroth-order/black-box optimization. This hints at the possibility of extending BO to the FL setting (FBO) for agents to collaborate in these black-box optimization tasks. This paper presents federated Thompson sampling (FTS) which overcomes a number of key challenges of FBO and FL in a principled way: We (a) use random Fourier features to approximate the Gaussian process surrogate model used in BO, which naturally produces the parameters to be exchanged between agents, (b) design FTS based on Thompson sampling, which significantly reduces the number of parameters to be exchanged, and (c) provide a theoretical convergence guarantee that is robust against heterogeneous agents, which is a major challenge in FL and FBO. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of FTS in terms of communication efficiency, computational efficiency, and practical performance.

paragraphs: Federated learning commonly coordinates agents through gradient-based training, but some collaborative tasks provide no useful gradients. Hyperparameter tuning is one example of expensive black-box optimization. This paper extends Bayesian optimization to such federated settings, allowing agents to collaborate on optimization tasks through a method called federated Thompson sampling.

The method approximates the Gaussian process surrogate using random Fourier features. This representation supplies parameters that agents can exchange. Building the algorithm around Thompson sampling substantially reduces how many parameters must be communicated, connecting the optimization strategy directly to the practical cost of collaboration.

The authors provide a convergence guarantee that is robust to heterogeneity among agents, addressing the challenge that participating agents need not be identical. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness in communication efficiency, computational efficiency, and practical performance. The contribution broadens federated collaboration to expensive function evaluations without gradients, while giving both a communication-conscious construction and theoretical support for convergence with heterogeneous participants.
summary.tldr: Federated Thompson sampling enables collaborative black-box optimization with reduced parameter exchange and a convergence guarantee robust to heterogeneous agents.

title: Federated Bayesian Optimization via Thompson Sampling

abstract: This paper explores useful modifications of the recent development in contrastive learning via novel probabilistic modeling. We derive a particular form of contrastive loss named Joint Contrastive Learning (JCL). JCL implicitly involves the simultaneous learning of an infinite number of query-key pairs, which poses tighter constraints when searching for invariant features. We derive an upper bound on this formulation that allows analytical solutions in an end-to-end training manner. While JCL is practically effective in numerous computer vision applications, we also theoretically unveil the certain mechanisms that govern the behavior of JCL. We demonstrate that the proposed formulation harbors an innate agency that strongly favors similarity within each instance-specific class, and therefore remains advantageous when searching for discriminative features among distinct instances. We evaluate these proposals on multiple benchmarks, demonstrating considerable improvements over existing algorithms. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/caiqi/Joint-Contrastive-Learning.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning seeks representations that capture similarities within an instance while distinguishing different instances. This paper introduces Joint Contrastive Learning, or JCL, through a probabilistic formulation of the training loss. Its objective implicitly considers an infinite number of query-key pairs together, placing tighter constraints on the search for invariant features.

The infinite-pair formulation is made usable by deriving an upper bound that permits analytical solutions within end-to-end training. This is the connection between the broad probabilistic objective and a practical learning procedure. The method can therefore account implicitly for many paired possibilities without treating the stated infinite collection as a list that must be explicitly processed.

The authors also analyze why the objective behaves as it does. Their theory identifies a tendency to favor similarity within each instance-specific class, which supports learning features that distinguish separate instances. Evaluations across multiple computer-vision benchmarks show considerable improvements over existing algorithms. The contribution combines a new contrastive objective, a tractable bound for training it, and a theoretical explanation of its preference for within-instance consistency.
summary.tldr: JCL uses a tractable bound on an implicit infinite-pair contrastive objective to encourage consistent, discriminative representations.

title: Joint Contrastive Learning with Infinite Possibilities

abstract: A recent line of work focused on making adversarial training computationally efficient for deep learning models. In particular, Wong et al. (2020) showed that $\ell_\infty$-adversarial training with fast gradient sign method (FGSM) can fail due to a phenomenon called catastrophic overfitting, when the model quickly loses its robustness over a single epoch of training. We show that adding a random step to FGSM, as proposed in Wong et al. (2020), does not prevent catastrophic overfitting, and that randomness is not important per se --- its main role being simply to reduce the magnitude of the perturbation. Moreover, we show that catastrophic overfitting is not inherent to deep and overparametrized networks, but can occur in a single-layer convolutional network with a few filters. In an extreme case, even a single filter can make the network highly non-linear locally, which is the main reason why FGSM training fails. Based on this observation, we propose a new regularization method, GradAlign, that prevents catastrophic overfitting by explicitly maximizing the gradient alignment inside the perturbation set and improves the quality of the FGSM solution. As a result, GradAlign allows to successfully apply FGSM training also for larger $\ell_\infty$-perturbations and reduce the gap to multi-step adversarial training. The code of our experiments is available at https://github.com/tml-epfl/understanding-fast-adv-training.

paragraphs: Fast adversarial training uses a single gradient-based perturbation to reduce training cost, but robustness can collapse within one epoch. This paper investigates that catastrophic overfitting in FGSM training. It shows that a random preliminary step does not prevent the problem and that randomness mainly helps by reducing perturbation magnitude.

The failure does not require a deep or heavily overparameterized model. The authors show it can occur in a single convolutional layer with few filters, with even one filter capable of creating strong local nonlinearity. This local behavior explains why a single gradient-based step can become an unreliable basis for adversarial training.

The proposed GradAlign regularizer explicitly encourages gradients to align within the allowed perturbation region. The authors report that this prevents catastrophic overfitting and improves FGSM training outcomes. It also enables training with larger maximum-coordinate perturbations and narrows the gap to multi-step adversarial training. The contribution links a concrete local failure mechanism to a regularizer designed to address it.
summary.tldr: GradAlign addresses catastrophic overfitting in fast adversarial training by encouraging locally aligned gradients.

title: Understanding and Improving Fast Adversarial Training

abstract: In this paper, we propose Patience-based Early Exit, a straightforward yet effective inference method that can be used as a plug-and-play technique to simultaneously improve the efficiency and robustness of a pretrained language model (PLM). To achieve this, our approach couples an internal-classifier with each layer of a PLM and dynamically stops inference when the intermediate predictions of the internal classifiers do not change for a pre-defined number of steps. Our approach improves inference efficiency as it allows the model to make a prediction with fewer layers. Meanwhile, experimental results with an ALBERT model show that our method can improve the accuracy and robustness of the model by preventing it from overthinking and exploiting multiple classifiers for prediction, yielding a better accuracy-speed trade-off compared to existing early exit methods.

To achieve this, our approach couples an internal-classifier with each layer of a PLM and dynamically stops inference when the intermediate predictions of the internal classifiers do not change for a pre-defined number of steps. Our approach improves inference efficiency as it allows the model to make a prediction with fewer layers. Meanwhile, experimental results with an ALBERT model show that our method can improve the accuracy and robustness of the model by preventing it from overthinking and exploiting multiple classifiers for prediction, yielding a better accuracy-speed trade-off compared to existing early exit methods.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an inference method that lets a pretrained language model stop processing an input before reaching its final layer. Called Patience-based Early Exit, it attaches an internal classifier to each layer and watches how the intermediate predictions change as computation proceeds.

The stopping rule depends on stability: inference ends once the prediction has remained unchanged for a predefined number of steps. That patience requirement uses agreement across successive classifiers to decide when additional layers may be unnecessary. By allowing predictions after fewer layers, the method reduces the computation needed for inference.

Experiments with ALBERT show benefits beyond speed. The authors report that early stopping can improve accuracy and robustness by preventing overthinking and using multiple classifiers in making predictions. They also find a better accuracy-speed trade-off than existing early-exit methods. These are experimental findings for the evaluated model, while the proposed technique is presented as a plug-and-play approach for pretrained language models more broadly.
summary.tldr: Patience-based Early Exit stops when successive layer predictions stabilize, improving ALBERT’s reported accuracy-speed trade-off and robustness.

title: BERT Loses Patience: Fast and Robust Inference with Early Exit

abstract: The extension of classical online algorithms when provided with predictions is a new and active research area. In this paper, we extend the primal-dual method for online algorithms in order to incorporate predictions that advise the online algorithm about the next action to take. We use this framework to obtain novel algorithms for a variety of online covering problems. We compare our algorithms to the cost of the true and predicted offline optimal solutions and show that these algorithms outperform any online algorithm when the prediction is accurate while maintaining good guarantees when the prediction is misleading.

paragraphs: Online algorithms make decisions as information arrives, without having the complete problem available in advance. Predictions can offer guidance about the next action, but their usefulness depends on their accuracy. This paper studies how to incorporate such advice while retaining performance guarantees when the guidance is misleading.

The authors extend the primal-dual method, a framework for designing online algorithms, so that predictions can influence its decisions. They use the extension to construct algorithms for a variety of online covering problems. The contribution is therefore a shared design framework rather than a prediction mechanism tailored to just one problem.

The analysis compares algorithmic costs with both the true offline optimum and the predicted offline optimum. These comparisons make the value of accurate advice and the consequences of inaccurate advice part of the same performance account. With accurate predictions, the resulting algorithms outperform what online algorithms can achieve without that advantage, while maintaining good guarantees when predictions mislead. The central result is this combination of improved performance under useful advice and protection under poor advice.
summary.tldr: A prediction-aware primal-dual framework improves online covering performance with accurate advice while retaining guarantees when advice is misleading.

title: The Primal-Dual method for Learning Augmented Algorithms

abstract: Recent studies show that private training data can be leaked through the gradients sharing mechanism deployed in distributed machine learning systems, such as federated learning (FL). Increasing batch size to complicate data recovery is often viewed as a promising defense strategy against data leakage. In this paper, we revisit this defense premise and propose an advanced data leakage attack with theoretical justification to efficiently recover batch data from the shared aggregated gradients. We name our proposed method as catastrophic data leakage in vertical federated learning (CAFE). Comparing to existing data leakage attacks, our extensive experimental results on vertical FL settings demonstrate the effectiveness of CAFE to perform large-batch data leakage attack with improved data recovery quality. We also propose a practical countermeasure to mitigate CAFE. Our results suggest that private data participated in standard FL, especially the vertical case, have a high risk of being leaked from the training gradients. Our analysis implies unprecedented and practical data leakage risks in those learning settings. The code of our work is available at https://github.com/DeRafael/CAFE.

paragraphs: Federated learning can expose private training examples through the gradients shared during training. A proposed defense is to increase batch size, combining information from more examples so that individual records become harder to recover. This paper revisits whether that strategy provides adequate protection, focusing its experiments on vertical federated learning.

The authors introduce CAFE, an attack that recovers batch data from shared, aggregated gradients. They provide theoretical justification for the method and evaluate its recovery behavior experimentally. Compared with existing leakage attacks, CAFE achieves improved reconstruction quality in the tested large-batch vertical federated learning settings. Aggregation therefore does not eliminate recoverable information in those experiments.

The paper also proposes a practical countermeasure intended to mitigate CAFE. Its broader finding is that shared training gradients can present substantial privacy risks, especially in the vertical setting studied. The evidence challenges confidence in larger batches as a defense by demonstrating that an attack can still extract private data from their combined gradients.
summary.tldr: CAFE recovers private data from large-batch aggregated gradients in vertical federated learning, challenging batch size as a privacy defense.

title: CAFE: Catastrophic Data Leakage in Vertical Federated Learning

abstract: Scientific observations may consist of a large number of variables (features). Selecting a subset of meaningful features is often crucial for identifying patterns hidden in the ambient space. In this paper, we present a method for unsupervised feature selection, and we demonstrate its advantage in clustering, a common unsupervised task. We propose a differentiable loss that combines a graph Laplacian-based score that favors low-frequency features with a gating mechanism for removing nuisance features. Our method improves upon the naive graph Laplacian score by replacing it with a gated variant computed on a subset of low-frequency features. We identify this subset by learning the parameters of continuously relaxed Bernoulli variables, which gate the entire feature space. We mathematically motivate the proposed approach and demonstrate that it is crucial to compute the graph Laplacian on the gated inputs rather than on the full feature set in the high noise regime. Using several real-world examples, we demonstrate the efficacy and advantage of the proposed approach over leading baselines.

Our method improves upon the naive graph Laplacian score by replacing it with a gated variant computed on a subset of low-frequency features. Using several real-world examples, we demonstrate the efficacy and advantage of the proposed approach over leading baselines.

paragraphs: Scientific datasets can contain many measured variables, only some of which reveal useful patterns. This paper develops a way to select features without labels and demonstrates its value for clustering. The method combines a graph-based feature score with learned gates that suppress nuisance variables, allowing selection to be optimized through a differentiable objective.

The score uses a graph Laplacian and favors low-frequency features, meaning features that vary smoothly over the graph. A crucial choice is to compute this graph-based quantity using gated inputs. Otherwise, nuisance features can influence the very structure used to judge which features are meaningful. The gates are learned through continuous relaxations of Bernoulli variables, making feature inclusion amenable to gradient-based optimization.

The authors mathematically motivate the approach and show that constructing the Laplacian from gated inputs is crucial in a high-noise regime. Several real-world examples demonstrate advantages over leading baselines. The findings emphasize that feature selection and the graph used to assess features should be considered together when irrelevant measurements strongly affect the data representation.
summary.tldr: Learned feature gates improve unsupervised selection by keeping nuisance variables out of the graph structure used to score features.

title: Differentiable Unsupervised Feature Selection based on a Gated Laplacian

abstract: When solving two-player zero-sum games, multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms often create populations of agents where, at each iteration, a new agent is discovered as the best response to a mixture over the opponent population. Within such a process, the update rules of "who to compete with" (i.e., the opponent mixture) and "how to beat them" (i.e., finding best responses) are underpinned by manually developed game theoretical principles such as fictitious play and Double Oracle. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework—Neural Auto-Curricula (NAC)—that leverages meta-gradient descent to automate the discovery of the learning update rule without explicit human design. Specifically, we parameterise the opponent selection module by neural networks and the best-response module by optimisation subroutines, and update their parameters solely via interaction with the game engine, where both players aim to minimise their exploitability. Surprisingly, even without human design, the discovered MARL algorithms achieve competitive or even better performance with the state-of-the-art population-based game solvers (e.g., PSRO) on Games of Skill, differentiable Lotto, non-transitive Mixture Games, Iterated Matching Pennies, and Kuhn Poker. Additionally, we show that NAC is able to generalise from small games to large games, for example training on Kuhn Poker and outperforming PSRO on Leduc Poker. Our work inspires a promising future direction to discover general MARL algorithms solely from data.

paragraphs: Population-based game solvers repeatedly decide which opponents to train against and how to respond to them. These decisions often follow manually designed game-theoretic rules. Neural Auto-Curricula, or NAC, instead learns the update procedure through interaction with two-player zero-sum games, making the training curriculum itself an object of optimisation.

NAC represents opponent selection with neural networks and best-response learning with optimisation subroutines. Meta-gradient descent adjusts their parameters, with both players seeking to reduce exploitability. The learned procedure therefore shapes the mixture of opponents and the response process according to how those choices affect the players’ vulnerability to exploitation.

Across the games studied, the discovered algorithms are competitive with or outperform state-of-the-art population-based solvers. The authors also demonstrate transfer from smaller to larger games: a procedure trained on Kuhn Poker outperforms PSRO on Leduc Poker. These findings support the possibility of learning useful game-solving rules from interactions, while the demonstrated generalisation concerns the specific transfers evaluated in the paper.
summary.tldr: NAC learns opponent-selection and response-update rules through game interaction, achieving competitive results and demonstrated transfer between poker games.

title: Neural Auto-Curricula in Two-Player Zero-Sum Games

abstract: Knowledge distillation is classically a procedure where a neural network is trained on the output of another network along with the original targets in order to transfer knowledge between the architectures. The special case of self-distillation, where the network architectures are identical, has been observed to improve generalization accuracy. In this paper, we consider an iterative variant of self-distillation in a kernel regression setting, in which successive steps incorporate both model outputs and the ground-truth targets. This allows us to provide the first theoretical results on the importance of using the weighted ground-truth targets in self-distillation. Our focus is on fitting nonlinear functions to training data with a weighted mean square error objective function suitable for distillation, subject to $\ell_2$ regularization of the model parameters. We show that any such function obtained with self-distillation can be calculated directly as a function of the initial fit, and that infinite distillation steps yields the same optimization problem as the original with amplified regularization. Furthermore, we provide a closed form solution for the optimal choice of weighting parameter at each step, and show how to efficiently estimate this weighting parameter for deep learning and significantly reduce the computational requirements compared to a grid search.

paragraphs: Self-distillation trains a network using predictions from another network with the same architecture, often alongside the original labels. It has been observed to improve generalization. This paper investigates why the weight assigned to those original targets matters, studying repeated self-distillation in a kernel regression setting.

The analysis considers nonlinear function fitting with a weighted squared-error objective and an ℓ₂ penalty on model parameters. Each distillation step combines model predictions with ground-truth targets. Within this setting, the authors show that the resulting function can be calculated directly from the initial fit. They also show that infinitely many distillation steps correspond to the original optimization problem with stronger regularization.

These results explain how repeated distillation changes regularization and why retaining weighted ground-truth guidance matters. The authors derive a closed-form optimal weighting parameter at each step in their analysis. They additionally show how to estimate that weight efficiently for deep learning, substantially reducing computation compared with grid search. The theoretical characterization is established in the stated kernel regression setting.
summary.tldr: A kernel regression analysis explains self-distillation as amplified regularization and derives how to weight ground-truth targets at each step.

title: Even your Teacher Needs Guidance: Ground-Truth Targets Dampen Regularization Imposed by Self-Distillation

abstract: Two-sided marketplaces are standard business models of many online platforms (e.g., Amazon, Facebook, LinkedIn), wherein the platforms have consumers, buyers or content viewers on one side and producers, sellers or content-creators on the other. Consumer side measurement of the impact of a treatment variant can be done via simple online A/B testing. Producer side measurement is more challenging because the producer experience depends on the treatment assignment of the consumers. Existing approaches for producer side measurement are either based on graph cluster-based randomization or on certain treatment propagation assumptions. The former approach results in low-powered experiments as the producer-consumer network density increases and the latter approach lacks a strict notion of error control. In this paper, we propose (i) a quantification of the quality of a producer side experiment design, and (ii) a new experiment design mechanism that generates high-quality experiments based on this quantification. Our approach, called UniCoRn (Unifying Counterfactual Rankings), provides explicit control over the quality of the experiment and its computation cost. Further, we prove that our experiment design is optimal to the proposed design quality measure. Our approach is agnostic to the density of the producer-consumer network and does not rely on any treatment propagation assumption. Moreover, unlike the existing approaches, we do not need to know the underlying network in advance, making this widely applicable to the industrial setting where the underlying network is unknown and challenging to predict a priori due to its dynamic nature. We use simulations to validate our approach and compare it against existing methods. We also deployed UniCoRn in an edge recommendation application that serves tens of millions of members and billions of edge recommendations daily.

paragraphs: Testing a recommendation change is complicated when a platform connects consumers with producers. A producer’s experience depends on which consumers receive the change, so consumer treatment assignments also affect producer outcomes. The paper addresses how to design experiments that measure effects on the producer side of this connected marketplace.

The authors introduce a measure of experiment design quality and a mechanism called UniCoRn that constructs experiments using that measure. They prove that the design is optimal according to their proposed criterion. The approach also gives explicit control over experiment quality and computational cost, making those considerations part of the design process.

UniCoRn does not require advance knowledge of the producer-consumer network or assumptions about treatment propagation, and its approach is independent of network density. These properties matter for platforms whose connections change over time. The authors validate the method through simulations and report deployment in an edge recommendation application serving tens of millions of members. The optimality claim concerns their specific design quality measure.
summary.tldr: UniCoRn designs producer-side recommendation experiments with explicit control over design quality and computation, without requiring a known consumer-producer network.

title: A/B Testing for Recommender Systems in a Two-sided Marketplace

abstract: Multi-agent behavior modeling and trajectory forecasting are crucial for the safe navigation of autonomous agents in interactive scenarios. Variational Autoencoder (VAE) has been widely applied in multi-agent interaction modeling to generate diverse behavior and learn a low-dimensional representation for interacting systems. However, existing literature did not formally discuss if a VAE-based model can properly encode interaction into its latent space. In this work, we argue that one of the typical formulations of VAEs in multi-agent modeling suffers from an issue we refer to as social posterior collapse, i.e., the model is prone to ignoring historical social context when predicting the future trajectory of an agent. It could cause significant prediction errors and poor generalization performance. We analyze the reason behind this under-explored phenomenon and propose several measures to tackle it. Afterward, we implement the proposed framework and experiment on real-world datasets for multi-agent trajectory prediction. In particular, we propose a novel sparse graph attention message-passing (sparse-GAMP) layer, which helps us detect social posterior collapse in our experiments. In the experiments, we verify that social posterior collapse indeed occurs. Also, the proposed measures are effective in alleviating the issue. As a result, the model attains better generalization performance when historical social context is informative for prediction.

paragraphs: Predicting an agent's movement in an interactive setting requires accounting for other agents. Variational autoencoders are used to represent these systems compactly and generate diverse possible trajectories. This paper asks whether a commonly used formulation actually encodes the history of social interactions in the representation used to predict future movement.

The authors identify a failure mode they call social posterior collapse: the model can ignore historical social context. They argue that this can produce substantial prediction errors and poor generalization, analyze why it happens, and propose measures to address it. Their framework also includes a sparse graph attention message-passing layer, called sparse-GAMP, which helps detect the failure in experiments.

Tests on real-world trajectory datasets confirm that social posterior collapse occurs and that the proposed measures alleviate it. The resulting generalization improvement is specifically reported when past social context contains information useful for prediction. This qualification matters: the contribution concerns making informative interactions count in the model, rather than asserting that social history improves every forecasting situation.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies and mitigates a VAE failure that ignores social history, improving generalization when that history informs trajectory prediction.

title: Exploring Social Posterior Collapse in Variational Autoencoder for Interaction Modeling

abstract: In online reinforcement learning (RL), efficient exploration remains particularly challenging in high-dimensional environments with sparse rewards. In low-dimensional environments, where tabular parameterization is possible, count-based upper confidence bound (UCB) exploration methods achieve minimax near-optimal rates. However, it remains unclear how to efficiently implement UCB in realistic RL tasks that involve non-linear function approximation. To address this, we propose a new exploration approach via *maximizing* the deviation of the occupancy of the next policy from the explored regions. We add this term as an adaptive regularizer to the standard RL objective to balance exploration vs. exploitation. We pair the new objective with a provably convergent algorithm, giving rise to a new intrinsic reward that adjusts existing bonuses. The proposed intrinsic reward is easy to implement and combine with other existing RL algorithms to conduct exploration. As a proof of concept, we evaluate the new intrinsic reward on tabular examples across a variety of model-based and model-free algorithms, showing improvements over count-only exploration strategies. When tested on navigation and locomotion tasks from MiniGrid and DeepMind Control Suite benchmarks, our approach significantly improves sample efficiency over state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Exploration is difficult when a reinforcement learning agent receives few rewards and operates in a large environment. Counting visits supports strong exploration methods in tabular problems, but extending those methods efficiently to nonlinear function approximation remains challenging. MADE introduces an objective based on moving beyond regions already explored.

The method encourages the next policy's occupancy, or pattern of visits, to deviate from previously explored regions. It adds this encouragement as an adaptive regularizer to the usual reinforcement learning objective, balancing information-seeking behavior with reward pursuit. A provably convergent algorithm for the objective produces an intrinsic reward that adjusts existing exploration bonuses.

The intrinsic reward can be combined with existing reinforcement learning algorithms. In tabular demonstrations, the authors report improvements over count-only exploration across model-based and model-free approaches. Tests on navigation and locomotion tasks from MiniGrid and the DeepMind Control Suite show significantly improved sample efficiency over state-of-the-art methods. These results support using the relationship between future occupancy and past exploration to guide additional exploration.
summary.tldr: MADE rewards policies for departing from explored regions, improving reported exploration and sample efficiency across several reinforcement learning settings.

title: MADE: Exploration via Maximizing Deviation from Explored Regions

abstract: This work studies the statistical limits of uniform convergence for offline policy evaluation (OPE) problems with model-based methods (for episodic MDP) and provides a unified framework towards optimal learning for several well-motivated offline tasks. Uniform OPE $\sup_\Pi|Q^\pi-\hat{Q}^\pi|<\epsilon$ is a stronger measure than the point-wise OPE and ensures offline learning when $\Pi$ contains all policies (the global class). In this paper, we establish an $\Omega(H^2 S/d_m\epsilon^2)$ lower bound (over model-based family) for the global uniform OPE and our main result establishes an upper bound of $\tilde{O}(H^2/d_m\epsilon^2)$ for the \emph{local} uniform convergence that applies to all \emph{near-empirically optimal} policies for the MDPs with \emph{stationary} transition. Here $d_m$ is the minimal marginal state-action probability. Critically, the highlight in achieving the optimal rate $\tilde{O}(H^2/d_m\epsilon^2)$ is our design of \emph{singleton absorbing MDP}, which is a new sharp analysis tool that works with the model-based approach. We generalize such a model-based framework to the new settings: offline task-agnostic and the offline reward-free with optimal complexity $\tilde{O}(H^2\log(K)/d_m\epsilon^2)$ ($K$ is the number of tasks) and $\tilde{O}(H^2S/d_m\epsilon^2)$ respectively. These results provide a unified solution for simultaneously solving different offline RL problems.

paragraphs: Offline policy evaluation estimates policy values from a fixed dataset. Uniform evaluation controls error across a policy class and can support learning, but covering every policy may require substantially more data than covering policies close to empirically optimal.

For episodic models with stationary transitions, the paper proves a global model-based lower bound of Omega(H²S/(d_m epsilon²)) and a local upper bound of roughly O(H²/(d_m epsilon²)), up to logarithmic factors. Here d_m is the minimum marginal state-action probability. A new singleton-absorbing-MDP construction enables the sharper local analysis.

The framework extends to task-agnostic and reward-free offline learning, with respective complexities roughly O(H² log(K)/(d_m epsilon²)) and O(H²S/(d_m epsilon²)). K is the number of tasks. These are statistical guarantees under the specified coverage and transition assumptions; the abstract does not report empirical performance or suggest that arbitrary offline datasets provide adequate coverage.
summary.tldr: Local uniform policy-evaluation bounds unify several model-based offline reinforcement-learning guarantees.

title: Optimal Uniform OPE and Model-based Offline Reinforcement Learning in Time-Homogeneous, Reward-Free and Task-Agnostic Settings

abstract: In classic auction theory, reserve prices are known to be effective for improving revenue for the auctioneer against quasi-linear utility maximizing bidders. The introduction of reserve prices, however, usually do not help improve total welfare of the auctioneer and the bidders. In this paper, we focus on value maximizing bidders with return on spend constraints---a paradigm that has drawn considerable attention recently as more advertisers adopt auto-bidding algorithms in advertising platforms---and show that the introduction of reserve prices has a novel impact on the market. Namely, by choosing reserve prices appropriately the auctioneer can improve not only the total revenue but also the total welfare. Our results also demonstrate that reserve prices are robust to bidder types, i.e., reserve prices work well for different bidder types, such as value maximizers and utility maximizers, without using bidder type information. We generalize these results for a variety of auction mechanisms such as VCG, GSP, and first-price auctions. Moreover, we show how to combine these results with additive boosts to improve the welfare of the outcomes of the auction further. Finally, we complement our theoretical observations with an empirical study confirming the effectiveness of these ideas using data from online advertising auctions.

paragraphs: Reserve prices are established tools for increasing auction revenue, but they do not usually improve the combined welfare of the auctioneer and bidders in the classical setting. This paper studies a different bidder objective relevant to automated advertising: maximize acquired value while satisfying a return-on-spend constraint.

For that setting, the authors show that appropriately chosen reserve prices can improve both revenue and total welfare. Their results also establish robustness across bidder types, including value maximizers and utility maximizers, without requiring the auctioneer to know each bidder's type. The choice of reserve prices remains central to the stated benefit.

The analysis extends across VCG, generalized second-price, and first-price auctions. The authors further show how additive boosts can be combined with these results to improve welfare. An empirical study using online advertising auction data supports the effectiveness of the ideas. Together, the findings show how automated bidding objectives can change the welfare consequences of a familiar auction-design tool.
summary.tldr: Appropriately chosen reserve prices can improve both revenue and welfare for return-constrained auto-bidders, with results spanning multiple auction mechanisms.

title: Robust Auction Design in the Auto-bidding World

abstract: Stochastic model-based methods have received increasing attention lately due to their appealing robustness to the stepsize selection and provable efficiency guarantee. We make two important extensions for improving model-based methods on stochastic weakly convex optimization. First, we propose new minibatch model- based methods by involving a set of samples to approximate the model function in each iteration. For the first time, we show that stochastic algorithms achieve linear speedup over the batch size even for non-smooth and non-convex (particularly, weakly convex) problems. To this end, we develop a novel sensitivity analysis of the proximal mapping involved in each algorithm iteration. Our analysis appears to be of independent interests in more general settings. Second, motivated by the success of momentum stochastic gradient descent, we propose a new stochastic extrapolated model-based method, greatly extending the classic Polyak momentum technique to a wider class of stochastic algorithms for weakly convex optimization. The rate of convergence to some natural stationarity condition is established over a fairly flexible range of extrapolation terms.While mainly focusing on weakly convex optimization, we also extend our work to convex optimization. We apply the minibatch and extrapolated model-based methods to stochastic convex optimization, for which we provide a new complexity bound and promising linear speedup in batch size. Moreover, an accelerated model-based method based on Nesterov’s momentum is presented, for which we establish an optimal complexity bound for reaching optimality.

paragraphs: Stochastic model-based optimization updates parameters using an approximate model of the objective. This paper extends such methods with minibatches and momentum for weakly convex problems, a class that includes nonsmooth and nonconvex objectives. The aim is to improve efficiency while retaining theoretical convergence guarantees.

For minibatches, each iteration constructs its approximation from several samples. A new sensitivity analysis of the proximal mapping establishes linear speedup with batch size in the studied setting. The authors also introduce an extrapolated method that extends Polyak momentum to a broader family of stochastic model-based algorithms. They prove convergence rates toward a stationarity condition over a flexible range of extrapolation choices.

The paper additionally develops results for convex optimization, including a new complexity bound and batch-size speedup. An accelerated method using Nesterov momentum achieves an optimal complexity bound for reaching optimality. The distinction matters: the weakly convex results concern stationarity, while the convex accelerated result concerns optimality. Together, the contributions give theoretical foundations for incorporating two widely useful optimization strategies into model-based methods.
summary.tldr: The paper extends stochastic model-based optimization with minibatching and momentum, proving batch-size speedups and convergence guarantees.

title: Minibatch and Momentum Model-based Methods for Stochastic Weakly Convex Optimization

abstract: Conventional meta-learning considers a set of tasks from a stationary distribution. In contrast, this paper focuses on a more complex online setting, where tasks arrive sequentially and follow a non-stationary distribution. Accordingly, we propose a Variational Continual Bayesian Meta-Learning (VC-BML) algorithm. VC-BML maintains a Dynamic Gaussian Mixture Model for meta-parameters, with the number of component distributions determined by a Chinese Restaurant Process. Dynamic mixtures at the meta-parameter level increase the capability to adapt to diverse tasks due to a larger parameter space, alleviating the negative knowledge transfer problem. To infer posteriors of model parameters, compared to the previously used point estimation method, we develop a more robust posterior approximation method -- structured variational inference for the sake of avoiding forgetting knowledge. Experiments on tasks from non-stationary distributions show that VC-BML is superior in transferring knowledge among diverse tasks and alleviating catastrophic forgetting in an online setting.

paragraphs: Conventional meta-learning assumes tasks come from a stable distribution. This paper considers tasks arriving sequentially from a changing distribution, where transferring earlier knowledge can be unhelpful and learning new tasks can erase useful old knowledge. VC-BML addresses both issues through a Bayesian representation of the meta-parameters.

The method maintains a dynamic Gaussian mixture, with a Chinese Restaurant Process determining the number of components. Multiple components enlarge the parameter space available for adapting to diverse tasks, helping reduce negative knowledge transfer. The model can therefore represent task diversity through a changing mixture rather than a single fixed parameter estimate.

To infer parameter posteriors, the authors introduce structured variational inference as a more robust alternative to point estimation, with the aim of preserving knowledge. Experiments on tasks from non-stationary distributions show better transfer across diverse tasks and reduced catastrophic forgetting. The contribution combines a flexible representation of meta-parameters with posterior approximation, addressing both adaptation to changing tasks and retention of knowledge in the online setting.
summary.tldr: VC-BML uses dynamic Bayesian mixtures and structured variational inference to improve transfer and reduce forgetting across changing task distributions.

title: Variational Continual Bayesian Meta-Learning

abstract: The visual system of mammals is comprised of parallel, hierarchical specialized pathways. Different pathways are specialized in so far as they use representations that are more suitable for supporting specific downstream behaviours. In particular, the clearest example is the specialization of the ventral ("what") and dorsal ("where") pathways of the visual cortex. These two pathways support behaviours related to visual recognition and movement, respectively. To-date, deep neural networks have mostly been used as models of the ventral, recognition pathway. However, it is unknown whether both pathways can be modelled with a single deep ANN. Here, we ask whether a single model with a single loss function can capture the properties of both the ventral and the dorsal pathways. We explore this question using data from mice, who like other mammals, have specialized pathways that appear to support recognition and movement behaviours. We show that when we train a deep neural network architecture with two parallel pathways using a self-supervised predictive loss function, we can outperform other models in fitting mouse visual cortex. Moreover, we can model both the dorsal and ventral pathways. These results demonstrate that a self-supervised predictive learning approach applied to parallel pathway architectures can account for some of the functional specialization seen in mammalian visual systems.

These two pathways support behaviours related to visual recognition and movement, respectively. To-date, deep neural networks have mostly been used as models of the ventral, recognition pathway. However, it is unknown whether both pathways can be modelled with a single deep ANN. Here, we ask whether a single model with a single loss function can capture the properties of both the ventral and the dorsal pathways. We explore this question using data from mice, who like other mammals, have specialized pathways that appear to support recognition and movement behaviours. We show that when we train a deep neural network architecture with two parallel pathways using a self-supervised predictive loss function, we can outperform other models in fitting mouse visual cortex. Moreover, we can model both the dorsal and ventral pathways. These results demonstrate that a self-supervised predictive learning approach applied to parallel pathway architectures can account for some of the functional specialization seen in mammalian visual systems.

paragraphs: Mammalian vision includes parallel pathways with different functional roles. The ventral pathway supports recognition, while the dorsal pathway supports movement-related behavior. Neural network models have mostly focused on the recognition pathway. This paper asks whether a single network trained with a single objective can capture properties of both pathways.

The authors investigate that question using mouse visual cortex data. They train a deep network with two parallel pathways and a self-supervised predictive loss. This combines an architectural feature resembling parallel visual processing with one shared learning objective, allowing the study to examine whether functional specialization can arise within that arrangement.

The trained model fits mouse visual cortex better than the comparison models and captures both dorsal and ventral pathways. These results support the claim that predictive self-supervised learning in a parallel architecture can account for some specialization seen in mammalian vision. The conclusion concerns the functional properties captured by this model and the mouse data studied; it establishes a successful modeling approach for aspects of both pathways.
summary.tldr: A network with parallel pathways and one self-supervised predictive objective captures aspects of both mouse visual pathways and improves cortical fits.

title: The functional specialization of visual cortex emerges from training parallel pathways with self-supervised predictive learning

abstract: This paper presents a novel federated linear contextual bandits model, where individual clients face different $K$-armed stochastic bandits coupled through common global parameters. By leveraging the geometric structure of the linear rewards, a collaborative algorithm called Fed-PE is proposed to cope with the heterogeneity across clients without exchanging local feature vectors or raw data. Fed-PE relies on a novel multi-client G-optimal design, and achieves near-optimal regrets for both disjoint and shared parameter cases with logarithmic communication costs. In addition, a new concept called collinearly-dependent policies is introduced, based on which a tight minimax regret lower bound for the disjoint parameter case is derived. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
