Each client chooses among K possible actions, with rewards having a linear structure. The challenge is to benefit from collaboration despite differences between clients, while avoiding exchanges of local feature vectors or raw data.

The proposed Fed-PE algorithm uses the geometry of those linear rewards to coordinate learning. A central component is a multi-client G-optimal design, which organizes information collection across clients. The resulting method achieves near-optimal regret for both disjoint and shared parameter cases, with logarithmic communication costs. Regret measures the reward lost through decisions made while learning.

The authors also introduce collinearly-dependent policies and use that concept to derive a tight minimax regret lower bound for the disjoint parameter case. This supplies a theoretical benchmark for assessing achievable performance in that setting. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the algorithms’ effectiveness, complementing the guarantees about decision quality and communication.
summary.tldr: Fed-PE enables heterogeneous bandit clients to collaborate with near-optimal regret and logarithmic communication without sharing raw data or local features.

title: Federated Linear Contextual Bandits

abstract: In the adversarial training framework of \cite{carmon2019unlabeled,gowal2021improving}, people use generated/real unlabeled data with pseudolabels to improve adversarial robustness. We provide statistical insights to explain why the artificially generated data improve adversarial training. In particular, we study how the attack strength and the quality of the unlabeled data affect adversarial robustness in this framework. Our results show that with a high-quality unlabeled data generator, adversarial training can benefit greatly from this framework under large attack strength, while a poor generator can still help to some extent. To make adaptions concerning the quality of generated data, we propose an algorithm that performs online adjustment to the weight between the labeled real data and the generated data, aiming to optimize the adversarial risk. Numerical studies are conducted to verify our theories and show the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can be supplemented with unlabeled real or generated examples that receive predicted labels. This paper investigates why artificially generated examples can improve robustness in that framework. Its statistical analysis focuses on two interacting factors: the strength of the adversarial attack and the quality of the unlabeled-data generator.

The results show that a high-quality generator can provide substantial benefits when attack strength is large. A poor generator can still help to some extent, so the analysis does not reduce the value of generated data to a simple useful-or-useless distinction. Instead, the expected contribution depends on the quality of the supplementary data and the adversarial training conditions.

The authors use these insights to propose an algorithm that adjusts the relative weights of labeled real data and generated data during training. The adjustment aims to optimize adversarial risk while accounting for generated-data quality. Numerical studies support the theoretical results and demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness. The work therefore combines an explanation of synthetic-data benefits with a practical mechanism for adapting how strongly training relies on them.
summary.tldr: The paper links synthetic-data benefits to generator quality and attack strength, then adaptively weights generated and real data during adversarial training.

title: Why Do Artificially Generated Data Help Adversarial Robustness

abstract: Recovering linear subspaces from data is a fundamental and important task in statistics and machine learning. Motivated by heterogeneity in Federated Learning settings, we study a basic formulation of this problem: the principal component analysis (PCA), with a focus on dealing with irregular noise. Our data come from $n$ users with user $i$ contributing data samples from a $d$-dimensional distribution with mean $\mu_i$. Our goal is to recover the linear subspace shared by $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n$ using the data points from all users, where every data point from user $i$ is formed by adding an independent mean-zero noise vector to $\mu_i$. If we only have one data point from every user, subspace recovery is information-theoretically impossible when the covariance matrices of the noise vectors can be non-spherical, necessitating additional restrictive assumptions in previous work. We avoid these assumptions by leveraging at least two data points from each user, which allows us to design an efficiently-computable estimator under non-spherical and user-dependent noise. We prove an upper bound for the estimation error of our estimator in general scenarios where the number of data points and amount of noise can vary across users, and prove an information-theoretic error lower bound that not only matches the upper bound up to a constant factor, but also holds even for spherical Gaussian noise. This implies that our estimator does not introduce additional estimation error (up to a constant factor) due to irregularity in the noise. We show additional results for a linear regression problem in a similar setup.

Motivated by federated learning, the setting allows users to contribute different numbers of samples and to have different amounts and shapes of noise.

With only one sample per user, recovery is information-theoretically impossible when noise covariance can be nonspherical, absent further restrictions. The authors instead use at least two samples from each user. This enables an efficiently computable estimator that handles both direction-dependent noise and differences in noise across users without the restrictive assumptions discussed for earlier work.

The estimator’s error upper bound matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to a constant factor. That lower bound holds even for spherical Gaussian noise, implying that irregular noise adds no extra estimation penalty beyond a constant factor in the stated bounds. The paper also supplies results for a related linear regression setting. Its key message is that repeated observations per user can overcome an identifiability obstacle created by irregular noise.
summary.tldr: Using at least two samples per user enables efficient shared-subspace recovery under irregular noise with error bounds optimal up to a constant factor.

title: Subspace Recovery from Heterogeneous Data with Non-isotropic Noise

abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are a popular framework for modeling complex data distributions; they can be efficiently trained via variational inference by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO), at the expense of a gap to the exact (log-)marginal likelihood. While VAEs are commonly used for representation learning, it is unclear why ELBO maximization would yield useful representations, since unregularized maximum likelihood estimation cannot invert the data-generating process. Yet, VAEs often succeed at this task. We seek to elucidate this apparent paradox by studying nonlinear VAEs in the limit of near-deterministic decoders. We first prove that, in this regime, the optimal encoder approximately inverts the decoder---a commonly used but unproven conjecture---which we refer to as self-consistency. Leveraging self-consistency, we show that the ELBO converges to a regularized log-likelihood. This allows VAEs to perform what has recently been termed independent mechanism analysis (IMA): it adds an inductive bias towards decoders with column-orthogonal Jacobians, which helps recovering the true latent factors. The gap between ELBO and log-likelihood is therefore welcome, since it bears unanticipated benefits for nonlinear representation learning. In experiments on synthetic and image data, we show that VAEs uncover the true latent factors when the data generating process satisfies the IMA assumption.

This paper asks whether that gap helps explain their useful representations. The puzzle is that unregularized maximum likelihood alone cannot invert the data-generating process, yet VAEs often recover meaningful latent factors.

Experiments on synthetic and image data demonstrate recovery when the data-generating process satisfies the IMA assumption. The argument therefore ties representation recovery to both a particular theoretical regime and a stated structural assumption.
summary.tldr: For nearly deterministic decoders, the VAE objective introduces a structural bias that helps recover latent factors when the IMA assumption holds.

title: Embrace the Gap: VAEs Perform Independent Mechanism Analysis

abstract: We propose a provable defense mechanism against backdoor policies in reinforcement learning under subspace trigger assumption. A backdoor policy is a security threat where an adversary publishes a seemingly well-behaved policy which in fact allows hidden triggers. During deployment, the adversary can modify observed states in a particular way to trigger unexpected actions and harm the agent. We assume the agent does not have the resources to re-train a good policy. Instead, our defense mechanism sanitizes the backdoor policy by projecting observed states to a `safe subspace', estimated from a small number of interactions with a clean (non-triggered) environment. Our sanitized policy achieves $\epsilon$ approximate optimality in the presence of triggers, provided the number of clean interactions is $O\left(\frac{D}{(1-\gamma)^4 \epsilon^2}\right)$ where $\gamma$ is the discounting factor and $D$ is the dimension of state space. Empirically, we show that our sanitization defense performs well on two Atari game environments.

paragraphs: A backdoored reinforcement-learning policy can behave normally until an adversary modifies its observations with a hidden trigger. The trigger then causes harmful or unexpected actions during deployment. This paper considers an agent that lacks the resources to retrain a good policy and instead needs to make an existing policy safer to use.

The defense assumes a particular subspace structure for triggers. It estimates a safe subspace using interactions with a clean environment, then projects observations into that subspace before the policy acts. The intervention therefore changes the observations supplied to the policy, using clean experience to identify the representation used for sanitization.

Under the stated assumption, the authors prove approximate optimality within epsilon despite triggers when the clean interaction count is O(D/((1−gamma)^4 epsilon²)). Here D is state dimension and gamma is the discount factor. They also report good empirical performance in two Atari environments. The guarantee links protection to a concrete trigger assumption and a sufficient amount of clean interaction.
summary.tldr: Under a subspace trigger assumption, projecting observations into an estimated safe subspace provides a provable defense without retraining the policy.

title: Provable Defense against Backdoor Policies in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Lightweight and efficiency are critical drivers for the practical application of image super-resolution (SR) algorithms. We propose a simple and effective approach, ShuffleMixer, for lightweight image super-resolution that explores large convolution and channel split-shuffle operation. In contrast to previous SR models that simply stack multiple small kernel convolutions or complex operators to learn representations, we explore a large kernel ConvNet for mobile-friendly SR design. Specifically, we develop a large depth-wise convolution and two projection layers based on channel splitting and shuffling as the basic component to mix features efficiently. Since the contexts of natural images are strongly locally correlated, using large depth-wise convolutions only is insufficient to reconstruct fine details. To overcome this problem while maintaining the efficiency of the proposed module, we introduce Fused-MBConvs into the proposed network to model the local connectivity of different features. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed ShuffleMixer is about $3 \times$ smaller than the state-of-the-art efficient SR methods, e.g. CARN, in terms of model parameters and FLOPs while achieving competitive performance.

paragraphs: ShuffleMixer aims to reconstruct higher-resolution images with a lightweight convolutional network suitable for mobile-oriented design. The paper explores large convolution kernels and channel splitting and shuffling as a way to mix image features efficiently. Its basic component combines a large depth-wise convolution with two projection layers built around those channel operations.

The design also addresses a limitation of relying on large depth-wise convolutions alone: they are insufficient for reconstructing fine details in locally correlated natural images. The authors add Fused-MBConv components to model local connections between different features while maintaining the module’s efficiency. The architecture therefore combines broad spatial processing with additional local feature interaction.

Experiments show competitive super-resolution performance while using about one-third the parameters and floating-point operations of efficient state-of-the-art methods such as CARN. Those reductions describe model size and operation counts, rather than a measured universal device speedup. The findings support the paper’s architectural argument that large kernels can fit an efficient super-resolution design when channel mixing and local connectivity are handled carefully.
summary.tldr: ShuffleMixer combines large depth-wise convolutions and channel mixing to deliver competitive super-resolution with substantially fewer parameters and operations.

title: ShuffleMixer: An Efficient ConvNet for Image Super-Resolution

abstract: The overwhelming vulnerability of deep neural networks to carefully crafted perturbations known as adversarial attacks has led to the development of various training techniques to produce robust models. While the primary focus of existing approaches has been directed toward addressing the worst-case performance achieved under a single-threat model, it is imperative that safety-critical systems are robust with respect to multiple threat models simultaneously. Existing approaches that address worst-case performance under the union of such threat models ($\ell_{\infty}, \ell_2, \ell_1$) either utilize adversarial training methods that require multi-step attacks which are computationally expensive in practice, or rely upon fine-tuning of pre-trained models that are robust with respect to a single-threat model. In this work, we show that by carefully choosing the objective function used for robust training, it is possible to achieve similar, or improved worst-case performance over a union of threat models while utilizing only single-step attacks, thereby achieving a significant reduction in computational resources necessary for training. Furthermore, prior work showed that adversarial training specific to the $\ell_1$ threat model is relatively difficult, to the extent that even multi-step adversarially trained models were shown to be prone to gradient-masking. However, the proposed method—when applied on the $\ell_1$ threat model specifically—enables us to obtain the first $\ell_1$ robust model trained solely with single-step adversaries. Finally, to demonstrate the merits of our approach, we utilize a modern set of attack evaluations to better estimate the worst-case performance under the considered union of threat models.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness is often trained against a single rule defining allowable input perturbations. This paper targets worst-case performance across the union of three threat models: l-infinity, l2, and l1. Covering them together matters because strength against one perturbation model does not by itself address the combined robustness objective.

Existing approaches discussed in the paper use expensive multistep attacks or fine-tune models already robust to a single threat. The authors show that carefully choosing the training objective makes it possible to obtain similar or better worst-case performance across the union using only single-step attacks. This substantially reduces the computational resources needed for training.

They also apply the method specifically to l1 robustness, a setting where prior adversarial training approaches encountered gradient masking. The paper reports the first l1-robust model trained solely with single-step adversaries. A modern collection of attack evaluations is used to better estimate worst-case performance under the considered union, supporting the claimed efficiency and robustness benefits within those threat models.
summary.tldr: A carefully chosen objective enables efficient single-step adversarial training against a union of l-infinity, l2, and l1 threats.

title: Toward Efficient Robust Training against Union of $\ell_p$ Threat Models

abstract: In distributed training of deep neural networks, people usually run Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) or its variants on each machine and communicate with other machines periodically. However, SGD might converge slowly in training some deep neural networks (e.g., RNN, LSTM) because of the exploding gradient issue. Gradient clipping is usually employed to address this issue in the single machine setting, but exploring this technique in the distributed setting is still in its infancy: it remains mysterious whether the gradient clipping scheme can take advantage of multiple machines to enjoy parallel speedup. The main technical difficulty lies in dealing with nonconvex loss function, non-Lipschitz continuous gradient, and skipping communication rounds simultaneously. In this paper, we explore a relaxed-smoothness assumption of the loss landscape which LSTM was shown to satisfy in previous works, and design a communication-efficient gradient clipping algorithm. This algorithm can be run on multiple machines, where each machine employs a gradient clipping scheme and communicate with other machines after multiple steps of gradient-based updates. Our algorithm is proved to have $O\left(\frac{1}{N\epsilon^4}\right)$ iteration complexity and $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^3})$ communication complexity for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary point in the homogeneous data setting, where $N$ is the number of machines. This indicates that our algorithm enjoys linear speedup and reduced communication rounds. Our proof relies on novel analysis techniques of estimating truncated random variables, which we believe are of independent interest. Our experiments on several benchmark datasets and various scenarios demonstrate that our algorithm indeed exhibits fast convergence speed in practice and thus validates our theory.

paragraphs: Training a neural network across several machines creates two connected challenges: unstable gradients can slow optimization, while frequent communication can reduce the benefit of parallel work. This paper studies whether gradient clipping, which limits unusually large updates, can address the first problem while allowing machines to communicate less often.

The proposed algorithm performs multiple clipped gradient updates on each machine before exchanging information. Its analysis uses a relaxed smoothness assumption on the loss landscape, rather than requiring the usual globally controlled gradient variation. This accommodates the combination of nonconvex optimization, large gradients, and skipped communication rounds that makes the distributed setting difficult.

For homogeneous data across machines, the authors prove an iteration complexity of O(1/(N epsilon^4)) and communication complexity of O(1/epsilon^3) for reaching an epsilon-stationary point. The dependence on the number of machines N establishes linear parallel speedup under those conditions. Experiments across several benchmark datasets and scenarios also show fast convergence, supporting the practical relevance of the theoretical result.
summary.tldr: Distributed gradient clipping achieves provable parallel speedup with fewer communication rounds under relaxed smoothness and homogeneous data assumptions.

title: A Communication-Efficient Distributed Gradient Clipping Algorithm for Training Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Despite the established convergence theory of Optimistic Gradient Descent Ascent (OGDA) and Extragradient (EG) methods for the convex-concave minimax problems, little is known about the theoretical guarantees of these methods in nonconvex settings. To bridge this gap, for the first time, this paper establishes the convergence of OGDA and EG methods under the nonconvex-strongly-concave (NC-SC) and nonconvex-concave (NC-C) settings by providing a unified analysis through the lens of single-call extra-gradient methods. We further establish lower bounds on the convergence of GDA/OGDA/EG, shedding light on the tightness of our analysis. We also conduct experiments supporting our theoretical results. We believe our results will advance the theoretical understanding of OGDA and EG methods for solving complicated nonconvex minimax real-world problems, e.g., Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) or robust neural networks training.

paragraphs: Minimax optimization involves minimizing over one set of variables while maximizing over another. Optimistic gradient descent-ascent and extragradient methods already had established convergence theory for convex-concave problems. This paper addresses the less understood case where the minimizing side can be nonconvex, as occurs in more complicated learning formulations.

The authors give a unified analysis through single-call extragradient methods. They establish convergence for both optimistic gradient descent-ascent and extragradient in nonconvex-strongly-concave and nonconvex-concave settings. These conditions retain concavity on the maximizing side, with strong concavity defining the more restrictive of the two settings. The guarantees therefore address specified nonconvex problem classes.

The paper also proves convergence lower bounds for gradient descent-ascent, optimistic gradient descent-ascent, and extragradient. These bounds help assess how tight the analysis is by showing constraints on the methods' convergence behavior. Experiments support the theoretical results. The contribution strengthens the theoretical basis for studying these algorithms in nonconvex minimax learning problems, with GANs and robust neural network training identified as motivating applications.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis establishes convergence and supporting lower bounds for extragradient and optimistic gradient methods in specified nonconvex minimax settings.

title: Tight Analysis of Extra-gradient and Optimistic Gradient Methods For Nonconvex Minimax Problems

abstract: In safety-critical applications of reinforcement learning such as healthcare and robotics, it is often desirable to optimize risk-sensitive objectives that account for tail outcomes rather than expected reward. We prove the first regret bounds for reinforcement learning under a general class of risk-sensitive objectives including the popular CVaR objective. Our theory is based on a novel characterization of the CVaR objective as well as a novel optimistic MDP construction.
originalAbstract: In safety-critical applications of reinforcement learning such as healthcare and robotics, it is often desirable to optimize risk-sensitive objectives that account for tail outcomes rather than expected reward. We prove the first regret bounds for reinforcement learning under a general class of risk-sensitive objectives including the popular CVaR objective. Our theory is based on a novel characterization of the CVaR objective as well as a novel optimistic MDP construction.

paragraphs: Optimizing average reward can leave a reinforcement-learning objective insensitive to outcomes in the tails of the reward distribution. In settings motivated by healthcare or robotics, those outcomes may deserve explicit attention. This paper studies learning objectives that account for risk, including Conditional Value at Risk, commonly called CVaR.

The main contribution is a set of regret bounds for a general class of risk-sensitive objectives. Regret measures the performance lost while learning relative to the relevant optimal benchmark. The authors identify these as the first such bounds for their class, extending theoretical performance analysis beyond an objective based solely on expected reward.

The theory rests on a new characterization of CVaR and a new construction of an optimistic Markov decision process. These provide the ingredients for analyzing learning under the risk-sensitive objective. The result offers a mathematical account of learning performance when tail outcomes matter. Its contribution is the regret theory itself, with healthcare and robotics serving as motivations for the objective.
summary.tldr: The paper proves regret bounds for a general class of risk-sensitive reinforcement-learning objectives, including CVaR.

title: Regret Bounds for Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce Resilient Multiple Choice Learning (rMCL), an extension of the MCL approach for conditional distribution estimation in regression settings where multiple targets may be sampled for each training input.Multiple Choice Learning is a simple framework to tackle multimodal density estimation, using the Winner-Takes-All (WTA) loss for a set of hypotheses. In regression settings, the existing MCL variants focus on merging the hypotheses, thereby eventually sacrificing the diversity of the predictions. In contrast, our method relies on a novel learned scoring scheme underpinned by a mathematical framework based on Voronoi tessellations of the output space, from which we can derive a probabilistic interpretation.After empirically validating rMCL with experiments on synthetic data, we further assess its merits on the sound source localization problem, demonstrating its practical usefulness and the relevance of its interpretation.

paragraphs: Some regression problems have several plausible outputs for the same input, and training may provide multiple targets per input. Multiple Choice Learning represents these possibilities with a set of predictions trained using a winner-takes-all loss. The paper argues that existing regression variants can sacrifice prediction diversity when they merge those hypotheses.

Resilient Multiple Choice Learning, or rMCL, introduces a learned scoring scheme for the hypotheses. Its mathematical foundation uses Voronoi tessellations, which divide the output space into regions associated with different predictions. This regional view supports a probabilistic interpretation of the scores and predictions, connecting the collection of hypotheses to a conditional distribution.

The authors first validate the method on synthetic data and then apply it to sound-source localization. These experiments demonstrate practical usefulness and support the proposed probabilistic interpretation. The contribution is a way to give diverse regression predictions meaningful scores, addressing distribution estimation without relying on the hypothesis merging that the authors identify as a source of lost diversity.
summary.tldr: rMCL adds probabilistically grounded learned scores to multiple regression hypotheses, with validation on synthetic data and sound-source localization.

title: Resilient Multiple Choice Learning: A learned scoring scheme with application to audio scene analysis

abstract: Combinatorial Optimization underpins many real-world applications and yet, designing performant algorithms to solve these complex, typically NP-hard, problems remains a significant research challenge. Reinforcement Learning (RL) provides a versatile framework for designing heuristics across a broad spectrum of problem domains. However, despite notable progress, RL has not yet supplanted industrial solvers as the go-to solution. Current approaches emphasize pre-training heuristics that construct solutions, but often rely on search procedures with limited variance, such as stochastically sampling numerous solutions from a single policy, or employing computationally expensive fine-tuning of the policy on individual problem instances. Building on the intuition that performant search at inference time should be anticipated during pre-training, we propose COMPASS, a novel RL approach that parameterizes a distribution of diverse and specialized policies conditioned on a continuous latent space. We evaluate COMPASS across three canonical problems - Travelling Salesman, Capacitated Vehicle Routing, and Job-Shop Scheduling - and demonstrate that our search strategy (i) outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in 9 out of 11 standard benchmarking tasks and (ii) generalizes better, surpassing all other approaches on a set of 18 procedurally transformed instance distributions.

paragraphs: Combinatorial optimization involves choosing among many possible arrangements, such as routes or schedules. Reinforcement learning can learn rules for constructing these solutions, but finding strong solutions also depends on how those rules are explored when a new problem arrives. The paper identifies two common approaches: repeatedly sampling from one policy, which can restrict search diversity, and fine-tuning a policy for each instance, which can be computationally expensive.

COMPASS builds the needs of this later search into pre-training. It represents a collection of diverse, specialized policies controlled by a continuous latent space. Searching that space provides a way to explore different solution-building behaviors. The central idea is that training should prepare a useful range of policies for search, so adaptation to an instance becomes part of how the learned solver is used.

The authors evaluate COMPASS on travelling salesman, capacitated vehicle routing, and job-shop scheduling problems. They report better performance than state-of-the-art approaches on 9 of 11 standard benchmark tasks. They also report stronger generalization across 18 procedurally transformed instance distributions, outperforming every comparison approach there. These findings support the value of preparing policy diversity during training for effective search on the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: COMPASS trains diverse policies organized by a continuous latent space, enabling search that outperforms comparison approaches on most tested benchmarks and all tested transformed distributions.

title: Combinatorial Optimization with Policy Adaptation using Latent Space Search

abstract: Learning feature interactions can be the key for multivariate predictive modeling. ReLU-activated neural networks create piecewise linear prediction models, and other nonlinear activation functions lead to models with only high-order feature interactions. Recent methods incorporate candidate polynomial terms of fixed orders into deep learning, which is subject to the issue of combinatorial explosion, or learn the orders that are difficult to adapt to different regions of the feature space. We propose a Polyhedron Attention Module (PAM) to create piecewise polynomial models where the input space is split into polyhedrons which define the different pieces and on each piece the hyperplanes that define the polyhedron boundary multiply to form the interactive terms, resulting in interactions of adaptive order to each piece. PAM is interpretable to identify important interactions in predicting a target. Theoretic analysis shows that PAM has stronger expression capability than ReLU-activated networks. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the superior classification performance of PAM on massive datasets of the click-through rate prediction and PAM can learn meaningful interaction effects in a medical problem.

paragraphs: Predictive models often need to capture interactions among several input features. Explicitly including polynomial terms of fixed orders can create a combinatorial explosion, while learned interaction orders may adapt poorly across different regions of the input space. This paper proposes varying the interaction structure locally through a Polyhedron Attention Module, or PAM.

PAM divides the input space into polyhedral regions and constructs a polynomial model within each region. The expressions defining the region's boundary hyperplanes are multiplied to form interaction terms. This makes the interaction order adaptive to the individual region. The resulting structure is also intended to identify which feature interactions matter for predicting the target.

Theoretical analysis establishes stronger expressive capability than ReLU-activated networks. Experiments report superior classification performance on large click-through-rate prediction datasets and meaningful interaction effects in a medical problem. These findings connect the architecture's mathematical construction to prediction and interpretation: different parts of the feature space can use different interaction orders, while exposing interactions relevant to the output.
summary.tldr: PAM builds piecewise polynomial models whose feature-interaction orders adapt to different regions of the input space.

title: Polyhedron Attention Module: Learning Adaptive-order Interactions

abstract: In-context learning is the ability of a pretrained model to adapt to novel and diverse downstream tasks by conditioning on prompt examples, without optimizing any parameters. While large language models have demonstrated this ability, how in-context learning could be performed over graphs is unexplored. In this paper, we develop \textbf{Pr}etraining \textbf{O}ver \textbf{D}iverse \textbf{I}n-Context \textbf{G}raph S\textbf{y}stems (PRODIGY), the first pretraining framework that enables in-context learning over graphs. The key idea of our framework is to formulate in-context learning over graphs with a novel \emph{prompt graph} representation, which connects prompt examples and queries. We then propose a graph neural network architecture over the prompt graph and a corresponding family of in-context pretraining objectives. With PRODIGY, the pretrained model can directly perform novel downstream classification tasks on unseen graphs via in-context learning. We provide empirical evidence of the effectiveness of our framework by showcasing its strong in-context learning performance on tasks involving citation networks and knowledge graphs. Our approach outperforms the in-context learning accuracy of contrastive pretraining baselines with hard-coded adaptation by 18\% on average across all setups. Moreover, it also outperforms standard finetuning with limited data by 33\% on average with in-context learning.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a pretrained model adapt to a task from examples supplied at prediction time, without updating its parameters. PRODIGY develops this capability for graphs. The intended outcome is a model that can perform new classification tasks on previously unseen graphs by using example-based context.

Its central representation is a prompt graph that connects demonstration examples with the queries to be answered. The authors design a graph neural network to operate on this representation and a corresponding family of pretraining objectives. Together, these components teach the model to use the relationship between examples and queries as the basis for task adaptation.

Experiments on citation networks and knowledge graphs show strong in-context performance. Across the evaluated setups, the authors report average accuracy improvements of 18% over contrastive pretraining baselines with hard-coded adaptation and 33% over standard fine-tuning with limited data. These comparisons support the value of pretraining explicitly for graph-based prompting, so that new examples can guide predictions without a separate parameter-optimization stage.
summary.tldr: PRODIGY pretrains graph networks to solve new classification tasks from connected prompt examples without updating model parameters.

title: PRODIGY: Enabling In-context Learning Over Graphs

abstract: Recent diffusion model advancements have enabled high-fidelity images to be generated using text prompts. However, a domain gap exists between generated images and real-world images, which poses a challenge in generating high-quality variations of real-world images. Our investigation uncovers that this domain gap originates from a latents' distribution gap in different diffusion processes. To address this issue, we propose a novel inference pipeline called Real-world Image Variation by ALignment (RIVAL) that utilizes diffusion models to generate image variations from a single image exemplar. Our pipeline enhances the generation quality of image variations by aligning the image generation process to the source image's inversion chain. Specifically, we demonstrate that step-wise latent distribution alignment is essential for generating high-quality variations. To attain this, we design a cross-image self-attention injection for feature interaction and a step-wise distribution normalization to align the latent features. Incorporating these alignment processes into a diffusion model allows RIVAL to generate high-quality image variations without further parameter optimization. Our experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms existing methods concerning semantic similarity and perceptual quality. This generalized inference pipeline can be easily applied to other diffusion-based generation tasks, such as image-conditioned text-to-image generation and stylization. Project page: https://rival-diff.github.io

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality images from text, but creating variations of a real photograph introduces a gap between real and generated images. The authors trace this gap to differences between latent distributions in the relevant diffusion processes. They propose RIVAL, an inference pipeline that generates variations from a single source image.

RIVAL aligns generation with the source image’s inversion chain, the sequence associated with reversing its diffusion process. The paper identifies alignment at each step as essential for high-quality variations. It combines cross-image self-attention injection, which enables feature interaction, with step-wise distribution normalization, which aligns the latent features. These operations work within a diffusion model without further parameter optimization.

Experiments show better semantic similarity and perceptual quality than existing methods. This means the reported variations improve both their relationship to the source image’s content and their visual quality. The authors also describe the pipeline as applicable to other diffusion tasks, including image-conditioned text-to-image generation and stylization.
summary.tldr: RIVAL improves real-image variations without further parameter optimization by aligning diffusion generation with the source image’s inversion chain.

title: Real-World Image Variation by Aligning Diffusion Inversion Chain

abstract: Large-scale pre-training and instruction tuning have been successful at creating general-purpose language models with broad competence. However, building general-purpose vision-language models is challenging due to the rich input distributions and task diversity resulting from the additional visual input. Although vision-language pretraining has been widely studied, vision-language instruction tuning remains under-explored. In this paper, we conduct a systematic and comprehensive study on vision-language instruction tuning based on the pretrained BLIP-2 models. We gather 26 publicly available datasets, covering a wide variety of tasks and capabilities, and transform them into instruction tuning format. Additionally, we introduce an instruction-aware Query Transformer, which extracts informative features tailored to the given instruction. Trained on 13 held-in datasets, InstructBLIP attains state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across all 13 held-out datasets, substantially outperforming BLIP-2 and larger Flamingo models. Our models also lead to state-of-the-art performance when finetuned on individual downstream tasks (e.g., 90.7% accuracy on ScienceQA questions with image contexts). Furthermore, we qualitatively demonstrate the advantages of InstructBLIP over concurrent multimodal models. All InstructBLIP models are open-source.

paragraphs: Vision-language systems face diverse tasks and visual inputs, making general-purpose instruction following challenging. This paper studies instruction tuning of pretrained BLIP-2 models using 26 public datasets converted into a common instruction-oriented format.

An instruction-aware Query Transformer extracts visual features suited to the current instruction. The model trains on 13 included datasets and is evaluated zero-shot on the other 13, explicitly testing transfer to held-out task data rather than only measuring training-task performance.

InstructBLIP achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot results on all 13 held-out datasets in the reported comparisons, surpassing BLIP-2 and larger Flamingo models. Individual-task fine-tuning also performs strongly, including 90.7% accuracy on ScienceQA questions with image contexts. The abstract adds qualitative comparisons with contemporary multimodal models. These results demonstrate broad evaluated transfer, while not establishing reliable instruction following for every possible visual task.
summary.tldr: InstructBLIP tunes a vision-language model to instructions and generalizes across held-out task datasets.

title: InstructBLIP: Towards General-purpose Vision-Language Models with Instruction Tuning

abstract: We present a novel approach for explaining Gaussian processes (GPs) that can utilize the full analytical covariance structure present in GPs. Our method is based on the popular solution concept of Shapley values extended to stochastic cooperative games, resulting in explanations that are random variables. The GP explanations generated using our approach satisfy similar favorable axioms to standard Shapley values and possess a tractable covariance function across features and data observations. This covariance allows for quantifying explanation uncertainties and studying the statistical dependencies between explanations. We further extend our framework to the problem of predictive explanation, and propose a Shapley prior over the explanation function to predict Shapley values for new data based on previously computed ones. Our extensive illustrations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Our method is based on the popular solution concept of Shapley values extended to stochastic cooperative games, resulting in explanations that are random variables. The GP explanations generated using our approach satisfy similar favorable axioms to standard Shapley values and possess a tractable covariance function across features and data observations. This covariance allows for quantifying explanation uncertainties and studying the statistical dependencies between explanations. We further extend our framework to the problem of predictive explanation, and propose a Shapley prior over the explanation function to predict Shapley values for new data based on previously computed ones. paragraphs: An explanation of a Gaussian process prediction can carry uncertainty, just as the prediction itself does. This paper develops a way to retain that uncertainty when assigning contributions to input features. It extends Shapley values to stochastic cooperative games, producing explanations that are random variables and can use the Gaussian process’s full analytical covariance structure.

The resulting explanations satisfy axioms similar to the favorable properties of ordinary Shapley values. They also have a tractable covariance function spanning both features and observations. This means the framework can describe uncertainty in individual contributions and statistical relationships among explanations. The explanation is therefore richer than a collection of separate feature scores: it can represent how those scores vary together.

The authors also address predictive explanation, where explanations for new data are estimated from previously computed ones. They introduce a Shapley prior over the explanation function to support that prediction. Extensive illustrations demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. The contribution is a unified treatment of feature attribution, uncertainty, and dependence for Gaussian processes, together with a way to extend computed explanations to additional observations.
summary.tldr: Stochastic Shapley values explain Gaussian processes while retaining uncertainty and dependencies between feature contributions.

title: Explaining the Uncertain: Stochastic Shapley Values for Gaussian Process Models

abstract: In this paper, we present EV-Eye, a first-of-its-kind large scale multimodal eye tracking dataset aimed at inspiring research on high-frequency eye/gaze tracking. EV-Eye utilizes an emerging bio-inspired event camera to capture independent pixel-level intensity changes induced by eye movements, achieving sub-microsecond latency. Our dataset was curated over a two-week period and collected from 48 participants encompassing diverse genders and age groups. It comprises over 1.5 million near-eye grayscale images and 2.7 billion event samples generated by two DAVIS346 event cameras. Additionally, the dataset contains 675 thousands scene images and 2.7 million gaze references captured by Tobii Pro Glasses 3 eye tracker for cross-modality validation. Compared with existing event-based high-frequency eye tracking datasets, our dataset is significantly larger in size, and the gaze references involve more natural eye movement patterns, i.e., fixation, saccade and smooth pursuit. Alongside the event data, we also present a hybrid eye tracking method as benchmark, which leverages both the near-eye grayscale images and event data for robust and high-frequency eye tracking. We show that our method achieves higher accuracy for both pupil and gaze estimation tasks compared to the existing solution.

paragraphs: EV-Eye provides a large multimodal dataset for studying high-frequency eye and gaze tracking. Its event cameras record intensity changes independently at individual pixels, capturing changes caused by eye movement with sub-microsecond latency. The dataset pairs these event measurements with conventional images and gaze references, giving researchers several complementary views of eye movement.

summary.tldr: EV-Eye pairs a large event-camera eye-tracking dataset with a hybrid method that improves pupil and gaze estimation accuracy.

title: EV-Eye: Rethinking High-frequency Eye Tracking through the Lenses of Event Cameras

abstract: We consider a contextual bandit problem with $S $ contexts and $K $ actions. In each round $t=1,2,\dots$ the learnerobserves a random context and chooses an action based on its past experience. The learner then observes a random reward whose mean is a function of the context and the action for the round. Under the assumption that the contexts can be lumped into $r\le \min(S ,K)$ groups such that the mean reward for the various actions is the same for any two contexts that are in the same group, we give an algorithm that outputs an $\epsilon$-optimal policy after using at most $\widetilde O(r (S +K )/\epsilon^2)$ samples with high probability and provide a matching $\widetilde\Omega(r (S +K )/\epsilon^2)$ lower bound. In the regret minimization setting, we give an algorithm whose cumulative regret up to time $T$ is bounded by $\widetilde O(\sqrt{r ^3(S +K )T})$. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to show the near-optimal sample complexity in the PAC setting and $\widetilde O{\sqrt{\text{poly}(r)(S+K)T}}$ minimax regret in the online setting for this problem. We also show our algorithms can be applied to more general low-rank bandits and get improved regret bounds in some scenarios.

paragraphs: In a contextual bandit problem, a learner sees a context, chooses an action, and observes a reward. This paper assumes that the S contexts can be grouped into r categories: within each category, every action has the same expected reward across contexts. The number of groups is at most the smaller of S and the number of actions, K.

Under this assumption, the authors give an algorithm that finds a policy within epsilon of optimal using roughly r(S + K)/epsilon² samples, with high probability and logarithmic factors suppressed. They prove a matching lower bound at that level of precision. This establishes nearly optimal data requirements for learning a good policy when the shared reward structure exists.

For learning while accumulating rewards, they provide a cumulative regret bound of roughly the square root of r³(S + K)T over T rounds, again suppressing logarithmic factors. They also extend their algorithms to more general low-rank bandits, improving regret bounds in some scenarios. The gains therefore depend on exploitable structure in how contexts and actions determine rewards.
summary.tldr: When contexts share action-reward profiles in groups, bandit algorithms can achieve nearly optimal sample requirements by exploiting that structure.

title: Context-lumpable stochastic bandits

abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) has attracted significant attention for its effectiveness in improving generalization across various tasks. However, its underlying principles remain poorly understood. In this work, we analyze SAM’s training dynamics using the maximum eigenvalue of the Hessian as a measure of sharpness and propose a third-order stochastic differential equation (SDE), which reveals that the dynamics are driven by a complex mixture of second- and third-order terms. We show that alignment between the perturbation vector and the top eigenvector is crucial for SAM’s effectiveness in regularizing sharpness, but find that this alignment is often inadequate in practice, which limits SAM's efficiency. Building on these insights, we introduce Eigen-SAM, an algorithm that explicitly aims to regularize the top Hessian eigenvalue by aligning the perturbation vector with the leading eigenvector. We validate the effectiveness of our theory and the practical advantages of our proposed approach through comprehensive experiments. Code is available at https://github.com/RitianLuo/EigenSAM.

paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, can improve generalization, but the reasons for its effectiveness remain incompletely understood. This paper studies its training dynamics using the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian as a measure of sharpness. That quantity captures the strongest local curvature of the training loss.

The authors develop a third-order stochastic differential equation describing SAM’s dynamics. Their analysis reveals a mixture of second- and third-order effects and highlights the direction of SAM’s perturbation. Effective sharpness regularization depends crucially on alignment between that perturbation and the Hessian’s leading eigenvector, the direction associated with its largest eigenvalue. They find that this alignment is often inadequate in practice, limiting SAM’s efficiency.

These insights motivate Eigen-SAM, which explicitly aligns the perturbation with the leading eigenvector to target the largest eigenvalue. The authors report comprehensive experiments supporting both their theoretical account and the practical benefits of the algorithm. The contribution connects an explanation of when SAM’s perturbations are effective with a concrete change intended to make that alignment more reliable.
summary.tldr: Eigen-SAM targets loss sharpness by aligning SAM’s perturbation with the leading Hessian eigenvector, addressing a weakness identified in its training dynamics.

title: Explicit Eigenvalue Regularization Improves Sharpness-Aware Minimization

abstract: Motion forecasting is an essential task for autonomous driving, and utilizing information from infrastructure and other vehicles can enhance forecasting capabilities.Existing research mainly focuses on leveraging single-frame cooperative information to enhance the limited perception capability of the ego vehicle, while underutilizing the motion and interaction context of traffic participants observed from cooperative devices. In this paper, we propose a forecasting-oriented representation paradigm to utilize motion and interaction features from cooperative information. Specifically, we present V2X-Graph, a representative framework to achieve interpretable and end-to-end trajectory feature fusion for cooperative motion forecasting. V2X-Graph is evaluated on V2X-Seq in vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) scenarios.To further evaluate on vehicle-to-everything (V2X) scenario, we construct the first real-world V2X motion forecasting dataset V2X-Traj, which contains multiple autonomous vehicles and infrastructure in every scenario.Experimental results on both V2X-Seq and V2X-Traj show the advantage of our method. We hope both V2X-Graph and V2X-Traj will benefit the further development of cooperative motion forecasting.Find the project at https://github.com/AIR-THU/V2X-Graph.

paragraphs: This paper studies motion forecasting when an autonomous vehicle can use observations from other vehicles and roadside infrastructure. The authors argue that existing cooperative methods emphasize single-frame information to improve perception, leaving much of the observed motion history and interaction context underused. Their approach makes those trajectory-related features central to the shared representation.

The proposed V2X-Graph framework fuses trajectory features end to end for cooperative forecasting. It is designed to make that fusion interpretable while using motion and interaction information from cooperating devices. This changes the purpose of information sharing: cooperative observations contribute directly to forecasting representations, extending their role beyond improving what the vehicle perceives in one frame.

The authors evaluate vehicle-to-infrastructure forecasting on V2X-Seq. They also introduce V2X-Traj, described as the first real-world V2X motion-forecasting dataset, with multiple autonomous vehicles and infrastructure in every scenario. Experiments on both datasets show advantages for their method. Together, the framework and dataset support studying prediction with richer cooperation among traffic-observation sources.
summary.tldr: V2X-Graph uses shared motion and interaction histories for cooperative forecasting, supported by the new real-world V2X-Traj dataset.

title: Learning Cooperative Trajectory Representations for Motion Forecasting

abstract: In this paper, we analyze the sample and communication complexity of the federated linear stochastic approximation (FedLSA) algorithm. We explicitly quantify the effects of local training with agent heterogeneity. We show that the communication complexity of FedLSA scales polynomially with the inverse of the desired accuracy ϵ. To overcome this, we propose SCAFFLSA a new variant of FedLSA that uses control variates to correct for client drift, and establish its sample and communication complexities. We show that for statistically heterogeneous agents, its communication complexity scales logarithmically with the desired accuracy, similar to Scaffnew. An important finding is that, compared to the existing results for Scaffnew, the sample complexity scales with the inverse of the number of agents, a property referred to as linear speed-up. Achieving this linear speed-up requires completely new theoretical arguments. We apply the proposed method to federated temporal difference learning with linear function approximation and analyze the corresponding complexity improvements.

paragraphs: Federated linear stochastic approximation lets multiple agents perform local learning while periodically communicating. When agents have different statistical characteristics, local updates can drift apart. The paper quantifies how this heterogeneity affects both the number of samples and the communication needed by the existing FedLSA algorithm.

The analysis shows that FedLSA's communication cost grows polynomially with inverse target accuracy. To improve this dependence, the authors introduce SCAFFLSA, which uses control variates to correct client drift. For statistically heterogeneous agents, its communication complexity grows logarithmically with inverse target accuracy, matching the type of dependence established for Scaffnew.

The sample analysis adds another benefit: complexity scales inversely with the number of agents, a property called linear speed-up. The authors emphasize that proving this improvement over existing Scaffnew results requires new theoretical arguments. They also apply SCAFFLSA to federated temporal-difference learning with linear function approximation and analyze the resulting complexity gains. The contribution therefore addresses communication and sample use together in the specified linear learning settings.
summary.tldr: SCAFFLSA corrects federated client drift, achieving logarithmic communication dependence on inverse accuracy and linear sample speed-up across agents.

title: SCAFFLSA: Taming Heterogeneity in Federated Linear Stochastic Approximation and TD Learning

abstract: This paper introduces FUNGI, **F**eatures from **UN**supervised **G**rad**I**ents, a method to enhance the features of transformer encoders by leveraging self-supervised gradients. Our method is simple: given any pretrained model, we first compute gradients from various self-supervised objectives for each input. These gradients are projected to a lower dimension and then concatenated with the model's output embedding. The resulting features are evaluated on k-nearest neighbor classification over 11 datasets from vision, 5 from natural language processing, and 2 from audio. Across backbones spanning various sizes and pretraining strategies, FUNGI features provide consistent performance improvements over the embeddings. We also show that using FUNGI features can benefit linear classification, clustering and image retrieval, and that they significantly improve the retrieval-based in-context scene understanding abilities of pretrained models, for example improving upon DINO by +17% for semantic segmentation - without any training. Code is available at https://github.com/WalterSimoncini/fungivision.

paragraphs: FUNGI improves the representations produced by pretrained transformer encoders without training their weights further. It extracts additional information from how self-supervised objectives respond to each input. The idea is to use the resulting gradients as features alongside the model's ordinary output embedding, expanding what a downstream method can use.

For each input, the method computes gradients from several self-supervised objectives, projects them into fewer dimensions, and concatenates them with the embedding. The authors evaluate these combined features using nearest-neighbor classification on 11 vision datasets, five language datasets, and two audio datasets. Across different backbone sizes and pretraining strategies, the combined features consistently improve on embeddings alone.

The paper also reports benefits for linear classification, clustering, and image retrieval. In retrieval-based in-context scene understanding, FUNGI improves DINO's semantic-segmentation performance by a reported 17% without training. The findings show that a frozen model can supply useful information beyond its standard forward representation: input-specific gradients can enrich the features available for several downstream uses.
summary.tldr: FUNGI augments frozen model embeddings with compressed self-supervised gradients, improving representations without additional training.

title: No Train, all Gain: Self-Supervised Gradients Improve Deep Frozen Representations

abstract: Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is vital for decision makers as it offers insights into the potential reliability of data and model, enabling more informed and risk-aware decision-making. Graphical models, capable of representing data with complex dependencies, are widely used across domains.Existing sampling-based UQ methods are unbiased but cannot guarantee convergence and are time-consuming on large-scale graphs. There are fast UQ methods for graphical models with closed-form solutions and convergence guarantee but with uncertainty underestimation.We propose *LinUProp*, a UQ method that utilizes a novel linear propagation of uncertainty to model uncertainty among related nodes additively instead of multiplicatively, to offer linear scalability, guaranteed convergence, and closed-form solutions without underestimating uncertainty.Theoretically, we decompose the expected prediction error of the graphical model and prove that the uncertainty computed by *LinUProp* is the *generalized variance component* of the decomposition.Experimentally, we demonstrate that *LinUProp* is consistent with the sampling-based method but with linear scalability and fast convergence.Moreover, *LinUProp* outperforms competitors in uncertainty-based active learning on four real-world graph datasets, achieving higher accuracy with a lower labeling budget.

Graphical models, capable of representing data with complex dependencies, are widely used across domains.Existing sampling-based UQ methods are unbiased but cannot guarantee convergence and are time-consuming on large-scale graphs. There are fast UQ methods for graphical models with closed-form solutions and convergence guarantee but with uncertainty underestimation.We propose *LinUProp*, a UQ method that utilizes a novel linear propagation of uncertainty to model uncertainty among related nodes additively instead of multiplicatively, to offer linear scalability, guaranteed convergence, and closed-form solutions without underestimating uncertainty.Theoretically, we decompose the expected prediction error of the graphical model and prove that the uncertainty computed by *LinUProp* is the *generalized variance component* of the decomposition.Experimentally, we demonstrate that *LinUProp* is consistent with the sampling-based method but with linear scalability and fast convergence.Moreover, *LinUProp* outperforms competitors in uncertainty-based active learning on four real-world graph datasets, achieving higher accuracy with a lower labeling budget.

paragraphs: Graphical models describe systems in which variables depend on one another, making uncertainty estimation more complicated than treating each prediction independently. The paper describes a tradeoff in existing methods: sampling-based approaches can be slow and lack convergence guarantees, while faster closed-form alternatives can underestimate uncertainty.

LinUProp changes how uncertainty moves between related nodes. It combines their uncertainty additively rather than multiplicatively, yielding a method with linear scalability, closed-form solutions, and guaranteed convergence without the stated underestimation problem. The authors also decompose expected prediction error and prove that LinUProp computes the generalized variance component of that decomposition, giving its uncertainty estimate a defined mathematical interpretation.

Experiments show agreement with the sampling-based method while retaining fast convergence and linear scalability. The authors further test whether these estimates help decide which examples to label in active learning. Across four real-world graph datasets, LinUProp achieves higher accuracy with a smaller labeling budget than competing methods. This connects the uncertainty calculation to a concrete decision benefit beyond computational efficiency alone.
summary.tldr: LinUProp propagates uncertainty additively across graphs, combining theoretical guarantees with efficient estimation and improved active-learning results.

title: Linear Uncertainty Quantification of Graphical Model Inference

abstract: Motivated by online display advertising, this work considers repeated second-price auctions, where agents sample their value from an unknown distribution with cumulative distribution function $F$. In each auction $t$, a decision-maker bound by limited observations selects $n_t$ agents from a coalition of $N$ to compete for a prize with $p$ other agents, aiming to maximize the cumulative reward of the coalition across all auctions.The problem is framed as an $N$-armed structured bandit, each number of player sent being an arm $n$, with expected reward $r(n)$ fully characterized by $F$ and $p+n$. We present two algorithms, Local-Greedy (LG) and Greedy-Grid (GG), both achieving *constant* problem-dependent regret. This relies on three key ingredients: **1.** an estimator of $r(n)$ from feedback collected from any arm $k$, **2.** concentration bounds of these estimates for $k$ within an estimation neighborhood of $n$ and **3.** the unimodality property of $r$ under standard assumptions on $F$. Additionally, GG exhibits problem-independent guarantees on top of best problem-dependent guarantees. However, by avoiding to rely on confidence intervals, LG practically outperforms GG, as well as standard unimodal bandit algorithms such as OSUB or multi-armed bandit algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies how many members of a coalition should enter each of a sequence of second-price auctions. A decision-maker has limited observations, while agents draw their values from an unknown distribution. The objective is to maximize the coalition’s cumulative reward as its selected members compete with a fixed number of outside agents.

The authors model each possible number of participating coalition members as an arm in a structured bandit problem. Their Local-Greedy and Greedy-Grid algorithms exploit relationships between these choices: feedback from one arm can estimate rewards for others. The analysis combines these estimates, concentration bounds within suitable neighborhoods, and a reward-unimodality property that holds under standard assumptions on the value distribution.

Both algorithms achieve constant problem-dependent regret under the stated framework. Greedy-Grid also has problem-independent guarantees. In practical comparisons, however, Local-Greedy performs better than Greedy-Grid and the tested standard bandit methods, avoiding reliance on confidence intervals. The results distinguish strong theoretical guarantees from observed performance and show how auction structure can make limited feedback useful across participation choices.
summary.tldr: Two structured-bandit algorithms learn coalition participation levels in repeated auctions, achieving constant problem-dependent regret under the stated assumptions.

title: Optimizing the coalition gain in Online Auctions with Greedy Structured Bandits

abstract: Pedestrian pre-collision pose is one of the key factors to determine the degree of pedestrian-vehicle injury in collision. Human pose estimation algorithm is an effective method to estimate pedestrian emergency pose from accident video. However, the pose estimation model trained by the existing daily human pose datasets has poor robustness under specific poses such as pedestrian pre-collision pose, and it is difficult to obtain human pose datasets in the wild scenes, especially lacking scarce data such as pedestrian pre-collision pose in traffic scenes. In this paper, we collect pedestrian-vehicle collision pose from the dashcam perspective of dashcam and construct the first Pedestrian-Vehicle Collision Pose dataset (PVCP) in a semi-automatic way, including 40k+ accident frames and 20K+ pedestrian pre-collision pose annotation (2D, 3D, Mesh). Further, we construct a Pedestrian Pre-collision Pose Estimation Network (PPSENet) to estimate the collision pose and shape sequence of pedestrians from pedestrian-vehicle accident videos. The PPSENet first estimates the 2D pose from the image (Image to Pose, ITP) and then lifts the 2D pose to 3D mesh (Pose to Mesh, PTM). Due to the small size of the dataset, we introduce a pre-training model that learns the human pose prior on a large number of pose datasets, and use iterative regression to estimate the pre-collision pose and shape of pedestrians. Further, we classify the pre-collision pose sequence and introduce pose class loss, which achieves the best accuracy compared with the existing relevant \textit{state-of-the-art} methods. Code and data are available for research at https://github.com/wmj142326/PVCP.

paragraphs: This paper focuses on estimating pedestrian pose and body shape immediately before a vehicle collision. Such poses matter for understanding injury severity, but models trained on everyday human poses are poorly suited to these unusual movements. Relevant real-world training data are also scarce, particularly from traffic scenes.

The authors construct PVCP from dashcam collision footage using a semi-automatic process. It contains more than 40,000 accident frames and over 20,000 pre-collision pose annotations covering 2D, 3D, and mesh representations. They also introduce PPSENet, which first estimates a 2D pose from an image and then converts that pose into a 3D body mesh.

Because the specialized dataset remains small, PPSENet uses a pretrained model that learns pose priors from broader pose datasets, followed by iterative pose and shape regression. The method also classifies pose sequences and adds a pose-class loss. The authors report the best accuracy among the relevant methods compared, supporting their combination of specialized collision data, broader pose knowledge, and sequence classification for this estimation task.
summary.tldr: PVCP and PPSENet support dashcam-based reconstruction of pedestrians' 3D poses and body shapes before collisions.

title: Pedestrian-Centric 3D Pre-collision Pose and Shape Estimation from Dashcam Perspective

abstract: A fundamental problem in quantum many-body physics is that of finding ground states of localHamiltonians. A number of recent works gave provably efficient machine learning (ML) algorithmsfor learning ground states. Specifically, [Huang et al. Science 2022], introduced an approach for learningproperties of the ground state of an $n$-qubit gapped local Hamiltonian $H$ from only $n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$ datapoints sampled from Hamiltonians in the same phase of matter. This was subsequently improvedby [Lewis et al. Nature Communications 2024], to $\mathcal{O}(\log 𝑛)$ samples when the geometry of the $n$-qubit system is known.In this work, we introduce two approaches that achieve a constant sample complexity, independentof system size $n$, for learning ground state properties. Our first algorithm consists of a simplemodification of the ML model used by Lewis et al. and applies to a property of interest known beforehand. Our second algorithm, which applies even if a description ofthe property is not known, is a deep neural network model. While empirical results showing theperformance of neural networks have been demonstrated, to our knowledge, this is the first rigoroussample complexity bound on a neural network model for predicting ground state properties. We also perform numerical experiments that confirm the improved scaling of our approach compared to earlier results.

paragraphs: Predicting properties of quantum ground states is a central problem in many-body physics. The paper builds on learning approaches for gapped local Hamiltonians, where examples come from Hamiltonians in the same phase of matter. Earlier results required sample counts growing polynomially with system size, later reduced to logarithmic growth when system geometry is known.

The authors introduce two approaches whose sample complexity is constant with respect to the number of qubits. The first modifies an earlier machine-learning model and applies when the property to be predicted is specified beforehand. The second uses a deep neural network and also applies when a description of the property is not known.

The neural-network result supplies a rigorous sample-complexity guarantee, which the authors identify as the first of its kind for this prediction problem to their knowledge. Numerical experiments confirm improved scaling relative to earlier results. The central advance concerns how the required number of examples scales with system size: it need not grow with the number of qubits in the setting studied.
summary.tldr: Two learning approaches predict quantum ground-state properties with sample requirements independent of system size, including a rigorously analyzed neural network.

title: Predicting Ground State Properties: Constant Sample Complexity and Deep Learning Algorithms

abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) typically encode an image into a fixed number of visual tokens (e.g., 576) and process these tokens with a language model. Despite their strong performance, LVLMs face challenges in adapting to varying computational constraints. This raises the question: can we achieve flexibility in the number of visual tokens to suit different tasks and computational resources? We answer this with an emphatic yes. Inspired by Matryoshka Representation Learning, we introduce the Matryoshka Query Transformer (MQT), capable of encoding an image into $m$ visual tokens during inference, where $m$ can be any number up to a predefined maximum. This is achieved by employing a query transformer with $M$ latent query tokens to compress the visual embeddings. During each training step, we randomly select $m \leq M$ latent query tokens and train the model using only these first $m$ tokens, discarding the rest.Combining MQT with LLaVA, we train a single model once, and flexibly and drastically reduce the number of inference-time visual tokens while maintaining similar or better performance compared to training independent models for each number of tokens. Our model, MQT-LLaVA, matches LLaVA-1.5 performance across 11 benchmarks using a maximum of 256 tokens instead of LLaVA’s fixed 576. Reducing to 16 tokens (8x less TFLOPs) only sacrifices the performance by 2.4 points on MMBench. On certain tasks such as ScienceQA and MMMU, we can even go down to only 2 visual tokens with performance drops of just 3\% and 6\% each.Our exploration of the trade-off between the accuracy and computational cost brought about by the number of visual tokens facilitates future research to achieve the best of both worlds.

paragraphs: Large vision–language models commonly represent every image with a fixed number of visual tokens, limiting their flexibility when computation budgets change. Matryoshka Query Transformer lets a single trained model use any number of visual tokens up to a chosen maximum. This makes the amount of image information passed to the language model adjustable at inference time.

MQT compresses visual embeddings through a query transformer with a maximum number of latent queries. During training, it randomly chooses a smaller count and uses only that prefix of queries. Repeating this process trains nested token sets, allowing one model to serve different token budgets with similar or better performance than separately trained models.

MQT-LLaVA matches LLaVA-1.5 across 11 benchmarks using at most 256 tokens instead of 576. At 16 tokens, it uses eight times fewer TFLOPs with a 2.4-point MMBench decline. With two tokens, reported performance drops are 3% on ScienceQA and 6% on MMMU. The results demonstrate a task-dependent tradeoff between computation and accuracy.
summary.tldr: MQT trains one vision–language model to work with adjustable visual-token counts, enabling substantial computational savings with task-dependent performance tradeoffs.

title: Matryoshka Query Transformer for Large Vision-Language Models

abstract: The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) has revolutionized text generation, producing outputs that closely mimic human writing. This blurring of lines between machine- and human-written text presents new challenges in distinguishing one from the other – a task further complicated by the frequent updates and closed nature of leading proprietary LLMs. Traditional logits-based detection methods leverage surrogate models for identifying LLM-generated content when the exact logits are unavailable from black-box LLMs. However, these methods grapple with the misalignment between the distributions of the surrogate and the often undisclosed target models, leading to performance degradation, particularly with the introduction of new, closed-source models. Furthermore, while current methodologies are generally effective when the source model is identified, they falter in scenarios where the model version remains unknown, or the test set comprises outputs from various source models. To address these limitations, we present \textbf{D}istribution-\textbf{A}ligned \textbf{L}LMs \textbf{D}etection (DALD), an innovative framework that redefines the state-of-the-art performance in black-box text detection even without logits from source LLMs. DALD is designed to align the surrogate model's distribution with that of unknown target LLMs, ensuring enhanced detection capability and resilience against rapid model iterations with minimal training investment. By leveraging corpus samples from publicly accessible outputs of advanced models such as ChatGPT, GPT-4 and Claude-3, DALD fine-tunes surrogate models to synchronize with unknown source model distributions effectively. Our approach achieves SOTA performance in black-box settings on different advanced closed-source and open-source models. The versatility of our method enriches widely adopted zero-shot detection frameworks (DetectGPT, DNA-GPT, Fast-DetectGPT) with a `plug-and-play' enhancement feature. Extensive experiments validate that our methodology reliably secures high detection precision for LLM-generated text and effectively detects text from diverse model origins through a singular detector.Our method is also robust under the revised text attack and non-English texts.

paragraphs: Detecting machine-written text becomes harder when the generating model hides its internal prediction scores. Existing detectors often substitute scores from an accessible surrogate model. However, differences between the surrogate's text distribution and the source model's distribution can undermine detection, particularly when the source is unknown, changes version, or varies across examples.
