The aim is to make the surrogate's distribution better reflect those of unknown source models without requiring their internal scores. This alignment can be added to existing detection frameworks, including DetectGPT, DNA-GPT, and Fast-DetectGPT.

The authors report state-of-the-art black-box detection performance across evaluated closed-source and open-source models, with a single detector handling text from multiple origins. They also report robustness on revised text and non-English text. These findings support distribution alignment as a way to strengthen existing detection methods while requiring only a modest training investment.
summary.tldr: DALD improves black-box AI-text detection by aligning surrogate models with publicly available outputs from source language models.

title: DALD: Improving Logits-based Detector without Logits from Black-box LLMs

paragraphs: M-natural-concave functions, also called gross substitute valuations, arise in discrete mathematics and economics. This paper studies how to maximize them when their values are initially unknown and must be learned through interaction. It separates settings with stochastic noisy observations from adversarial settings, asking what learning guarantees are computationally achievable in each.

With T queries to an unbiased noisy value oracle, the authors provide stochastic-bandit algorithms with simple regret of order T^(-1/2) and cumulative regret of order T^(2/3). These address the quality of a recommended solution and losses accumulated during learning, respectively. A key technical result shows that greedy maximization remains robust to local errors, supporting optimization from imperfect feedback.

The adversarial result draws a different boundary. Unless P equals NP, no algorithm running in polynomial time per round can guarantee regret of order T^(1−c) for any fixed positive c, even with full-information feedback. The proof reduces a three-matroid intersection problem to this setting, showing that richer feedback alone does not remove the stated computational barrier.
summary.tldr: Stochastic noisy feedback permits provable learning for M-natural-concave maximization, while adversarial learning faces a conditional polynomial-time barrier.

title: No-Regret M${}^{\natural}$-Concave Function Maximization: Stochastic Bandit Algorithms and NP-Hardness of Adversarial Full-Information Setting

abstract: Multi-modal domain generalization (MMDG) requires that models trained on multi-modal source domains can generalize to unseen target distributions with the same modality set. Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) is an effective technique for traditional uni-modal domain generalization (DG), however, with limited improvement in MMDG. In this paper, we identify that modality competition and discrepant uni-modal flatness are two main factors that restrict multi-modal generalization. To overcome these challenges, we propose to construct consistent flat loss regions and enhance knowledge exploitation for each modality via cross-modal knowledge transfer. Firstly, we turn to the optimization on representation-space loss landscapes instead of traditional parameter space, which allows us to build connections between modalities directly. Then, we introduce a novel method to flatten the high-loss region between minima from different modalities by interpolating mixed multi-modal representations. We implement this method by distilling and optimizing generalizable interpolated representations and assigning distinct weights for each modality considering their divergent generalization capabilities. Extensive experiments are performed on two benchmark datasets, EPIC-Kitchens and Human-Animal-Cartoon (HAC), with various modality combinations, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method under multi-source and single-source settings. Our code is open-sourced.

paragraphs: This paper studies models that learn from several modalities and must work on unfamiliar data distributions containing the same modalities. The authors identify two obstacles: modalities compete during learning, and their individual loss landscapes have different degrees of flatness. A technique that improves generalization for a single modality therefore offers only limited gains in this multimodal setting.

The proposed method optimizes the loss landscape over learned representations rather than model parameters. This makes it possible to connect modalities directly by mixing their representations. The method seeks to flatten high-loss regions between minima associated with different modalities, using interpolated representations to support knowledge transfer. It distills and optimizes these representations while assigning different weights to modalities according to their differing generalization capabilities.

Experiments on EPIC-Kitchens and Human-Animal-Cartoon cover multiple modality combinations and both single-source and multiple-source training. The reported results support the effectiveness of this representation-based approach in those settings. Its central contribution is to make cross-modal relationships part of the generalization objective, instead of relying only on flatness measures developed for individual modalities.
summary.tldr: The method improves multimodal generalization by flattening loss regions between modalities through mixed representations and cross-modal knowledge transfer.

title: Cross-modal Representation Flattening for Multi-modal Domain Generalization

abstract: Data is a critical resource for machine learning (ML), yet working with data remains a key friction point. This paper introduces Croissant, a metadata format for datasets that creates a shared representation across ML tools, frameworks, and platforms. Croissant makes datasets more discoverable, portable, and interoperable, thereby addressing significant challenges in ML data management. Croissant is already supported by several popular dataset repositories, spanning hundreds of thousands of datasets, enabling easy loading into the most commonly-used ML frameworks, regardless of where the data is stored. Our initial evaluation by human raters shows that Croissant metadata is readable, understandable, complete, yet concise.

paragraphs: Croissant addresses the practical friction of finding and using datasets across different machine-learning tools. The paper introduces a shared metadata format: a common way to describe datasets so repositories, frameworks, and platforms can work with the same representation. Its contribution concerns the information surrounding a dataset and how that information supports access and use.

A shared description helps make datasets discoverable, portable, and interoperable. These goals connect different parts of the workflow: locating suitable data, moving between tools, and loading data into a framework. The paper reports support from several popular repositories spanning hundreds of thousands of datasets, with loading into commonly used machine-learning frameworks regardless of where the data is stored.

The authors also report an initial human evaluation of the metadata itself. Raters found the descriptions readable, understandable, complete, and concise. That finding matters because the format is intended to serve people as well as software. Together, repository support and the initial evaluation provide evidence for Croissant's practical role as shared infrastructure for dataset use.
summary.tldr: Croissant standardizes dataset metadata to make machine-learning data easier to discover, move between tools, and load.

title: Croissant: A Metadata Format for ML-Ready Datasets

abstract: Multi-distribution or collaborative learning involves learning a single predictor that works well across multiple data distributions, using samples from each during training. Recent research on multi-distribution learning, focusing on binary loss and finite VC dimension classes, has shown near-optimal sample complexity that is achieved with oracle efficient algorithms. That is, these algorithms are computationally efficient given an efficient ERM for the class. Unlike in classical PAC learning, where the optimal sample complexity is achieved with deterministic predictors, current multi-distribution learning algorithms output randomized predictors. This raises the question: can these algorithms be derandomized to produce a deterministic predictor for multiple distributions? Through a reduction to discrepancy minimization, we show that derandomizing multi-distribution learning is computationally hard, even when ERM is computationally efficient. On the positive side, we identify a structural condition enabling an efficient black-box reduction, converting existing randomized multi-distribution predictors into deterministic ones.

paragraphs: Multi-distribution learning seeks a single predictor that performs well across several data distributions, using training samples from each. For binary losses and hypothesis classes with finite VC dimension, existing approaches achieve nearly optimal sample requirements. Their computational efficiency assumes access to an efficient empirical risk minimizer, which finds a good predictor for observed training data.

However, those approaches produce randomized predictors. The paper asks whether their randomness can be removed while retaining useful guarantees across all distributions. This differs from classical PAC learning, where deterministic predictors can already achieve optimal sample complexity. The distinction matters because efficient training does not automatically imply efficient conversion to a deterministic decision rule.

The authors establish a computational barrier through a reduction to discrepancy minimization: derandomization can be hard even when empirical risk minimization is efficient. They also identify a structural condition under which conversion is possible through an efficient black-box procedure. The result separates the general difficulty from a setting where existing randomized predictors can be systematically made deterministic.
summary.tldr: Removing randomness from multi-distribution predictors can be computationally hard, but a structural condition enables efficient conversion.

title: Derandomizing Multi-Distribution Learning

abstract: Due to the exponential growth of agent interactions and the curse of dimensionality, learning efficient coordination from scratch is inherently challenging in large-scale multi-agent systems. While agents' learning is data-driven, sampling from millions of steps, human learning processes are quite different. Inspired by the concept of Human-on-the-Loop and the daily human hierarchical control, we propose a novel knowledge-guided multi-agent reinforcement learning framework (hhk-MARL), which combines human abstract knowledge with hierarchical reinforcement learning to address the learning difficulties among a large number of agents. In this work, fuzzy logic is applied to represent human suboptimal knowledge, and agents are allowed to freely decide how to leverage the proposed prior knowledge. Additionally, a graph-based group controller is built to enhance agent coordination. The proposed framework is end-to-end and compatible with various existing algorithms. We conduct experiments in challenging domains of the StarCraft Multi-agent Challenge combined with three famous algorithms: IQL, QMIX, and Qatten. The results show that our approach can greatly accelerate the training process and improve the final performance, even based on low-performance human prior knowledge.

paragraphs: Learning coordination from scratch becomes difficult as a multiagent system grows, because the number of interactions and the size of the learning problem expand rapidly. This paper asks whether imperfect human knowledge can help agents learn more efficiently. Its hhk-MARL framework combines abstract human guidance with hierarchical reinforcement learning to support coordination among many agents.

The framework represents suboptimal human knowledge through fuzzy logic, allowing guidance to express less rigid rules. Agents retain the ability to decide how to use that prior knowledge. A graph-based group controller provides an additional mechanism for coordinating agents. The overall system is trained end to end and is designed to work with multiple existing reinforcement learning algorithms.

Experiments use challenging StarCraft Multi-agent Challenge settings with IQL, QMIX, and Qatten. The authors report substantially faster training and improved final performance, even when the human prior knowledge performs poorly on its own. This suggests that human guidance can be useful as a resource agents learn to incorporate, without requiring that the supplied knowledge already constitute a strong solution.
summary.tldr: hhk-MARL combines imperfect human guidance, hierarchical learning, and graph-based coordination to improve multiagent training.

title: Integrating Suboptimal Human Knowledge with Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Large-Scale Multiagent Systems

abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is a prevalent approach to align AI systems with human values by learning rewards from human preference data. Due to various reasons, however, such data typically takes the form of rankings over pairs of trajectory segments, which fails to capture the varying strengths of preferences across different pairs. In this paper, we propose a novel adaptive preference loss, underpinned by distributionally robust optimization (DRO), designed to address this uncertainty in preference strength. By incorporating an adaptive scaling parameter into the loss for each pair, our method increases the flexibility of the reward function. Specifically, it assigns small scaling parameters to pairs with ambiguous preferences, leading to more comparable rewards, and large scaling parameters to those with clear preferences for more distinct rewards. Computationally, our proposed loss function is strictly convex and univariate with respect to each scaling parameter, enabling its efficient optimization through a simple second-order algorithm. Our method is versatile and can be readily adapted to various preference optimization frameworks, including direct preference optimization (DPO). Our experiments with robotic control and natural language generation with large language models (LLMs) show that our method not only improves policy performance but also aligns reward function selection more closely with policy optimization, simplifying the hyperparameter tuning process.

paragraphs: Human preference data often says which of two behavior segments is preferred without recording how strongly one is preferred. This leaves reward learning with an important ambiguity: a close choice and an obvious choice can receive the same kind of ranking label. The paper introduces an adaptive preference loss to account for this missing information about preference strength.

The loss is grounded in distributionally robust optimization and assigns a separate scaling parameter to each pair. Ambiguous pairs receive smaller scales, encouraging similar rewards, while clearer preferences receive larger scales, encouraging greater reward separation. For each scaling parameter, the optimization problem is strictly convex and involves only one variable, allowing an efficient second-order optimization procedure.

The method can also be incorporated into other preference optimization frameworks, including direct preference optimization. Experiments in robotic control and language generation report improved policy performance. They also indicate that reward-function selection becomes more closely aligned with policy optimization, simplifying hyperparameter tuning. These findings support treating preference strength as something to adapt during learning rather than assuming that every ranking conveys equally decisive evidence.
summary.tldr: An adaptive preference loss adjusts reward differences to reflect ambiguous versus clear preferences, improving policy learning in robotic control and language-generation experiments.

title: Adaptive Preference Scaling for Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback

abstract: Cognitive processes usually take place at a macroscopic scale in systems characterised by emergent properties, which make the whole ‘more than the sum of its parts.’ While recent proposals have provided quantitative, information-theoretic metrics to detect emergence in time series data, it is often highly non-trivial to identify the relevant macroscopic variables a priori. In this paper we leverage recent advances in representation learning and differentiable information estimators to put forward a data-driven method to find emergent variables. The proposed method successfully detects emergent variables and recovers the ground-truth emergence values in a synthetic dataset. Furthermore, we show the method can be extended to learn multiple independent features, extracting a diverse set of emergent quantities. We finally show that a modified method scales to real experimental data from primate brain activity, paving the ground for future analyses uncovering the emergent structure of cognitive representations in biological and artificial intelligence systems.

paragraphs: Studying emergence in a time series requires choosing variables that describe the system at a larger scale. That choice is difficult when the relevant collective patterns are not known beforehand. Although information-theoretic measures can quantify emergence, researchers still need a way to find the representations to which those measures should be applied.

The paper combines representation learning with differentiable information estimators to discover emergent variables directly from data. This links the search for a useful representation to quantitative information about emergence. The authors also extend the method to learn several independent features, allowing it to extract a varied collection of emergent quantities rather than a single representation.

On synthetic data, the method identifies emergent variables and recovers the known emergence values. A modified version also scales to experimental recordings of primate brain activity. These results establish a route from controlled validation to biological data analysis. The broader prospect is to use learned variables to investigate emergent cognitive structure in biological and artificial systems.
summary.tldr: The method learns diverse emergent variables from time series and is demonstrated on synthetic data and primate brain recordings.

title: Learning diverse causally emergent representations from time series data

abstract: Time series forecasting has attracted significant attention in recent decades. Previous studies have demonstrated that the Channel-Independent (CI) strategy improves forecasting performance by treating different channels individually, while it leads to poor generalization on unseen instances and ignores potentially necessary interactions between channels. Conversely, the Channel-Dependent (CD) strategy mixes all channels with even irrelevant and indiscriminate information, which, however, results in oversmoothing issues and limits forecasting accuracy. There is a lack of channel strategy that effectively balances individual channel treatment for improved forecasting performance without overlooking essential interactions between channels. Motivated by our observation of a correlation between the time series model's performance boost against channel mixing and the intrinsic similarity on a pair of channels, we developed a novel and adaptable \textbf{C}hannel \textbf{C}lustering \textbf{M}odule (CCM). CCM dynamically groups channels characterized by intrinsic similarities and leverages cluster information instead of individual channel identities, combining the best of CD and CI worlds. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that CCM can (1) boost the performance of CI and CD models by an average margin of 2.4% and 7.2% on long-term and short-term forecasting, respectively; (2) enable zero-shot forecasting with mainstream time series forecasting models; (3) uncover intrinsic time series patterns among channels and improve interpretability of complex time series models.

paragraphs: Forecasting several time series together requires deciding which channels should share information. Treating each channel separately can miss useful interactions and generalize poorly to unseen instances. Mixing every channel can introduce irrelevant information and oversmooth the representations. This paper seeks a way to preserve useful relationships without indiscriminately combining all channels.

The authors observe a connection between similarity within a pair of channels and the performance benefit obtained from mixing them. Their Channel Clustering Module dynamically groups channels according to intrinsic similarities. It then uses information about those groups instead of relying on individual channel identities, providing a shared organization for related signals.

Experiments on real-world datasets report average improvements of 2.4% for long-term forecasting and 7.2% for short-term forecasting when enhancing channel-independent and channel-dependent models. The module also enables zero-shot forecasting with mainstream forecasting models. Its clusters reveal patterns shared across channels, offering interpretability alongside the measured forecasting improvements and a more selective approach to information sharing.
summary.tldr: Dynamically clustering similar time-series channels improves forecasting and enables information sharing based on relationships rather than channel identity.

title: From Similarity to Superiority: Channel Clustering for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Semantic correspondence (SC) aims to establish semantically meaningful matches across different instances of an object category. We illustrate how recent supervised SC methods remain limited in their ability to generalize beyond sparsely annotated training keypoints, effectively acting as keypoint detectors. To address this, we propose a novel approach for learning dense correspondences by lifting 2D keypoints into a canonical 3D space using monocular depth estimation. Our method constructs a continuous canonical manifold that captures object geometry without requiring explicit 3D supervision or camera annotations. Additionally, we introduce SPair-U, an extension of SPair-71k with novel keypoint annotations, to better assess generalization. Experiments not only demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms supervised baselines on unseen keypoints, highlighting its effectiveness in learning robust correspondences, but that unsupervised baselines outperform supervised counterparts when generalized across different datasets.

paragraphs: Semantic correspondence finds meaningfully matching locations across different instances of an object category. This paper shows that recent supervised methods can remain tied to the sparse keypoints used for training, behaving effectively as keypoint detectors. Success on familiar annotated locations therefore does not necessarily establish an ability to match other parts of an object.

The proposed method lifts two-dimensional keypoints into a shared canonical three-dimensional space using monocular depth estimation. It constructs a continuous canonical manifold that represents object geometry, without requiring explicit three-dimensional supervision or camera annotations. Separately, unsupervised baselines outperform supervised counterparts in cross-dataset generalization experiments. These findings make the evaluation target central: matching known keypoints, matching unseen locations, and transferring between datasets test different aspects of correspondence learning.
summary.tldr: A canonical 3D representation improves correspondence on unseen keypoints, while new evaluations expose generalization weaknesses in supervised methods.

title: Jamais Vu: Exposing the Generalization Gap in Supervised Semantic Correspondence

abstract: Single-positive multi-label learning (SPMLL) is a weakly supervised multi-label learning problem, where each training example is annotated with only one positive label. Existing SPMLL methods typically assign pseudo-labels to unannotated labels with the assumption that prior probabilities of all classes are identical. However, the class-prior of each category may differ significantly in real-world scenarios, which makes the predictive model not perform as well as expected due to the unrealistic assumption on real-world application. To alleviate this issue, a novel framework named Crisp, i.e., Class-pRiors Induced Single-Positive multi-label learning, is proposed. Specifically, a class-priors estimator is introduced, which can estimate the class-priors that are theoretically guaranteed to converge to the ground-truth class-priors. In addition, based on the estimated class-priors, an unbiased risk estimator for classification is derived, and the corresponding risk minimizer can be guaranteed to approximately converge to the optimal risk minimizer on fully supervised data. Experimental results on ten MLL benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of our method over existing SPMLL approaches.

paragraphs: In single-positive multi-label learning, an example may have several correct labels, but training reveals only one positive label. The remaining labels therefore contain unresolved information. This paper questions a common assumption used when assigning them pseudo-labels: that every category has the same underlying prevalence, even though real categories can occur at very different rates.

The proposed framework, Crisp, estimates these category-specific class priors and uses them to construct the learning objective. The authors provide a theoretical guarantee that their prior estimates converge to the true priors. They also derive an unbiased estimator of classification risk, connecting the estimated label frequencies to the quantity that the model is trained to minimize.

The corresponding risk minimizer is guaranteed to approximately converge to the optimal minimizer available with fully supervised data. That is an approximate convergence claim, rather than a promise of identical predictions with limited annotations. Experiments across ten multi-label benchmarks report improvements over existing single-positive methods, supporting the value of explicitly accounting for unequal class frequencies.
summary.tldr: Crisp estimates unequal class frequencies to improve learning when each training example has only one observed positive label.

title: Can Class-Priors Help Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning?

abstract: With increasingly powerful large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents tackling an ever-growing list of tasks, we envision a future where numerous LLM agents work seamlessly with other AI agents and humans to solve complex problems and enhance daily life. To achieve these goals, LLM agents must develop collaborative skills such as effective persuasion, assertion and disagreement, which are often overlooked in the prevalent single-turn training and evaluation of LLMs. In this work, we present Collaborative Reasoner (Coral), a framework to evaluate and improve the collaborative reasoning abilities of language models. In particular, tasks and metrics in Coral necessitate agents to disagree with incorrect solutions, convince their partners of a correct solution, and ultimately agree as a team to commit to a final solution, all through a natural multi-turn conversation. Through comprehensive evaluation on six collaborative reasoning tasks covering domains of coding, math, scientific QA and social reasoning, we show that current models cannot effectively collaborate due to undesirable social behaviors, collapsing even on problems that they can solve singlehandedly. To improve the collaborative reasoning capabilities of LLMs, we propose a self-play method to generate synthetic multi-turn preference data and further train the language models to be better collaborators. Experiments with Llama-3.1, Ministral and Qwen-2.5 models show that our proposed self-improvement approach consistently outperforms finetuned chain-of-thought performance of the same base model, yielding gains up to 16.7% absolute. Human evaluations show that the models exhibit more effective disagreement and produce more natural conversations after training on our synthetic interaction data.

paragraphs: Solving a problem alone and reaching a correct answer through discussion require different skills. A useful collaborator must challenge mistakes, explain why a solution is right, and eventually commit to a shared answer. Collaborative Reasoner, or Coral, evaluates these abilities through multi-turn conversations instead of measuring only an individual model's response.

The framework includes six collaborative reasoning tasks spanning coding, mathematics, scientific questions, and social reasoning. Its evaluations find that undesirable social behaviors can make current models fail together even on problems they can solve independently. To improve collaboration, the authors use self-play to generate synthetic conversations with preference information, then train models on that interaction data.

Experiments with Llama-3.1, Ministral, and Qwen-2.5 show consistent improvements over chain-of-thought fine-tuning of the same base models, with gains reaching 16.7 percentage points. Human evaluations also find more effective disagreement and more natural dialogue after training. The results indicate that conversational collaboration benefits from dedicated training objectives: individual reasoning competence does not by itself ensure that a group will use its members' knowledge effectively.
summary.tldr: Coral uses self-play conversations to train models to disagree constructively, persuade partners, and reach better joint solutions.

title: Collaborative Reasoner: Self-Improving Social Agents with Synthetic Conversations

abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promise for end-to-end autonomous driving by leveraging world knowledge and reasoning capabilities. However, current VLA models often struggle with physically infeasible action outputs, complex model structures, or unnecessarily long reasoning. In this paper, we propose AutoVLA, a novel VLA model that unifies reasoning and action generation within a single autoregressive generation model for end-to-end autonomous driving. AutoVLA performs semantic reasoning and trajectory planning directly from raw visual inputs and language instructions. We tokenize continuous trajectories into discrete, feasible actions, enabling direct integration into the language model. For training, we employ supervised fine-tuning to equip the model with dual thinking modes: fast thinking (trajectory-only) and slow thinking (enhanced with chain-of-thought reasoning). To further enhance planning performance and efficiency, we introduce a reinforcement fine-tuning method based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), reducing unnecessary reasoning in straightforward scenarios. Extensive experiments across real-world and simulated datasets and benchmarks, including nuPlan, nuScenes, Waymo, and CARLA, demonstrate the competitive performance of AutoVLA in both open-loop and closed-loop settings. Qualitative results showcase the adaptive reasoning and accurate planning capabilities of AutoVLA in diverse scenarios.

paragraphs: AutoVLA addresses three difficulties in vision-language-action driving models: physically infeasible outputs, complicated architectures, and excessive reasoning. It combines semantic reasoning and trajectory planning in one autoregressive model that takes raw visual inputs and language instructions. Continuous trajectories are represented as discrete, feasible action tokens, allowing driving actions to fit directly into the language model's generation process.

Supervised fine-tuning teaches two operating modes. Fast thinking produces a trajectory alone, while slow thinking includes chain-of-thought reasoning. A subsequent reinforcement fine-tuning stage uses Group Relative Policy Optimization to improve planning and efficiency, including reducing unnecessary reasoning in straightforward situations. The training design makes the amount of reasoning part of the model's adaptive behavior.

Experiments across nuPlan, nuScenes, Waymo, and CARLA demonstrate competitive results in both open-loop and closed-loop evaluation. Qualitative examples also show adaptive reasoning and accurate planning across varied scenarios. These findings support combining action generation and selective reasoning within one driving model; the reported outcome is competitive benchmark performance rather than a universal claim about driving reliability.
summary.tldr: AutoVLA combines driving actions and adaptive reasoning in one model, using reinforcement fine-tuning to reduce unnecessary deliberation.

title: AutoVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Adaptive Reasoning and Reinforcement Fine-Tuning

abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence technologies, the demand for training data has surged, exacerbating risks of data leakage. Despite increasing incidents and costs associated with such leaks, data leakage prevention (DLP) technologies lag behind evolving evasion techniques that bypass existing sensitive information recognition (SIR) models. Current datasets lack comprehensive coverage of these adversarial transformations, limiting the evaluation of robust SIR systems. To address this gap, we introduce DataSIR, a benchmark dataset specifically designed to evaluate SIR models on sensitive data subjected to diverse format transformations. We curate 26 sensitive data categories based on multiple international regulations, and collect 131,890 original samples correspondingly. Through empirical analysis of real-world evasion tactics, we implement 21 format transformation methods, which are applied to the original samples, expanding the dataset to 1,647,501 samples to simulate adversarial scenarios. We evaluated DataSIR using four traditional NLP models and four large language models (LLMs). For LLMs, we design structured prompts with varying degrees of contextual hints to assess the impact of prior knowledge on recognition accuracy. These evaluations demonstrate that our dataset effectively differentiates the performance of various SIR algorithms. Combined with its rich category and format diversity, the dataset can serve as a benchmark for evaluating related models and help develop future more advanced SIR models. Our dataset and experimental code are publicly available at https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/fanmo1/datasir and https://github.com/Fan-Mo-ZJU/DataSIR.

paragraphs: Sensitive information recognition systems must detect protected data even when its formatting has been altered to evade detection. The authors argue that existing datasets do not adequately cover these transformations, making it difficult to assess robustness. DataSIR supplies a benchmark focused specifically on recognition under diverse changes to data format.

The dataset starts with 131,890 original samples spanning 26 sensitive data categories drawn from multiple international regulations. Based on an empirical analysis of real-world evasion tactics, the authors implement 21 transformation methods. Applying these methods expands the collection to 1,647,501 samples, providing a much broader set of adversarial formatting scenarios for evaluation.

The authors evaluate four traditional natural language processing models and four large language models. For the latter, structured prompts vary the amount of contextual guidance to examine how prior knowledge affects recognition accuracy. Results show that DataSIR distinguishes performance among recognition algorithms. Its contribution is a shared evaluation resource for comparing systems across sensitive categories and transformed formats.
summary.tldr: DataSIR tests sensitive information recognition using more than 1.6 million examples covering adversarial format transformations.

title: DataSIR: A Benchmark Dataset for Sensitive Information Recognition

abstract: Ultra-high dynamic range (UHDR) scenes exhibit pronounced exposure disparities between bright and dark regions. Such conditions are Ultra-high dynamic range (UHDR) scenes exhibit significant exposure disparities between bright and dark regions. Such conditions are commonly encountered in nighttime scenes with light sources. Even with standard exposure settings, a bimodal intensity distribution with boundary peaks often emerges, making it difficult to preserve both highlight and shadow details simultaneously. RGB-based bracketing methods can capture details at both ends using short-long exposure pairs, but are susceptible to misalignment and ghosting artifacts. We found that a short-exposure image already retains sufficient highlight detail. The main challenge of UHDR reconstruction lies in denoising and recovering information in dark regions. In comparison to the RGB images, RAW images, thanks to their higher bit depth and more predictable noise characteristics, offer greater potential for addressing this challenge. This raises a key question: can we learn to see everything in UHDR scenes using only a single short-exposure RAW image? In this study, we rely solely on a single short-exposure frame, which inherently avoids ghosting and motion blur, making it particularly robust in dynamic scenes. To achieve that, we introduce UltraLED, a two-stage framework that performs exposure correction via a ratio map to balance dynamic range, followed by a brightness-aware RAW denoiser to enhance detail recovery in dark regions. To support this setting, we design a 9-stop bracketing pipeline to synthesize realistic UHDR images and contribute a corresponding dataset based on diverse scenes, using only the shortest exposure as input for reconstruction. Extensive experiments show that UltraLED significantly outperforms existing single-frame approaches. Our code and dataset are made publicly available at https://srameo.github.io/projects/ultraled.

paragraphs: UltraLED reconstructs scenes containing extremely bright and dark regions from a single short-exposure RAW image. Combining short and long exposures can preserve both ends of the brightness range, but moving content can cause misalignment and ghosting. The paper observes that short exposures already retain useful highlight detail, making recovery of dark regions the main challenge.

The method uses RAW data because its higher bit depth and more predictable noise offer greater potential for this recovery. Its first stage corrects exposure through a ratio map that balances the dynamic range. A second, brightness-aware RAW denoiser then targets detail recovery in dark regions. Relying on one short exposure avoids the need to align separate input frames.

The authors also develop a nine-stop exposure-bracketing pipeline to synthesize realistic ultra-high-dynamic-range images and construct a dataset spanning diverse scenes. Reconstruction uses only the shortest exposure as input. Experiments show significant improvements over existing single-frame approaches, supporting the combination of exposure correction and brightness-aware denoising for recovering detail from this constrained input.
summary.tldr: UltraLED recovers bright and dark scene detail from one short-exposure RAW image using exposure correction followed by brightness-aware denoising.

title: UltraLED: Learning to See Everything in Ultra-High Dynamic Range Scenes

abstract: Recent years have revealed an unprecedented demand for AI-based technology, leading to a common setting where immense data is distributed across multiple locations. This creates a communication bottleneck among the storage facilities, often aiming to jointly solve tasks of small solution size $k$ from input of astronomically large size $n$. Motivated by federated and distributed machine learning applications, we study two fundamental optimization problems, maximum weight matroid independent set (MW-IS) and maximum weight matching (MWM), in a zero communication computational model. In this model, the data is dispersed between $m$ servers. Without any communication, each server has to send a message to a central server, which is required to compute an optimal solution for the original (large) instance. The goal is to minimize the size of the maximum message sent. For this natural restrictive model, we obtain deterministic algorithms that use $k$-data per server for MW-IS and $O(k^2)$-data per server for MWM, where $k$ is the solution size. We complement these results with tight lower bounds -- ruling out any asymptotic improvement even if randomization is allowed. Our algorithms are simple and run in nearly linear time. Interestingly, we show how our zero communication algorithms yield deterministic parallel algorithms with running times $O\left(\sqrt{k} \cdot \log n\right)$ and $O\left(k^4 \cdot \log n\right)$ for MW-IS and MWM, respectively.

paragraphs: Large distributed datasets can overwhelm communication channels even when the desired solution is small. This paper studies a setting where servers cannot coordinate with each other and each sends one summary to a central server, which must recover an optimal global solution.

For maximum-weight matroid independent set, deterministic algorithms need k data items per server; for maximum-weight matching, they need O(k²), where k is solution size. Matching lower bounds rule out asymptotic improvement even with randomization, and the algorithms run in nearly linear time.

The constructions also yield deterministic parallel algorithms with running times O(sqrt(k) log(n)) and O(k⁴ log(n)), respectively. The phrase zero communication refers to no interserver coordination before the summaries, not to sending no information at all. The result precisely characterizes the local summary size required for these two global optimization tasks.
summary.tldr: Small independent server messages suffice for exact matroid and matching optimization, with tight size bounds.

title: Tight Bounds for Maximum Weight Matroid Independent Set and Matching in the Zero Communication Model

abstract: Operating rooms (ORs) demand precise coordination among surgeons, nurses, and equipment in a fast-paced, occlusion-heavy environment, necessitating advanced perception models to enhance safety and efficiency. Existing datasets either provide partial egocentric views or sparse exocentric multi-view context, but do not explore the comprehensive combination of both. We introduce EgoExOR, the first OR dataset and accompanying benchmark to fuse first-person and third-person perspectives. Spanning 94 minutes (84,553 frames at 15 FPS) of two emulated spine procedures, Ultrasound-Guided Needle Insertion and Minimally Invasive Spine Surgery, EgoExOR integrates egocentric data (RGB, gaze, hand tracking, audio) from wearable glasses, exocentric RGB and depth from RGB-D cameras, and ultrasound imagery. Its detailed scene graph annotations, covering 36 entities and 22 relations (568,235 triplets), enable robust modeling of clinical interactions, supporting tasks like action recognition and human-centric perception. We evaluate the surgical scene graph generation performance of two adapted state-of-the-art models and offer a new baseline that explicitly leverages EgoExOR’s multimodal and multi-perspective signals. This new dataset and benchmark set a new foundation for OR perception, offering a rich, multimodal resource for next-generation clinical perception. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ardamamur/EgoExOR.

paragraphs: Understanding activity in an operating room requires following interactions among people and equipment despite frequent visual obstruction. EgoExOR combines first-person recordings with third-person views to provide complementary perspectives on those interactions. The dataset is designed to support surgical activity understanding and human-centered perception through a richer combination of views and sensor signals.

Its recordings cover 94 minutes of two emulated spine procedures: ultrasound-guided needle insertion and minimally invasive spine surgery. Wearable glasses supply RGB video, gaze, hand tracking, and audio, while external cameras provide RGB and depth; ultrasound imagery is also included. Scene graph annotations describe entities and their relationships, covering 36 entities, 22 relation types, and 568,235 annotated triplets.

The paper evaluates two adapted models for surgical scene graph generation and introduces a baseline that explicitly uses the dataset's multiple modalities and perspectives. Its main contribution is therefore both a resource and an evaluation setting for modeling clinical interactions. The recordings come from two emulated procedures, which defines the concrete procedural setting represented by the dataset rather than a broad collection of operating-room cases.
summary.tldr: EgoExOR combines wearable and external sensor views with detailed interaction annotations for studying activity in two emulated surgical procedures.

title: EgoExOR: An Ego-Exo-Centric Operating Room Dataset for Surgical Activity Understanding

abstract: AI agents are rapidly being deployed across diverse industries, but can they adhere to deployment policies under attacks? We organized a one-month red teaming challenge---the largest of its kind to date---involving expert red teamers attempting to elicit policy violations from AI agents powered by $22$ frontier LLMs. Our challenge collected $1.8$ million prompt injection attacks, resulting in over $60,000$ documented successful policy violations, revealing critical vulnerabilities. Utilizing this extensive data, we construct a challenging AI agent red teaming benchmark, currently achieving near $100\%$ attack success rates across all tested agents and associated policies. Our further analysis reveals high transferability and universality of successful attacks, underscoring the scale and criticality of existing AI agent vulnerabilities. We also observe minimal correlation between agent robustness and factors such as model capability, size, or inference compute budget, highlighting the necessity of substantial improvements in defense. We hope our benchmark and insights drive further research toward more secure and reliable AI agents.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether deployed AI agents follow their policies when people deliberately try to make them violate those policies. The authors organized a month-long public red-teaming competition involving agents powered by 22 frontier language models. The challenge collected 1.8 million prompt-injection attacks and documented more than 60,000 successful policy violations.

Using this collection, the authors construct a demanding benchmark for evaluating agent security. They report attack success rates near 100% across the agents and associated policies tested on that benchmark. This result concerns the benchmark assembled from the competition data; it is distinct from the proportion of successful attacks among all competition submissions. Their analysis also finds that successful attacks often transfer and apply broadly across tested settings.

The study observes little correlation between robustness and model capability, model size, or inference compute budget. Within this evaluation, those attributes therefore provide limited guidance about resistance to attacks. The benchmark and analysis expose substantial deployment-policy vulnerabilities and provide evidence for the need to improve agent defenses.
summary.tldr: A large public attack competition exposes widespread agent policy violations and yields a benchmark with near-total attack success across the tested agents and policies.

title: Security Challenges in AI Agent Deployment: Insights from a Large Scale Public Competition

abstract: Human-like agents have long been one of the goals in pursuing artificial intelligence. Although reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved superhuman performance in many domains, relatively little attention has been focused on designing human-like RL agents. As a result, many reward-driven RL agents often exhibit unnatural behaviors compared to humans, raising concerns for both interpretability and trustworthiness. To achieve human-like behavior in RL, this paper first formulates human-likeness as trajectory optimization, where the objective is to find an action sequence that closely aligns with human behavior while also maximizing rewards, and adapts the classic receding-horizon control to human-like learning as a tractable and efficient implementation. To achieve this, we introduce Macro Action Quantization (MAQ), a human-like RL framework that distills human demonstrations into macro actions via Vector-Quantized VAE. Experiments on D4RL Adroit benchmarks show that MAQ significantly improves human-likeness, increasing trajectory similarity scores, and achieving the highest human-likeness rankings among all RL agents in the human evaluation study. Our results also demonstrate that MAQ can be easily integrated into various off-the-shelf RL algorithms, opening a promising direction for learning human-like RL agents. Our code is available at https://rlg.iis.sinica.edu.tw/papers/MAQ.

paragraphs: An agent can earn high rewards while moving or acting in ways people find unnatural. This paper makes resemblance to human behavior an explicit part of reinforcement learning. It formulates the problem as choosing action sequences that both align with human trajectories and maximize reward, bringing behavioral style into the optimization objective.

The proposed Macro Action Quantization framework learns macro actions from human demonstrations using a vector-quantized variational autoencoder. These learned action units carry patterns from demonstrated behavior into the agent’s available choices. The framework also adapts receding-horizon control to make the trajectory-based objective tractable and efficient to implement.

On D4RL Adroit benchmarks, MAQ improves trajectory similarity scores and receives the highest human-likeness rankings among the RL agents included in a human evaluation. The authors also demonstrate integration with several existing RL algorithms. These findings support using demonstration-derived macro actions to encourage recognizable human behavior while retaining reward maximization as part of the learning problem.
summary.tldr: MAQ learns macro actions from human demonstrations to help reinforcement-learning agents optimize reward while behaving more like humans.

title: Learning Human-Like RL Agents Through Trajectory Optimization With Action Quantization

abstract: We introduce Time-Conditioned Contraction Matching (TCCM), a novel method for semi-supervised anomaly detection in tabular data. TCCM is inspired by flow matching, a recent generative modeling framework that learns velocity fields between probability distributions and has shown strong performance compared to diffusion models and generative adversarial networks. Instead of directly applying flow matching as originally formulated, TCCM builds on its core idea—learning velocity fields between distributions—but simplifies the framework by predicting a time-conditioned contraction vector toward a fixed target (the origin) at each sampled time step. This design offers three key advantages: (1) a lightweight and scalable training objective that removes the need for solving ordinary differential equations during training and inference; (2) an efficient scoring strategy called one time-step deviation, which quantifies deviation from expected contraction behavior in a single forward pass, addressing the inference bottleneck of existing continuous-time models such as DTE (a diffusion-based model with leading anomaly detection accuracy but heavy inference cost); and (3) explainability and provable robustness, as the learned velocity field operates directly in input space, making the anomaly score inherently feature-wise attributable; moreover, the score function is Lipschitz-continuous with respect to the input, providing theoretical guarantees under small perturbations. Extensive experiments on the ADBench benchmark show that TCCM strikes a favorable balance between detection accuracy and inference cost, outperforming state-of-the-art methods—especially on high-dimensional and large-scale datasets. The source code is provided at https://github.com/ZhongLIFR/TCCM-NIPS.

paragraphs: Time-Conditioned Contraction Matching, or TCCM, detects anomalies in tabular data using a simplified idea from flow matching. Instead of learning a general flow between distributions, it predicts a time-dependent vector that contracts an input toward the origin. This gives the model a specific expected behavior against which unusual examples can be evaluated.

Its anomaly score measures deviation from that expected contraction at one time step. Scoring needs a single forward pass, and neither training nor inference requires solving ordinary differential equations. Because the learned vector field operates directly on input features, the score can be attributed feature by feature. The authors also establish Lipschitz continuity of the score, providing a theoretical stability guarantee under small input perturbations.

Experiments on ADBench report a favorable balance between detection accuracy and inference cost, with improvements over state-of-the-art methods especially on large and high-dimensional datasets. The contribution links efficient scoring, feature-level explanations, and a formal perturbation guarantee within one design. Its robustness claim concerns the score's behavior under small changes to the input.
summary.tldr: TCCM detects tabular anomalies in one forward pass using contraction deviations, with feature-level attribution and small-perturbation stability guarantees.

title: Scalable, Explainable and Provably Robust Anomaly Detection with One-Step Flow Matching

abstract: The application of machine learning (ML) to electroencephalography (EEG) has great potential to advance both neuroscientific research and clinical applications. However, the generalisability and robustness of EEG-based ML models often hinge on the amount and diversity of training data. It is common practice to split EEG recordings into small segments, thereby increasing the number of samples substantially compared to the number of individual recordings or participants. We conceptualise this as a multi-level data generation process and investigate the scaling behaviour of model performance with respect to the overall sample size and the participant diversity through large-scale empirical studies. We then use the same framework to investigate the effectiveness of different ML strategies designed to address limited data problems: data augmentations and self-supervised learning. Our findings show that model performance scaling can be severely constrained by participant distribution shifts and provide actionable guidance for data collection and ML research. The code for our experiments is publicly available online.

paragraphs: An EEG dataset can contain many training samples while representing relatively few people. Researchers commonly divide recordings into short segments, greatly increasing the sample count without adding participants. This paper asks how that distinction affects the ability of machine learning models to improve with more data and generalize across people.

The authors describe EEG data through a multilevel generation process that distinguishes samples from the recordings and participants behind them. Large-scale empirical studies then examine performance scaling with both total sample size and participant diversity. The same framework is used to study data augmentation and self-supervised learning, two strategies intended to help when data are limited.

The findings show that shifts in the participant distribution can severely constrain performance scaling. Consequently, a growing number of segments need not remove the difficulties associated with transferring a model across participant populations. The paper's contribution is a framework for separating these sources of data growth and examining their consequences, providing guidance for EEG data collection and research on learning from limited data.
summary.tldr: The study shows that participant distribution shifts can severely limit EEG model improvements even as the number of segmented training samples grows.

title: Is Limited Participant Diversity Impeding EEG-based Machine Learning?

abstract: Quantized training of Large Language Models (LLMs) remains an open challenge, as maintaining accuracy while performing all matrix multiplications in low precision has proven difficult. This is particularly the case when fine-tuning pre-trained models, which can have large weight, activation, and error (output gradient) outlier values that make lower-precision optimization difficult. To address this, we present HALO, a new quantization-aware training approach for Transformers that enables accurate and efficient low-precision training by combining 1) strategic placement of Hadamard rotations in both forward and backward passes, which mitigate outliers, 2) high-performance kernel support, and 3) FSDP integration for low-precision communication. Our approach ensures that all large matrix multiplications during the forward and backward passes are executed in lower precision. Applied to LLaMa models, HALO achieves near-full-precision-equivalent results during fine-tuning on various tasks, while delivering up to 1.41x end-to-end speedup for full fine-tuning on RTX 4090 GPUs. HALO efficiently supports both standard and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). Our results demonstrate the first practical approach to fully quantized LLM fine-tuning that maintains accuracy in INT8 and FP6 precision, while delivering performance benefits.

abstract: Time-resolved single-cell omics data offers high-throughput, genome-wide measurements of cellular states, which are instrumental to reverse-engineer the processes underpinning cell fate. Such technologies are inherently destructive, allowing only cross-sectional measurements of the underlying stochastic dynamical system. Furthermore, cells may divide or die in addition to changing their molecular state. Collectively these present a major challenge to inferring realistic biophysical models. We present a novel approach, unbalanced probability flow inference, that addresses this challenge for biological processes modelled as stochastic dynamics with growth. By leveraging a Lagrangian formulation of the Fokker-Planck equation, our method accurately disentangles drift from intrinsic noise and growth. We showcase the applicability of our approach through evaluation on a range of simulated and real single-cell RNA-seq datasets. Comparing to several existing methods, we find our method achieves higher accuracy while enjoying a simple two-step training scheme.

paragraphs: Single-cell measurements can reveal molecular states at different times, but the measurement process destroys the cells. Researchers therefore observe successive population snapshots rather than following the same cells continuously. Inferring how cells change is further complicated by division and death, which alter the population as molecular states evolve.

The paper introduces unbalanced probability flow inference for processes modeled as stochastic dynamics with growth. It uses a Lagrangian formulation of the Fokker–Planck equation to separate three contributions: systematic changes in state, intrinsic randomness, and population growth. Distinguishing these contributions matters because a changing population distribution can reflect several different underlying processes, rather than cellular state changes alone.

The authors evaluate the approach on simulated data and real single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets. They report more accurate inference than several existing methods, together with a simple two-step training procedure. The contribution is a way to recover richer dynamical descriptions from destructive snapshots while explicitly accounting for the changing number of cells.
summary.tldr: Unbalanced probability flow inference separates cellular drift, randomness, and growth when learning dynamics from destructive population snapshots.

title: Inferring stochastic dynamics with growth from cross-sectional data

abstract: The real world is dynamic, yet most image fusion methods process static frames independently, ignoring temporal correlations in videos and leading to flickering and temporal inconsistency. To address this, we propose Unified Video Fusion (UniVF), a novel and unified framework for video fusion that leverages multi-frame learning and optical flow-based feature warping for informative, temporally coherent video fusion. To support its development, we also introduce Video Fusion Benchmark (VF-Bench), the first comprehensive benchmark covering four video fusion tasks: multi-exposure, multi-focus, infrared-visible, and medical fusion. VF-Bench provides high-quality, well-aligned video pairs obtained through synthetic data generation and rigorous curation from existing datasets, with a unified evaluation protocol that jointly assesses the spatial quality and temporal consistency of video fusion. Extensive experiments show that UniVF achieves state-of-the-art results across all tasks on VF-Bench. Project page: [vfbench.github.io](https://vfbench.github.io).

paragraphs: Video fusion combines complementary visual information into a single video. Processing each frame independently can produce individually useful images whose appearance changes inconsistently over time. This paper addresses that mismatch with UniVF, a framework that explicitly uses neighboring frames to produce informative fused videos with greater temporal coherence.

UniVF combines multi-frame learning with optical flow-based feature warping. Optical flow supplies motion information so that features from different frames can be brought into correspondence. This makes temporal relationships part of the fusion process, rather than treating the video as a collection of unrelated images. The approach targets both the information retained within frames and the consistency between them.

The paper also introduces VF-Bench, covering multi-exposure, multi-focus, infrared-visible, and medical video fusion. Its aligned video pairs come from synthetic generation and curated existing datasets. A shared evaluation protocol measures spatial quality alongside temporal consistency. The authors report state-of-the-art results across all four tasks on this benchmark, supporting the value of evaluating and learning video fusion as a temporal problem.
summary.tldr: UniVF combines motion-aware multi-frame learning with a four-task benchmark to improve video fusion quality and temporal consistency.

title: A Unified Solution to Video Fusion: From Multi-Frame Learning to Benchmarking

abstract: Recent work on latent diffusion models (LDMs) has focused almost exclusively on generative tasks, leaving their potential for discriminative transfer largely unexplored. We introduce Discriminative Vicinity Diffusion (DVD), a novel LDM-based framework for a more practical variant of source-free domain adaptation (SFDA): the source provider may share not only a pre-trained classifier but also an auxiliary latent diffusion module, trained once on the source data and never exposing raw source samples. DVD encodes each source feature’s label information into its latent vicinity by fitting a Gaussian prior over its k-nearest neighbors and training the diffusion network to drift noisy samples back to label-consistent representations. During adaptation, we sample from each target feature’s latent vicinity, apply the frozen diffusion module to generate source-like cues, and use a simple InfoNCE loss to align the target encoder to these cues, explicitly transferring decision boundaries without source access. Across standard SFDA benchmarks, DVD outperforms state-of-the-art methods. We further show that the same latent diffusion module enhances the source classifier’s accuracy on in-domain data and boosts performance in supervised classification and domain generalization experiments. DVD thus reinterprets LDMs as practical, privacy-preserving bridges for explicit knowledge transfer, addressing a core challenge in source-free domain adaptation that prior methods have yet to solve. Code is available on our Github: https://github.com/JingWang18/DVD-SFDA.

The same diffusion module also improves source-domain classifier accuracy and performance in supervised classification and domain generalization experiments. Its adaptation setting specifically permits that additional module alongside the classifier.
summary.tldr: DVD uses a shared, frozen latent diffusion module to transfer source decision-boundary information without accessing raw source samples.

title: Vicinity-Guided Discriminative Latent Diffusion for Privacy-Preserving Domain Adaptation

abstract: This work establishes that sparse Bayesian neural networks achieve optimal posterior contraction rates over anisotropic Besov spaces and their hierarchical compositions. These structures reflect the intrinsic dimensionality of the underlying function, thereby mitigating the curse of dimensionality. Our analysis shows that Bayesian neural networks equipped with either sparse or continuous shrinkage priors attain the optimal rates which are dependent on the intrinsic dimension of the true structures. Moreover, we show that these priors enable rate adaptation, allowing the posterior to contract at the optimal rate even when the smoothness level of the true function is unknown. The proposed framework accommodates a broad class of functions, including additive and multiplicative Besov functions as special cases. These results advance the theoretical foundations of Bayesian neural networks and provide rigorous justification for their practical effectiveness in high-dimensional, structured estimation problems.

paragraphs: This paper provides theoretical guarantees for how quickly a Bayesian neural network's posterior concentrates around a true function as data accumulate. It studies anisotropic Besov spaces, which allow function regularity to differ across directions, and hierarchical compositions of such functions. These structures can have a lower intrinsic dimension than the full input dimension suggests.

The authors show that networks using either sparse priors or continuous shrinkage priors attain optimal posterior contraction rates for the studied function classes. The rates depend on the intrinsic dimension of the underlying structure, helping mitigate the curse of dimensionality. The priors also support adaptation: the optimal rate can be attained even when the true function's smoothness is unknown.

The framework includes additive and multiplicative Besov functions as special cases, covering multiple forms of structured dependence. Its contribution is a mathematical explanation of how Bayesian neural networks can exploit structure in high-dimensional estimation. The guarantee concerns the specified function classes and priors, linking statistical accuracy to intrinsic complexity and unknown smoothness rather than treating all high-dimensional functions as equally difficult.
summary.tldr: Sparse Bayesian neural networks achieve optimal, smoothness-adaptive posterior contraction rates governed by intrinsic dimension for the studied Besov function classes.

title: Posterior Contraction for Sparse Neural Networks in Besov Spaces with Intrinsic Dimensionality

abstract: This paper introduces the Real-DRL framework for safety-critical autonomous systems, enabling runtime learning of a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agent to develop safe and high-performance action policies in real plants while prioritizing safety. The Real-DRL consists of three interactive components: a DRL-Student, a PHY-Teacher, and a Trigger. The DRL-Student is a DRL agent that innovates in the dual self-learning and teaching-to-learn paradigm and the safety-status-dependent batch sampling. On the other hand, PHY-Teacher is a physics-model-based design of action policies that focuses solely on safety-critical functions. PHY-Teacher is novel in its real-time patch for two key missions: i) fostering the teaching-to-learn paradigm for DRL-Student and ii) backing up the safety of real plants. The Trigger manages the interaction between the DRL-Student and the PHY-Teacher. Powered by the three interactive components, the Real-DRL can effectively address safety challenges that arise from the unknown unknowns and the Sim2Real gap. Additionally, Real-DRL notably features i) assured safety, ii) automatic hierarchy learning (i.e., safety-first learning and then high-performance learning), and iii) safety-informed batch sampling to address the experience imbalance caused by corner cases. Experiments with a real quadruped robot, a quadruped robot in Nvidia Isaac Gym, and a cart-pole system, along with comparisons and ablation studies, demonstrate the Real-DRL's effectiveness and unique features.

Experiments include a physical quadruped, a quadruped in Nvidia Isaac Gym, and a cart-pole system, alongside comparisons and ablations. These evaluations support the effectiveness of coordinating physics-based safety actions with a student that continues learning at runtime.
summary.tldr: Real-DRL coordinates a learning agent, physics-based safety teacher, and trigger to support safety-first policy learning during operation.

title: Real-DRL: Teach and Learn at Runtime

abstract: We propose the first framework capable of computing a 4D spatio-temporal grid of video frames and 3D Gaussian particles for each time step using a feed-forward architecture. Our architecture has two main components, a 4D video model and a 4D reconstruction model. In the first part, we analyze current 4D video diffusion architectures that perform spatial and temporal attention either sequentially or in parallel within a two-stream design. We highlight the limitations of existing approaches and introduce a novel fused architecture that performs spatial and temporal attention within a single layer. The key to our method is a sparse attention pattern, where tokens attend to others in the same frame, at the same timestamp, or from the same viewpoint. In the second part, we extend existing 3D reconstruction algorithms by introducing a Gaussian head, a camera token replacement algorithm, and additional dynamic layers and training. Overall, we establish a new state of the art for 4D generation, improving both visual quality and reconstruction capability.

In the second part, we extend existing 3D reconstruction algorithms by introducing a Gaussian head, a camera token replacement algorithm, and additional dynamic layers and training. paragraphs: Generating a dynamic 3D scene requires coordinating its appearance across both viewpoints and time. This paper presents a framework that produces a grid of video frames spanning those dimensions and reconstructs 3D Gaussian particles for each time step. It connects a 4D video model with a feedforward reconstruction model.

The video component changes how information is shared through attention. Instead of handling spatial and temporal attention sequentially or in separate parallel streams, it combines them within one layer. A sparse attention pattern lets tokens interact when they share a frame, timestamp, or viewpoint. These relationships directly connect the different views and moments that the model needs to coordinate.

The reconstruction component extends existing 3D reconstruction methods with a Gaussian output head, a camera-token replacement procedure, and additional layers and training for dynamics. The authors report a new state of the art in 4D generation, improving visual quality and reconstruction capability. The contribution links multi-view video generation to an explicit, time-varying 3D representation through the proposed architecture.
summary.tldr: A fused view-time attention model and feedforward Gaussian reconstruction improve generation of scenes that change over time.

title: Fused View-Time Attention and Feedforward Reconstruction for 4D Scene Generation

abstract: Collecting ground-truth rewards or human demonstrations for multi-step reasoning tasks is often prohibitively expensive, especially in interactive domains such as web tasks. We introduce Self-Taught Lookahead (STL), a reward-free framework that improves language model–based value functions by reasoning explicitly about state transitions. STL can be viewed as a chain-of-thought analogue of the value iteration algorithm: instead of regressing directly on numeric values, a value LLM is trained to simulate a step of lookahead in natural language—predicting the next action, resulting state, and rationale for its value. This process refines value estimates without any labeled data. The self-supervised procedure yields more accurate state-value predictions, which in turn enable lightweight search algorithms to expand fewer states while maintaining strong performance. Empirically, STL-trained value models built on moderately sized (8B-parameter) open-weight LLMs boost web agent success rates by over 39%, achieving performance comparable to proprietary models. STL also generalizes to multi-hop question answering and math puzzles. Overall, STL enables small open-source models to guide efficient search, reducing inference costs by integrating explicit reasoning with value learning.

paragraphs: Search-based agents need to judge which intermediate states are promising, but collecting rewards or human demonstrations for that judgment can be expensive. Self-Taught Lookahead improves language-model value functions without labeled data by training them to reason explicitly about what could happen next.

Instead of directly fitting a numerical value, the value model learns a natural-language lookahead step: it predicts an action, the resulting state, and a rationale for that state's value. These results connect self-supervised value learning to practical search efficiency: a smaller model can guide which possibilities deserve computation, reducing inference costs through more useful evaluations.
summary.tldr: Self-Taught Lookahead trains language models without labeled rewards to evaluate states through explicit lookahead, improving search efficiency and task success.

title: Language Models can Self-Improve at State-Value Estimation for Better Search

abstract: Adversarial input attacks can cause a significant shift of CLIP embeddings. This can affect the downstream robustness of models incorporating CLIP in the pipeline, such as text-to-image generative models or large vision language models. While some efforts have been done towards making the CLIP image encoders robust, the robustness of text encoders remains unexplored. In this work, we cover this gap in the literature. We propose LEAF: an efficient adversarial finetuning method for the text domain, with the ability to scale to large CLIP models. Our models significantly improve the zero-shot adversarial accuracy in the text domain, while maintaining the vision performance provided by robust image encoders. When combined with text-to-image diffusion models, we can improve the generation quality under adversarial noise. In multimodal retrieval tasks, LEAF improves the recall under adversarial noise over standard CLIP models. Finally, we show that robust text encoders facilitate better reconstruction of input text from its embedding via direct optimization. We open-source our code and models.

paragraphs: Adversarial inputs can shift CLIP embeddings enough to affect systems that depend on them, including image generators and large vision-language models. Work on robust CLIP models has focused on image encoders. This paper addresses the text side with LEAF, an adversarial fine-tuning method designed to scale to large CLIP models.

LEAF significantly improves zero-shot adversarial accuracy for text while maintaining the visual performance supplied by robust image encoders. This matters for a model whose image and text representations are used together: improving the image component alone leaves the text component as another source of sensitivity.

The authors examine several downstream effects. Combined with text-to-image diffusion models, robust text encoders improve generation quality under adversarial noise. LEAF also improves multimodal retrieval recall under such noise compared with standard CLIP. Finally, direct optimization reconstructs input text more effectively from the robust embeddings. These findings show benefits across several evaluated uses of the text representation, connecting encoder robustness to the behavior of systems built around CLIP.
summary.tldr: LEAF strengthens CLIP's text encoder against adversarial inputs while retaining robust vision performance and improving evaluated downstream tasks.

title: Robustness in Both Domains: CLIP Needs a Robust Text Encoder

abstract: We study the problem of approximate inference in collective graphical models (CGMs), which were recently introduced to model the problem of learning and inference with noisy aggregate observations. We first analyze the complexity of inference in CGMs: unlike inference in conventional graphical models, exact inference in CGMs is NP-hard even for tree-structured models. We then develop a tractable convex approximation to the NP-hard MAP inference problem in CGMs, and show how to use MAP inference for approximate marginal inference within the EM framework. We demonstrate empirically that these approximation techniques can reduce the computational cost of inference by two orders of magnitude and the cost of learning by at least an order of magnitude while providing solutions of equal or better quality.
