We first analyze the complexity of inference in CGMs: unlike inference in conventional graphical models, exact inference in CGMs is NP-hard even for tree-structured models. We then develop a tractable convex approximation to the NP-hard MAP inference problem in CGMs, and show how to use MAP inference for approximate marginal inference within the EM framework. We demonstrate empirically that these approximation techniques can reduce the computational cost of inference by two orders of magnitude and the cost of learning by at least an order of magnitude while providing solutions of equal or better quality.

paragraphs: Collective graphical models address learning from noisy aggregate observations. Their inference problem differs substantially from that of conventional graphical models: the paper proves that exact inference is NP-hard even when the model has a tree structure. This establishes that a seemingly simple dependency structure does not, by itself, make aggregate inference computationally manageable.

The authors develop a tractable convex approximation to maximum a posteriori inference, which seeks the most probable explanation of the observations. They also show how this approximate MAP computation can support approximate marginal inference within expectation-maximization. The approach therefore addresses both making inferences with a model and learning its parameters.

In the reported experiments, the approximations reduce inference cost by two orders of magnitude and learning cost by at least one order of magnitude, while producing solutions of equal or better quality. These empirical results show that the computational savings need not come with poorer solutions in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A convex approximation makes inference and learning in collective graphical models substantially cheaper in experiments while maintaining or improving solution quality.

title: Approximate Inference in Collective Graphical Models

abstract: Motivated by an application of eliciting users’ preferences, we investigate the problem of learning hemimetrics, i.e., pairwise distances among a set of n items that satisfy triangle inequalities and non-negativity constraints. In our application, the (asymmetric) distances quantify private costs a user incurs when substituting one item by another. We aim to learn these distances (costs) by asking the users whether they are willing to switch from one item to another for a given incentive offer. Without exploiting structural constraints of the hemimetric polytope, learning the distances between each pair of items requires Θ(n^2) queries. We propose an active learning algorithm that substantially reduces this sample complexity by exploiting the structural constraints on the version space of hemimetrics. Our proposed algorithm achieves provably-optimal sample complexity for various instances of the task. For example, when the items are embedded into K tight clusters, the sample complexity of our algorithm reduces to O(n K). Extensive experiments on a restaurant recommendation data set support the conclusions of our theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a user’s costs for switching between items by asking whether a particular incentive would persuade them to switch. These costs can be asymmetric: replacing one item with another need not have the same cost as reversing the substitution. The authors model them as hemimetrics, which satisfy non-negativity and triangle inequalities.

Learning every pairwise cost without using this structure requires a number of queries proportional to the square of the number of items. The proposed active learning algorithm uses constraints among the distances to restrict the set of still-possible hemimetrics. This allows answers about some substitutions to inform what remains possible for others.

The authors prove optimal sample complexity for various instances of the problem. In particular, when the items form K tight clusters, the query requirement falls to O(nK) for n items. That improvement depends on the stated cluster structure. Experiments with restaurant recommendation data support the theoretical analysis, showing the value of exploiting relationships among costs when eliciting preferences.
summary.tldr: An active learning algorithm reduces preference queries by exploiting structural constraints on asymmetric item-switching costs.

title: Actively Learning Hemimetrics with Applications to Eliciting User Preferences

abstract: Sparse matrix factorization is a popular tool to obtain interpretable data decompositions, which are also effective to perform data completion or denoising. Its applicability to large datasets has been addressed with online and randomized methods, that reduce the complexity in one of the matrix dimension, but not in both of them. In this paper, we tackle very large matrices in both dimensions. We propose a new factorization method that scales gracefully to terabyte-scale datasets. Those could not be processed by previous algorithms in a reasonable amount of time. We demonstrate the efficiency of our approach on massive functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data, and on matrix completion problems for recommender systems, where we obtain significant speed-ups compared to state-of-the art coordinate descent methods.

Their starting observation is that existing online and randomized approaches reduce complexity along one matrix dimension without doing so along both. The authors report significant speed improvements over state-of-the-art coordinate descent methods. summary.tldr: A sparse matrix factorization method handles matrices that are massive in both dimensions, with substantial reported speedups on imaging and recommendation tasks.

title: Dictionary Learning for Massive Matrix Factorization

abstract: Analysis of categorical data is a challenging task. In this paper, we propose to compute topographical features of high-dimensional categorical data. We propose an efficient algorithm to extract modes of the underlying distribution and their attractive basins. These topographical features provide a geometric view of the data and can be applied to visualization and clustering of real world challenging datasets. Experiments show that our principled method outperforms state-of-the-art clustering methods while also admits an embarrassingly parallel property.

Its approach is to construct topographical features of the underlying distribution, giving these data a geometric interpretation. This representation is intended to reveal how the observations are organized, making distributional structure useful for subsequent analysis.

The proposed algorithm efficiently extracts modes and their attractive basins. Modes represent peaks in the distribution, while attractive basins describe the regions associated with those peaks. Together, these features describe more than isolated representative points: they connect prominent parts of the distribution with the surrounding data regions. The resulting view supports both grouping observations and visualizing their organization.

Experiments on challenging real-world datasets report better clustering performance than state-of-the-art methods. The algorithm also has an embarrassingly parallel structure, meaning its work is particularly amenable to parallel execution. The stated contribution combines a distribution-based way to describe categorical data with an efficient computational method, with the reported experiments supporting its value for clustering.
summary.tldr: An efficient, highly parallel algorithm clusters categorical data using distributional peaks and their associated regions.

title: Clustering High Dimensional Categorical Data via Topographical Features

abstract: We present a probabilistic framework for overlapping community discovery and link prediction for relational data, given as a graph. The proposed framework has: (1) a deep architecture which enables us to infer multiple layers of latent features/communities for each node, providing superior link prediction performance on more complex networks and better interpretability of the latent features; and (2) a regression model which allows directly conditioning the node latent features on the side information available in form of node attributes. Our framework handles both (1) and (2) via a clean, unified model, which enjoys full local conjugacy via data augmentation, and facilitates efficient inference via closed form Gibbs sampling. Moreover, inference cost scales in the number of edges which is attractive for massive but sparse networks. Our framework is also easily extendable to model weighted networks with count-valued edges. We compare with various state-of-the-art methods and report results, both quantitative and qualitative, on several benchmark data sets.

paragraphs: The paper presents a probabilistic model for discovering overlapping communities and predicting links in graph data. Each node can have multiple layers of hidden features or community memberships. This deep organization is intended to capture more complex network structure while making the learned features more interpretable.

The framework also uses information attached to nodes, such as their attributes. A regression component directly conditions the hidden node features on this side information, bringing attributes and graph structure into one model. Through data augmentation, the authors obtain full local conjugacy, enabling an efficient Gibbs sampling procedure with closed-form updates.

The authors report superior link prediction on more complex networks and provide quantitative and qualitative comparisons with existing methods on benchmark datasets. Together, these contributions connect layered community representations, node attributes, and computationally efficient inference within a unified probabilistic framework.
summary.tldr: A deep probabilistic graph model combines layered community memberships with node attributes for link prediction and interpretable relational modeling.

title: Deep Generative Models for Relational Data with Side Information

abstract: We present a model for random simple graphs with power law (i.e., heavy-tailed) degree distributions. To attain this behavior, the edge probabilities in the graph are constructed from Bertoin–Fujita–Roynette–Yor (BFRY) random variables, which have been recently utilized in Bayesian statistics for the construction of power law models in several applications. Our construction readily extends to capture the structure of latent factors, similarly to stochastic block-models, while maintaining its power law degree distribution. The BFRY random variables are well approximated by gamma random variables in a variational Bayesian inference routine, which we apply to several network datasets for which power law degree distributions are a natural assumption. By learning the parameters of the BFRY distribution via probabilistic inference, we are able to automatically select the appropriate power law behavior from the data. In order to further scale our inference procedure, we adopt stochastic gradient ascent routines where the gradients are computed on minibatches (i.e., subsets) of the edges in the graph.

This paper develops a random simple-graph model designed to capture power-law degree behavior. It constructs edge probabilities using Bertoin–Fujita–Roynette–Yor random variables, whose distribution provides the mechanism for producing the desired tail.

The construction can also represent latent factors in a way similar to stochastic block models while retaining its power-law degree distribution. This allows hidden network structure and heavy-tailed connectivity to coexist in one model. Rather than fixing the precise power-law behavior in advance, the method learns parameters of the underlying random-variable distribution through probabilistic inference.

For computation, the authors use gamma approximations to the BFRY variables within variational Bayesian inference. They apply this procedure to network datasets where power-law degrees are a natural assumption. To improve scalability further, they estimate gradients from subsets of graph edges and use stochastic gradient ascent, connecting a flexible probabilistic construction with an inference procedure suited to larger networks.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian graph model learns power-law connectivity from data while accommodating latent structure and minibatch inference.

title: Bayesian inference on random simple graphs with power law degree distributions

abstract: Many loss functions in representation learning are invariant under a continuous symmetry transformation. For example, the loss function of word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013) remains unchanged if we simultaneously rotate all word and context embedding vectors. We show that representation learning models for time series possess an approximate continuous symmetry that leads to slow convergence of gradient descent. We propose a new optimization algorithm that speeds up convergence using ideas from gauge theory in physics. Our algorithm leads to orders of magnitude faster convergence and to more interpretable representations, as we show for dynamic extensions of matrix factorization and word embedding models. We further present an example application of our proposed algorithm that translates modern words into their historic equivalents.

paragraphs: Representation-learning losses can remain unchanged under continuous transformations of their parameters. This means different coordinate arrangements can express the same quality of solution, making symmetry relevant to the geometry of optimization.

The authors show that representation models for time series have an approximate continuous symmetry that causes gradient descent to converge slowly. They develop an optimization algorithm inspired by gauge theory in physics to address this behavior. The approach uses the symmetry structure as information for improving optimization, connecting a property of the model's parameterization to its training dynamics.

For dynamic matrix factorization and word-embedding models, the authors demonstrate convergence that is faster by orders of magnitude, together with more interpretable representations. They also present an application that translates modern words into historical equivalents. These findings show how addressing approximate symmetry can improve both computational behavior and the usefulness of representations in models that track changes over time.
summary.tldr: A gauge-theory-inspired optimizer addresses approximate continuous symmetries to accelerate temporal representation learning and improve interpretability.

title: Improving Optimization for Models With Continuous Symmetry Breaking

abstract: It is a known fact that training recurrent neural networks for tasks that have long term dependencies is challenging. One of the main reasons is the vanishing or exploding gradient problem, which prevents gradient information from propagating to early layers. In this paper we propose a simple recurrent architecture, the Fourier Recurrent Unit (FRU), that stabilizes the gradients that arise in its training while giving us stronger expressive power. Specifically, FRU summarizes the hidden states $h^{(t)}$ along the temporal dimension with Fourier basis functions. This allows gradients to easily reach any layer due to FRU’s residual learning structure and the global support of trigonometric functions. We show that FRU has gradient lower and upper bounds independent of temporal dimension. We also show the strong expressivity of sparse Fourier basis, from which FRU obtains its strong expressive power. Our experimental study also demonstrates that with fewer parameters the proposed architecture outperforms other recurrent architectures on many tasks.

paragraphs: Recurrent networks can struggle to learn relationships across long sequences because training gradients shrink or grow excessively before reaching earlier steps. The Fourier Recurrent Unit addresses this by changing how information from hidden states is summarized over time. It uses Fourier basis functions to represent that temporal information.

The architecture combines this summary with a residual learning structure. Because trigonometric functions have support across time, the authors explain that gradients can reach earlier layers more readily. They establish upper and lower gradient bounds that do not depend on the temporal dimension, directly addressing the role of sequence length in gradient stability.

The paper also analyzes the expressive strength of sparse Fourier bases, linking that property to the architecture’s ability to represent temporal patterns. Experiments show that the proposed network outperforms other recurrent architectures on many tasks while using fewer parameters. The contribution brings together a theoretical argument for stable gradient propagation, an expressivity analysis, and empirical evidence of effective sequence learning.
summary.tldr: Fourier Recurrent Units summarize hidden states with Fourier functions, yielding sequence-length-independent gradient bounds and strong reported performance.

title: Learning Long Term Dependencies via Fourier Recurrent Units

abstract: We establish, for the first time, explicit connections between feedforward neural networks with ReLU activation and tropical geometry — we show that the family of such neural networks is equivalent to the family of tropical rational maps. Among other things, we deduce that feedforward ReLU neural networks with one hidden layer can be characterized by zonotopes, which serve as building blocks for deeper networks; we relate decision boundaries of such neural networks to tropical hypersurfaces, a major object of study in tropical geometry; and we prove that linear regions of such neural networks correspond to vertices of polytopes associated with tropical rational functions. An insight from our tropical formulation is that a deeper network is exponentially more expressive than a shallow network.

Its central result identifies the family of such networks with the family of tropical rational maps. That correspondence lets questions about network structure be expressed through geometric objects.

They also relate decision boundaries to tropical hypersurfaces. A further result connects the network’s linear regions with vertices of polytopes associated with tropical rational functions, translating the subdivision of its input space into a geometric relationship.

These connections make the representation of shallow and deep networks accessible through the same mathematical framework. One insight is an exponential expressivity advantage for deeper networks over shallow ones. The contribution concerns what the networks can represent and how that capacity is organized geometrically; its stated findings are mathematical connections and expressivity results.
summary.tldr: Tropical geometry characterizes ReLU networks through geometric objects and reveals an exponential expressivity advantage of depth.

title: Tropical Geometry of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Deep learning has shown that learned functions can dramatically outperform hand-designed functions on perceptual tasks. Analogously, this suggests that learned optimizers may similarly outperform current hand-designed optimizers, especially for specific problems. However, learned optimizers are notoriously difficult to train and have yet to demonstrate wall-clock speedups over hand-designed optimizers, and thus are rarely used in practice. Typically, learned optimizers are trained by truncated backpropagation through an unrolled optimization process. The resulting gradients are either strongly biased (for short truncations) or have exploding norm (for long truncations). In this work we propose a training scheme which overcomes both of these difficulties, by dynamically weighting two unbiased gradient estimators for a variational loss on optimizer performance. This allows us to train neural networks to perform optimization of a specific task faster than tuned first-order methods. Moreover, by training the optimizer against validation loss (as opposed to training loss), we are able to learn optimizers that train networks to generalize better than first order methods. We demonstrate these results on problems where our learned optimizer trains convolutional networks faster in wall-clock time compared to tuned first-order methods and with an improvement in test loss.

These difficulties obstruct learning useful optimization behavior.

The authors demonstrate convolutional-network training problems with faster wall-clock optimization and improved test loss. These are task-specific empirical results, supporting the value of both the gradient-estimation scheme and the choice to optimize validation performance.
summary.tldr: Dynamically combining unbiased gradient estimators enables learned optimizers that outperform tuned first-order methods in wall-clock time and test loss on demonstrated tasks.

title: Understanding and correcting pathologies in the training of learned optimizers

abstract: Randomized Newton methods have recently become the focus of intense research activity in large-scale and distributed optimization. In general, these methods are based on a “computation-accuracy trade-off”, which allows the user to gain scalability in exchange for error in the solution. However, the user does not know how much error is created by the randomized approximation, which can be detrimental in two ways: On one hand, the user may try to assess the unknown error with theoretical worst-case error bounds, but this approach is impractical when the bounds involve unknown constants, and it often leads to excessive computation. On the other hand, the user may select the “sketch size” and stopping criteria in a heuristic manner, but this can lead to unreliable results. Motivated by these difficulties, we show how bootstrapping can be used to directly estimate the unknown error, which prevents excessive computation, and offers more confidence about the quality of a randomized solution.

paragraphs: Randomized Newton methods make large-scale and distributed optimization more manageable by replacing expensive calculations with randomized approximations. This creates a trade-off: computation becomes cheaper, but the resulting solution contains approximation error. The practical difficulty is that users often do not know how large that error is for the solution they actually obtain.

The paper explains why two common ways of managing this uncertainty can be unsatisfactory. Worst-case theoretical bounds may contain unknown constants and can encourage unnecessary computation. Alternatively, choosing the sketch size and stopping rule through heuristics can leave the quality of a result uncertain. Both difficulties arise from lacking a direct assessment of the approximation error.

The authors show how bootstrapping can estimate that unknown error directly. This gives users a more concrete basis for judging the quality of a randomized solution and avoiding excessive computation. The contribution concerns the reliability of the computation-accuracy trade-off itself: estimating the error helps make the computational savings of randomized optimization more usable.
summary.tldr: Bootstrapping estimates randomized Newton methods’ approximation error directly, helping users assess solution quality without unnecessary computation.

title: Estimating the Error of Randomized Newton Methods: A Bootstrap Approach

abstract: This paper presents the private-outsourced-Gaussian process-upper confidence bound (PO-GP-UCB) algorithm, which is the first algorithm for privacy-preserving Bayesian optimization (BO) in the outsourced setting with a provable performance guarantee. We consider the outsourced setting where the entity holding the dataset and the entity performing BO are represented by different parties, and the dataset cannot be released non-privately. For example, a hospital holds a dataset of sensitive medical records and outsources the BO task on this dataset to an industrial AI company. The key idea of our approach is to make the BO performance of our algorithm similar to that of non-private GP-UCB run using the original dataset, which is achieved by using a random projection-based transformation that preserves both privacy and the pairwise distances between inputs. Our main theoretical contribution is to show that a regret bound similar to that of the standard GP-UCB algorithm can be established for our PO-GP-UCB algorithm. We empirically evaluate the performance of our PO-GP-UCB algorithm with synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Outsourced Bayesian optimization separates the party holding a dataset from the party performing optimization. This creates a problem when the original data cannot be released without privacy protection. The paper addresses that setting with PO-GP-UCB, an algorithm designed to support private outsourcing while retaining a provable optimization guarantee.

Preserving those distances helps maintain the information used by the optimization procedure. The aim is to make behavior comparable to non-private GP-UCB operating on the original dataset, even though the optimization party receives transformed information.

The main theoretical result establishes a regret bound similar to that of standard GP-UCB. The authors also evaluate the method on synthetic and real-world datasets. The significance is the combination of a privacy-preserving transformation with a formal performance analysis for outsourced optimization. Similarity of the regret bounds supports the approach without asserting that every private run reproduces the exact decisions or outcomes of a non-private run.
summary.tldr: PO-GP-UCB uses a privacy-preserving distance transformation to enable outsourced Bayesian optimization with a regret bound similar to non-private GP-UCB.

title: Private Outsourced Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Safe reinforcement learning has been a promising approach for optimizing the policy of an agent that operates in safety-critical applications. In this paper, we propose an algorithm, SNO-MDP, that explores and optimizes Markov decision processes under unknown safety constraints. Specifically, we take a step-wise approach for optimizing safety and cumulative reward. In our method, the agent first learns safety constraints by expanding the safe region, and then optimizes the cumulative reward in the certified safe region. We provide theoretical guarantees on both the satisfaction of the safety constraint and the near-optimality of the cumulative reward under proper regularity assumptions. In our experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SNO-MDP through two experiments: one uses a synthetic data in a new, openly-available environment named GP-Safety-Gym, and the other simulates Mars surface exploration by using real observation data.

paragraphs: This paper considers reinforcement learning when an agent must respect safety constraints that are initially unknown. The challenge is to learn about the environment and pursue reward while accounting for uncertainty about which behavior is safe. The proposed algorithm, SNO-MDP, separates learning the safety constraints from optimizing cumulative reward.

First, the agent learns about safety by expanding its safe region. It then optimizes reward within the region that has been certified safe. This step-wise design makes the learned safety boundary part of the reward optimization problem. The paper provides theoretical guarantees for satisfying the safety constraint and achieving near-optimal cumulative reward, explicitly under appropriate regularity assumptions.

The evaluation uses two experiments: synthetic data in the openly available GP-Safety-Gym environment and a simulation of Mars surface exploration based on real observation data. These experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness in the tested settings. The theoretical contribution is conditional safety and reward assurance, with reward optimization carried out inside the certified safe region.
summary.tldr: SNO-MDP learns a certified safe region before optimizing reward, with safety and near-optimality guarantees under regularity assumptions.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning in Constrained Markov Decision Processes

abstract: A dynamic treatment regime (DTR) consists of a sequence of decision rules, one per stage of intervention, that dictates how to determine the treatment assignment to patients based on evolving treatments and covariates’ history. These regimes are particularly effective for managing chronic disorders and is arguably one of the critical ingredients underlying more personalized decision-making systems. All reinforcement learning algorithms for finding the optimal DTR in online settings will suffer O(\sqrt{|D_{X, S}|T}) regret on some environments, where T is the number of experiments, and D_{X, S} is the domains of treatments X and covariates S. This implies T = O (|D_{X, S}|) trials to generate an optimal DTR. In many applications, domains of X and S could be so enormous that the time required to ensure appropriate learning may be unattainable. We show that, if the causal diagram of the underlying environment is provided, one could achieve regret that is exponentially smaller than D_{X, S}. In particular, we develop two online algorithms that satisfy such regret bounds by exploiting the causal structure underlying the DTR; one is based on the principle of optimism in the face of uncertainty (OFU-DTR), and the other uses the posterior sampling learning (PS-DTR). Finally, we introduce efficient methods to accelerate these online learning procedures by leveraging the abundant, yet biased observational (non-experimental) data.

paragraphs: A dynamic treatment regime specifies a sequence of treatment decisions based on a patient’s evolving treatment and covariate history. Learning such rules online can require extensive experimentation when the possible combinations of treatments and covariates are numerous. The paper describes a worst-case regret dependence on the size of this combined domain, explaining why ordinary exploration can become impractical.

The proposed improvement relies on having the causal diagram of the environment. By exploiting this structure, the authors show that regret can have an exponentially smaller dependence on the treatment-and-covariate domain. The paper also introduces methods for accelerating these online procedures with abundant observational data, while recognizing that such data are biased. The contribution is a causal approach to reducing the burden of sequential experimentation. Its theoretical advantage is conditional on the supplied causal structure, rather than a claim that arbitrary treatment problems become easy to learn.
summary.tldr: Given a causal diagram, two reinforcement learning algorithms can substantially reduce regret when learning sequential treatment rules.

title: Designing Optimal Dynamic Treatment Regimes: A Causal Reinforcement Learning Approach

abstract: An ambitious goal for machine learning is to create agents that behave ethically: The capacity to abide by human moral norms would greatly expand the context in which autonomous agents could be practically and safely deployed, e.g. fully autonomous vehicles will encounter charged moral decisions that complicate their deployment. While ethical agents could be trained by rewarding correct behavior under a specific moral theory (e.g. utilitarianism), there remains widespread disagreement about the nature of morality. Acknowledging such disagreement, recent work in moral philosophy proposes that ethical behavior requires acting under moral uncertainty, i.e. to take into account when acting that one’s credence is split across several plausible ethical theories. This paper translates such insights to the field of reinforcement learning, proposes two training methods that realize different points among competing desiderata, and trains agents in simple environments to act under moral uncertainty. The results illustrate (1) how such uncertainty can help curb extreme behavior from commitment to single theories and (2) several technical complications arising from attempting to ground moral philosophy in RL (e.g. how can a principled trade-off between two competing but incomparable reward functions be reached). The aim is to catalyze progress towards morally-competent agents and highlight the potential of RL to contribute towards the computational grounding of moral philosophy.

This paper instead considers moral uncertainty: an agent assigns credence to several plausible ethical theories and takes that uncertainty into account when acting. It translates this philosophical idea into a reinforcement learning setting.

The authors propose two training methods that make different tradeoffs among competing desiderata, then train agents in simple environments. These experiments illustrate how uncertainty across theories can help restrain extreme behavior associated with commitment to a single theory. The findings concern these demonstrations rather than establishing ethical competence for autonomous deployment.

One central issue is how to make a principled tradeoff between reward functions that compete but lack a common basis for comparison. By making such problems computationally explicit, the paper both advances methods for acting under moral uncertainty and uses reinforcement learning to investigate questions from moral philosophy.
summary.tldr: Two reinforcement learning methods explore acting under moral uncertainty, illustrating reduced extremes and difficulties in comparing competing ethical rewards.

title: Reinforcement Learning Under Moral Uncertainty

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has made a lot of advances for solving a single problem in a given environment; but learning policies that generalize to unseen variations of a problem remains challenging. To improve sample efficiency for learning on such instances of a problem domain, we present Self-Paced Context Evaluation (SPaCE). Based on self-paced learning, SPaCE automatically generates instance curricula online with little computational overhead. To this end, SPaCE leverages information contained in state values during training to accelerate and improve training performance as well as generalization capabilities to new \tasks from the same problem domain. Nevertheless, SPaCE is independent of the problem domain at hand and can be applied on top of any RL agent with state-value function approximation. We demonstrate SPaCE’s ability to speed up learning of different value-based RL agents on two environments, showing better generalization capabilities and up to 10x faster learning compared to naive approaches such as round robin or SPDRL, as the closest state-of-the-art approach.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can solve one environment yet struggle with unseen variations of the same problem. Self-Paced Context Evaluation addresses this by choosing a curriculum of problem instances during training. The aim is to use training interactions more efficiently while improving the policy’s ability to handle new tasks from the same domain.

SPaCE builds its curriculum online using information already contained in state-value estimates. This lets training progress inform which instances the agent encounters, with little additional computational overhead. The approach is independent of the particular problem domain and can be added to any reinforcement learning agent that approximates a state-value function.

Experiments with different value-based agents in two environments demonstrate faster learning and improved generalization. The reported acceleration reaches up to tenfold compared with the evaluated approaches, including round-robin selection and SPDRL. These findings support using the agent’s own value information to organize its training experiences. The claimed generalization concerns new variations within the same problem domain, matching the curriculum’s intended role.
summary.tldr: SPaCE uses state-value estimates to build training curricula, improving same-domain generalization and achieving up to tenfold faster learning in the reported experiments.

title: Self-Paced Context Evaluation for Contextual Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Meta-learning algorithms adapt quickly to new tasks that are drawn from the same task distribution as the training tasks. The mechanism leading to fast adaptation is the conditioning of a downstream predictive model on the inferred representation of the task’s underlying data generative process, or \emph{function}. This \emph{meta-representation}, which is computed from a few observed examples of the underlying function, is learned jointly with the predictive model. In this work, we study the implications of this joint training on the transferability of the meta-representations. Our goal is to learn meta-representations that are robust to noise in the data and facilitate solving a wide range of downstream tasks that share the same underlying functions. To this end, we propose a decoupled encoder-decoder approach to supervised meta-learning, where the encoder is trained with a contrastive objective to find a good representation of the underlying function. In particular, our training scheme is driven by the self-supervision signal indicating whether two sets of examples stem from the same function. Our experiments on a number of synthetic and real-world datasets show that the representations we obtain outperform strong baselines in terms of downstream performance and noise robustness, even when these baselines are trained in an end-to-end manner.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses a few examples to infer a representation of the process underlying a task, allowing a predictive model to adapt quickly. Usually, this representation and the downstream predictor are trained together. The paper examines how that joint training affects the representation’s usefulness for other downstream tasks sharing the same underlying functions.

The authors propose separating encoder and decoder training. The encoder learns through a contrastive objective, using a self-supervision signal that indicates whether two sets of examples came from the same function. This directs representation learning toward the underlying function identified by the example sets. The goal is to obtain representations that remain useful across downstream tasks and tolerate noise in the observations.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show better downstream performance and noise robustness than strong baselines, including baselines trained end to end. The findings support learning the function representation as a distinct objective. The relevant transfer setting is a range of downstream tasks that share underlying functions, which explains why identifying those functions can provide reusable information.
summary.tldr: Contrastive training on whether example sets share an underlying function produces meta-representations with stronger reported transfer performance and noise robustness.

title: Function Contrastive Learning of Transferable Meta-Representations

abstract: A recent series of theoretical works showed that the dynamics of neural networks with a certain initialisation are well-captured by kernel methods. Concurrent empirical work demonstrated that kernel methods can come close to the performance of neural networks on some image classification tasks. These results raise the question of whether neural networks only learn successfully if kernels also learn successfully, despite being the more expressive function class. Here, we show that two-layer neural networks with *only a few neurons* achieve near-optimal performance on high-dimensional Gaussian mixture classification while lazy training approaches such as random features and kernel methods do not. Our analysis is based on the derivation of a set of ordinary differential equations that exactly track the dynamics of the network and thus allow to extract the asymptotic performance of the network as a function of regularisation or signal-to-noise ratio. We also show how over-parametrising the neural network leads to faster convergence, but does not improve its final performance.

paragraphs: Some neural networks, under particular initializations, have learning dynamics closely described by kernel methods. This raises a question about whether successful neural learning depends on a corresponding kernel method also succeeding. The paper investigates that question through classification of high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures, providing a setting where the two approaches behave differently.

The authors show that two-layer networks with only a few neurons can achieve near-optimal performance in this setting, while lazy training methods, including random features and kernel methods, do not. Their analysis derives ordinary differential equations that exactly track the network dynamics. These equations make it possible to determine asymptotic performance as regularization or the signal-to-noise ratio changes.

The analysis also separates the speed of learning from its final outcome. Adding more network parameters speeds convergence in the studied problem without improving the final performance. Together, these findings establish a concrete separation between neural networks and the kernel approaches considered, while showing that larger networks can offer an optimization benefit even when the eventual classification performance stays the same.
summary.tldr: In a high-dimensional Gaussian mixture problem, small two-layer networks achieve near-optimal classification where the studied kernel and random-feature methods do not.

title: Classifying high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures: Where kernel methods fail and neural networks succeed

abstract: This paper considers classification problems with hierarchically organized classes. We force the classifier (hyperplane) of each class to belong to a sphere manifold, whose center is the classifier of its super-class. Then, individual sphere manifolds are connected based on their hierarchical relations. Our technique replaces the last layer of a neural network by combining a spherical fully-connected layer with a hierarchical layer. This regularization is shown to improve the performance of widely used deep neural network architectures (ResNet and DenseNet) on publicly available datasets (CIFAR100, CUB200, Stanford dogs, Stanford cars, and Tiny-ImageNet).

paragraphs: Classification labels often form a hierarchy, such as fine-grained categories grouped under broader classes. A standard output layer does not necessarily encode those relationships. This paper uses the class hierarchy to regularize how the final classifiers are positioned relative to one another.

Each class’s classifier is constrained to a sphere manifold centered on the classifier of its parent class. These spheres are connected according to the hierarchy. The implementation replaces the network’s final layer with a combination of a spherical fully connected layer and a hierarchical layer, making the relationship between broad and specific classes part of the model structure.

The regularization improves ResNet and DenseNet performance on CIFAR100, CUB200, Stanford Dogs, Stanford Cars, and Tiny-ImageNet. These results support using hierarchical geometry as a useful constraint in classification. The approach presupposes hierarchically organized classes; the abstract does not describe discovering a hierarchy automatically or report the exact improvement for each dataset.
summary.tldr: Hierarchically connected spherical classifier constraints improve classification in the reported ResNet and DenseNet experiments.

title: Connecting Sphere Manifolds Hierarchically for Regularization

abstract: Games are abstractions of the real world, where artificial agents learn to compete and cooperate with other agents. While significant achievements have been made in various perfect- and imperfect-information games, DouDizhu (a.k.a. Fighting the Landlord), a three-player card game, is still unsolved. DouDizhu is a very challenging domain with competition, collaboration, imperfect information, large state space, and particularly a massive set of possible actions where the legal actions vary significantly from turn to turn. Unfortunately, modern reinforcement learning algorithms mainly focus on simple and small action spaces, and not surprisingly, are shown not to make satisfactory progress in DouDizhu. In this work, we propose a conceptually simple yet effective DouDizhu AI system, namely DouZero, which enhances traditional Monte-Carlo methods with deep neural networks, action encoding, and parallel actors. Starting from scratch in a single server with four GPUs, DouZero outperformed all the existing DouDizhu AI programs in days of training and was ranked the first in the Botzone leaderboard among 344 AI agents. Through building DouZero, we show that classic Monte-Carlo methods can be made to deliver strong results in a hard domain with a complex action space. The code and an online demo are released at https://github.com/kwai/DouZero with the hope that this insight could motivate future work.

paragraphs: DouZero tackles DouDizhu, a three-player card game involving both competition and collaboration. That last feature makes the game difficult for reinforcement learning methods designed around small, simple action spaces.

The system combines traditional Monte Carlo methods with deep neural networks, an encoding of actions, and parallel actors. Through self-play, this combination brings a classic learning approach to a setting with a particularly complicated set of possible moves. The contribution is a conceptually simple system showing that these ingredients can work effectively together in a demanding game.

Starting from scratch on one server with four GPUs, DouZero surpassed the existing DouDizhu programs described in the abstract after days of training. It also ranked first among 344 agents on the Botzone leaderboard. These results demonstrate strong performance in this domain and support revisiting Monte Carlo methods for problems whose action spaces challenge modern reinforcement learning algorithms.
summary.tldr: DouZero combines Monte Carlo learning, neural networks, action encoding, and parallel self-play to achieve leading reported performance in DouDizhu.

title: DouZero: Mastering DouDizhu with Self-Play Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Multiscale feature hierarchies have been witnessed the success in the computer vision area. This further motivates researchers to design multiscale Transformer for natural language processing, mostly based on the self-attention mechanism. For example, restricting the receptive field across heads or extracting local fine-grained features via convolutions. However, most of existing works directly modeled local features but ignored the word-boundary information. This results in redundant and ambiguous attention distributions, which lacks of interpretability. In this work, we define those scales in different linguistic units, including sub-words, words and phrases. We built a multiscale Transformer model by establishing relationships among scales based on word-boundary information and phrase-level prior knowledge. The proposed \textbf{U}niversal \textbf{M}ulti\textbf{S}cale \textbf{T}ransformer, namely \textsc{Umst}, was evaluated on two sequence generation tasks. Notably, it yielded consistent performance gains over the strong baseline on several test sets without sacrificing the efficiency.

paragraphs: Sequence models can process language at several levels of detail, but a small attention region does not necessarily correspond to a meaningful linguistic unit. This paper argues that earlier multiscale Transformers often modeled local features without respecting word boundaries. Such representations can produce redundant or ambiguous attention patterns that are difficult to interpret.

The proposed Universal MultiScale Transformer defines its scales explicitly as subwords, words, and phrases. It connects those scales using word-boundary information and prior knowledge about phrases. The approach therefore gives the hierarchy a linguistic basis, linking fine-grained pieces of text to the larger units they form rather than defining scale only through receptive-field size.

The model is evaluated on two sequence-generation tasks and achieves consistent gains over a strong baseline across several test sets without sacrificing efficiency. These findings support the usefulness of incorporating linguistic boundaries into multiscale generation models. The stated evaluation establishes performance and efficiency benefits; the interpretability concern motivates the design rather than supplying a separate quantified result in the abstract.
summary.tldr: UMST links subword, word, and phrase representations using linguistic boundaries, improving evaluated sequence-generation performance without sacrificing efficiency.

title: Learning Multiscale Transformer Models for Sequence Generation

abstract: Recent papers have developed alternating least squares (ALS) methods for CP and tensor ring decomposition with a per-iteration cost which is sublinear in the number of input tensor entries for low-rank decomposition. However, the per-iteration cost of these methods still has an exponential dependence on the number of tensor modes when parameters are chosen to achieve certain worst-case guarantees. In this paper, we propose sampling-based ALS methods for the CP and tensor ring decompositions whose cost does not have this exponential dependence, thereby significantly improving on the previous state-of-the-art. We provide a detailed theoretical analysis and also apply the methods in a feature extraction experiment.

However, the per-iteration cost of these methods still has an exponential dependence on the number of tensor modes when parameters are chosen to achieve certain worst-case guarantees. In this paper, we propose sampling-based ALS methods for the CP and tensor ring decompositions whose cost does not have this exponential dependence, thereby significantly improving on the previous state-of-the-art. We provide a detailed theoretical analysis and also apply the methods in a feature extraction experiment.

paragraphs: This paper improves sampling-based algorithms for CP and tensor ring decomposition. The starting point is alternating least squares, or ALS, methods whose work per iteration can be sublinear in the number of tensor entries when seeking a low-rank decomposition. That property makes the input’s sheer size less costly, but it does not resolve every source of computational growth.

Earlier methods still have a per-iteration cost that grows exponentially with the number of tensor modes when their parameters are chosen to obtain certain worst-case guarantees. The proposed sampling-based ALS methods remove that exponential dependence. This distinction matters because efficiency with respect to the number of entries can coexist with unfavorable scaling in the number of modes.

The authors provide a detailed theoretical analysis and apply their methods in a feature-extraction experiment. The main stated advance is the improved computational dependence while addressing the worst-case-guarantee setting. The experiment supplies an application of the methods, while the theoretical analysis supports the central claim about scaling. Together, they address an efficiency obstacle that remains even after sampling reduces dependence on total tensor size.
summary.tldr: New sampling-based ALS methods remove exponential dependence on tensor modes in the cost of CP and tensor ring decomposition under worst-case-guarantee parameter choices.

title: More Efficient Sampling for Tensor Decomposition With Worst-Case Guarantees

abstract: We approach the graph generation problem from a spectral perspective by first generating the dominant parts of the graph Laplacian spectrum and then building a graph matching these eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Spectral conditioning allows for direct modeling of the global and local graph structure and helps to overcome the expressivity and mode collapse issues of one-shot graph generators. Our novel GAN, called SPECTRE, enables the one-shot generation of much larger graphs than previously possible with one-shot models. SPECTRE outperforms state-of-the-art deep autoregressive generators in terms of modeling fidelity, while also avoiding expensive sequential generation and dependence on node ordering. A case in point, in sizable synthetic and real-world graphs SPECTRE achieves a 4-to-170 fold improvement over the best competitor that does not overfit and is 23-to-30 times faster than autoregressive generators.

paragraphs: Generating a graph in one step avoids expensive sequential construction, but one-shot models can struggle to represent varied global structures. SPECTRE approaches the problem through the graph’s spectrum. Instead of producing connectivity directly from an unconstrained latent representation, it first generates important spectral information.

The model generates dominant eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian, then constructs a graph matching them. This spectral conditioning gives its generative adversarial network access to both global and local structure. The approach is intended to reduce expressivity limits and mode collapse while avoiding dependence on a chosen node ordering.

On sizable synthetic and real graphs, the abstract reports a 4-to-170-fold improvement in modeling performance over the best non-overfitting competitor and 23-to-30-fold faster generation than autoregressive models. It also enables larger one-shot outputs than earlier approaches. The precise fidelity metric is not given in the abstract, so the reported multiplicative gain should not be interpreted as an accuracy percentage.
summary.tldr: SPECTRE conditions graph generation on Laplacian eigenstructure to improve fidelity and speed without sequential node generation.

title: SPECTRE: Spectral Conditioning Helps to Overcome the Expressivity Limits of One-shot Graph Generators

abstract: Normalizing flows model complex probability distributions using maps obtained by composing invertible layers. Special linear layers such as masked and 1{\texttimes}1 convolutions play a key role in existing architectures because they increase expressive power while having tractable Jacobians and inverses. We propose a new family of invertible linear layers based on butterfly layers, which are known to theoretically capture complex linear structures including permutations and periodicity, yet can be inverted efficiently. This representational power is a key advantage of our approach, as such structures are common in many real-world datasets. Based on our invertible butterfly layers, we construct a new class of normalizing flow mod- els called ButterflyFlow. Empirically, we demonstrate that ButterflyFlows not only achieve strong density estimation results on natural images such as MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-32{\texttimes}32, but also obtain significantly better log-likelihoods on structured datasets such as galaxy images and MIMIC-III patient cohorts{—}all while being more efficient in terms of memory and computation than relevant baselines.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows represent complicated probability distributions by composing transformations that can be reversed. Their linear layers must balance expressive power with the ability to compute inverses and track changes in probability density. This paper introduces a family of invertible linear layers based on butterfly matrices to address that balance.

Butterfly layers can theoretically represent complex linear structures, including permutations and periodic patterns, while allowing efficient inversion. The authors use this combination to construct ButterflyFlow. The motivation is that a layer capable of expressing these structures can better match patterns found in data without making the flow prohibitively expensive to run.

The experiments report strong density estimation on natural-image datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet at 32-by-32 resolution. On structured datasets involving galaxy images and MIMIC-III patient cohorts, ButterflyFlow achieves significantly better log-likelihoods than the relevant baselines. It also uses less memory and computation in the reported comparisons. These findings support butterfly layers as a practical way to combine structured expressiveness with computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: ButterflyFlow uses efficiently invertible butterfly layers to improve density modeling and reduce computational costs in the reported comparisons.

title: ButterflyFlow: Building Invertible Layers with Butterfly Matrices

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a promising framework for performing privacy-preserving, distributed learning with a set of clients. However, the data distribution among clients often exhibits non-IID, i.e., distribution shift, which makes efficient optimization difficult. To tackle this problem, many FL algorithms focus on mitigating the effects of data heterogeneity across clients by increasing the performance of the global model. However, almost all algorithms leverage Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) to be the local optimizer, which is easy to make the global model fall into a sharp valley and increase a large deviation of parts of local clients. Therefore, in this paper, we revisit the solutions to the distribution shift problem in FL with a focus on local learning generality. To this end, we propose a general, effective algorithm, \texttt{FedSAM}, based on Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) local optimizer, and develop a momentum FL algorithm to bridge local and global models, \texttt{MoFedSAM}. Theoretically, we show the convergence analysis of these two algorithms and demonstrate the generalization bound of \texttt{FedSAM}. Empirically, our proposed algorithms substantially outperform existing FL studies and significantly decrease the learning deviation.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines learning across clients whose data may follow different distributions. Those differences complicate optimization and can leave some clients far from the behavior of the shared model. This paper examines the local optimizer as a source of that problem, arguing that ordinary empirical risk minimization can lead the global model into a sharp loss valley.

The authors propose FedSAM, which uses Sharpness Aware Minimization for local learning. This shifts attention toward the generalization of each client’s learning procedure, rather than focusing only on the global model’s performance. They also introduce MoFedSAM, a momentum-based federated algorithm intended to connect local and global models more effectively.

The theoretical contribution includes convergence analyses for both algorithms and a generalization bound for FedSAM. Empirically, the authors report substantial improvements over existing federated learning methods and a significant reduction in learning deviation. The findings support changing local optimization as a way to address heterogeneous client data, with separate evidence for optimization behavior, generalization, and the performance observed in experiments.
summary.tldr: FedSAM and MoFedSAM use sharpness-aware local learning to improve federated learning with heterogeneous client data, supported by theory and reported empirical gains.

title: Generalized Federated Learning via Sharpness Aware Minimization

abstract: Data clipping is crucial in reducing noise in quantization operations and improving the achievable accuracy of quantization-aware training (QAT). Current practices rely on heuristics to set clipping threshold scalars and cannot be shown to be optimal. We propose Optimally Clipped Tensors And Vectors (OCTAV), a recursive algorithm to determine MSE-optimal clipping scalars. Derived from the fast Newton-Raphson method, OCTAV finds optimal clipping scalars on the fly, for every tensor, at every iteration of the QAT routine. Thus, the QAT algorithm is formulated with provably minimum quantization noise at each step. In addition, we reveal limitations in common gradient estimation techniques in QAT and propose magnitude-aware differentiation as a remedy to further improve accuracy. Experimentally, OCTAV-enabled QAT achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on multiple tasks. These include training-from-scratch and retraining ResNets and MobileNets on ImageNet, and Squad fine-tuning using BERT models, where OCTAV-enabled QAT consistently preserves accuracy at low precision (4-to-6-bits). Our results require no modifications to the baseline training recipe, except for the insertion of quantization operations where appropriate.

abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are a popular choice for modeling sequential data. Modern RNN architectures assume constant time-intervals between observations. However, in many datasets (e.g. medical records) observation times are irregular and can carry important information. To address this challenge, we propose continuous recurrent units (CRUs) {–} a neural architecture that can naturally handle irregular intervals between observations. The CRU assumes a hidden state, which evolves according to a linear stochastic differential equation and is integrated into an encoder-decoder framework. The recursive computations of the CRU can be derived using the continuous-discrete Kalman filter and are in closed form. The resulting recurrent architecture has temporal continuity between hidden states and a gating mechanism that can optimally integrate noisy observations. We derive an efficient parameterization scheme for the CRU that leads to a fast implementation f-CRU. We empirically study the CRU on a number of challenging datasets and find that it can interpolate irregular time series better than methods based on neural ordinary differential equations.

paragraphs: Sequential datasets often contain unequal gaps between observations, and those gaps can carry useful information. Standard recurrent architectures commonly assume constant intervals. Continuous recurrent units, or CRUs, address this mismatch by allowing the hidden state to evolve continuously between measurements while incorporating observations when they arrive.

A CRU places a hidden state governed by a linear stochastic differential equation inside an encoder-decoder architecture. Its recursive calculations follow from a continuous-discrete Kalman filter and have closed-form expressions. This connects continuous evolution between observations with discrete updates at measurement times. The resulting gating mechanism can optimally integrate noisy observations within this modeling framework, making observation uncertainty part of the recurrent computation.

The authors also derive an efficient parameterization that produces a faster implementation called f-CRU. Across the challenging datasets studied, CRUs interpolate irregular time series better than methods based on neural ordinary differential equations. The results support combining structured stochastic dynamics with learned encoding and decoding to handle unevenly timed observations, while retaining closed-form recurrent calculations.
summary.tldr: Continuous recurrent units combine continuous stochastic hidden-state evolution with Kalman-filter updates to model irregularly timed observations.

title: Modeling Irregular Time Series with Continuous Recurrent Units

abstract: In cross-device Federated Learning (FL), the communication cost of transmitting full-precision models between edge devices and a central server is a significant bottleneck, due to expensive, unreliable, and low-bandwidth wireless connections. As a solution, we propose a novel FL framework named QSFL, towards optimizing FL uplink (client-to-server) communication at both client and model levels. At the client level, we design a Qualification Judgment (QJ) algorithm to sample high-qualification clients to upload models. At the model level, we explore a Sparse Cyclic Sliding Segment (SCSS) algorithm to further compress transmitted models. We prove that QSFL can converge over wall-to-wall time, and develop an optimal hyperparameter searching algorithm based on theoretical analysis to enable QSFL to make the best trade-off between model accuracy and communication cost. Experimental results show that QSFL achieves state-of-the-art compression ratios with marginal model accuracy degradation.

paragraphs: Sending full-precision models from edge devices to a central server can be a major cost in federated learning. Wireless links may be slow, unreliable, and expensive, making communication a practical bottleneck. QSFL addresses this client-to-server traffic through two coordinated decisions: which clients upload and how much model information they transmit.

At the client level, a Qualification Judgment algorithm samples clients assessed as highly qualified to upload their models. At the model level, a Sparse Cyclic Sliding Segment algorithm compresses the transmitted models further. The framework therefore reduces communication through participation selection as well as compression, rather than relying on a single mechanism.

The authors prove convergence over elapsed training time and derive a hyperparameter search algorithm from their theoretical analysis to optimize the tradeoff between accuracy and communication cost. Experiments report state-of-the-art compression ratios with only marginal accuracy degradation. These findings suggest that coordinating client selection and model compression can substantially reduce uplink demands while retaining much of the predictive quality in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: QSFL combines client selection and model compression to reduce federated uplink communication with marginal reported accuracy loss.

title: QSFL: A Two-Level Uplink Communication Optimization Framework for Federated Learning

abstract: Sparse coding, which refers to modeling a signal as sparse linear combinations of the elements of a learned dictionary, has proven to be a successful (and interpretable) approach in applications such as signal processing, computer vision, and medical imaging. While this success has spurred much work on provable guarantees for dictionary recovery when the learned dictionary is the same size as the ground-truth dictionary, work on the setting where the learned dictionary is larger (or $\textit{over-realized}$) with respect to the ground truth is comparatively nascent. Existing theoretical results in this setting have been constrained to the case of noise-less data. We show in this work that, in the presence of noise, minimizing the standard dictionary learning objective can fail to recover the elements of the ground-truth dictionary in the over-realized regime, regardless of the magnitude of the signal in the data-generating process. Furthermore, drawing from the growing body of work on self-supervised learning, we propose a novel masking objective for which recovering the ground-truth dictionary is in fact optimal as the signal increases for a large class of data-generating processes. We corroborate our theoretical results with experiments across several parameter regimes showing that our proposed objective also enjoys better empirical performance than the standard reconstruction objective.

paragraphs: Sparse coding represents a signal using a small number of elements from a learned dictionary. This paper examines what happens when the learned dictionary contains more elements than the dictionary that actually generated the data. That larger-dictionary setting becomes particularly challenging when observations contain noise.

The authors show that minimizing the standard dictionary-learning objective can fail to recover the true dictionary elements in this setting. Increasing the strength of the underlying signal does not necessarily resolve that failure. The result separates successful optimization of the usual objective from successful recovery of the structure that produced the observations.

Inspired by self-supervised learning, the authors introduce a masking objective. For a large class of data-generating processes, recovering the true dictionary becomes optimal as signal strength increases. This establishes a property of the objective, rather than claiming that every training run must recover the dictionary. Experiments across several parameter regimes support the theory and show better empirical performance than the standard reconstruction objective.
summary.tldr: A masking objective can favor true dictionary recovery where standard noisy, over-realized sparse coding objectives can fail.

title: Hiding Data Helps: On the Benefits of Masking for Sparse Coding

abstract: Recently, the study of linear misspecified bandits has generated intriguing implications of the hardness of learning in bandits and reinforcement learning (RL). In particular, Du et al. (2020) shows that even if a learner is given linear features in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that approximate the rewards in a bandit or RL with a uniform error of $\varepsilon$, searching for an $O(\varepsilon)$-optimal action requires pulling at least $\Omega(\exp(d))$ queries. Furthermore, Lattimore et al. (2020) show that a degraded $O(\varepsilon\sqrt{d})$-optimal solution can be learned within $\operatorname{poly}(d/\varepsilon)$ queries. Yet it is unknown whether a structural assumption on the ground-truth parameter, such as sparsity, could break $\varepsilon\sqrt{d}$ barrier. In this paper, we address this question by showing that algorithms can obtain $O(\varepsilon)$-optimal actions by querying $\tilde{O}(\exp(m\varepsilon))$ actions, where $m$ is the sparsity parameter, removing the $\exp(d)$-dependence. We further show (with an information-theoretical lower bound) that this is the best possible if one demands an error $ m^{\delta}\varepsilon$ for $0<\delta<1$. We further show that $\operatorname{poly}(m/\varepsilon)$ bounds are possible when the linear features are "good”. These results provide a nearly complete picture of how sparsity can help in misspecified bandit learning and provide a deeper understanding of when linear features are “useful” for bandit and reinforcement learning with misspecification.

paragraphs: A misspecified linear bandit provides features that approximate action rewards but leave a uniform error of epsilon. The paper asks whether sparsity in the underlying parameter makes finding a good action easier. Without such structure, prior results require exponentially many queries in feature dimension d for O(epsilon) accuracy, while polynomially many queries permit a weaker O(epsilon times square root of d) guarantee.

The authors show that sparsity changes this dependence. When m measures sparsity, an O(epsilon)-optimal action can be obtained with a query bound that, suppressing logarithmic factors, scales as exp(m epsilon). This removes the exponential dependence on the full dimension, although it does not make the general query requirement polynomial in sparsity.

Polynomial bounds in m/epsilon become possible when the features satisfy the paper’s additional “good” feature condition. Thus, sparsity helps, and feature quality further determines the achievable efficiency.
summary.tldr: Sparsity removes exponential dependence on full feature dimension in misspecified bandits, while polynomial query bounds require additional feature structure.

title: Does Sparsity Help in Learning Misspecified Linear Bandits?

abstract: In this work, we initiate the idea of using denoising diffusion models to learn priors for online decision making problems. We specifically focus on bandit meta-learning, aiming to learn a policy that performs well across bandit tasks of a same class. To this end, we train a diffusion model that learns the underlying task distribution and combine Thompson sampling with the learned prior to deal with new tasks at test time. Our posterior sampling algorithm carefully balances between the learned prior and the noisy observations that come from the learner’s interaction with the environment. To capture realistic bandit scenarios, we propose a novel diffusion model training procedure that trains from incomplete and noisy data, which could be of independent interest. Finally, our extensive experiments clearly demonstrate the potential of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: This paper explores diffusion models as a way to learn prior knowledge for online decisions. It focuses on bandit meta-learning, where experience across tasks from one class should help a learner handle new tasks from that class. The aim is to capture the task distribution in a form useful for subsequent decision-making.

The authors train a denoising diffusion model on that distribution and combine its learned prior with Thompson sampling at test time. Their posterior-sampling algorithm balances information from the prior against noisy observations collected through interaction with the environment. This allows the learned distribution and the accumulating evidence from the current task to jointly inform decisions.

The paper also introduces a diffusion-training procedure for incomplete and noisy data, reflecting the observations available in realistic bandit settings. Extensive experiments demonstrate the potential of the overall approach. The contribution is a connection between generative modeling and adaptive decision-making: a diffusion model supplies transferable distributional knowledge, while posterior sampling incorporates the evidence needed for each new task.
summary.tldr: The method learns a diffusion-model prior across bandit tasks and combines it with Thompson sampling and noisy observations on new tasks.

title: Thompson Sampling with Diffusion Generative Prior

abstract: Current visual detectors, though impressive within their training distribution, often fail to parse out-of-distribution scenes into their constituent entities. Recent test-time adaptation methods use auxiliary self-supervised losses to adapt the network parameters to each test example independently and have shown promising results towards generalization outside the training distribution for the task of image classification. In our work, we find evidence that these losses are insufficient for the task of scene decomposition, without also considering architectural inductive biases. Recent slot-centric generative models attempt to decompose scenes into entities in a self-supervised manner by reconstructing pixels. Drawing upon these two lines of work, we propose Slot-TTA, a semi-supervised slot-centric scene decomposition model that at test time is adapted per scene through gradient descent on reconstruction or cross-view synthesis objectives. We evaluate Slot-TTA across multiple input modalities, images or 3D point clouds, and show substantial out-of-distribution performance improvements against state-of-the-art supervised feed-forward detectors, and alternative test-time adaptation methods. Project Webpage: http://slot-tta.github.io/

paragraphs: Breaking a scene into individual entities becomes difficult when its appearance differs from the training data. Test-time adaptation updates a model using the current test example, often through a self-supervised objective. This paper finds evidence that such objectives alone are insufficient for scene decomposition unless the architecture also provides useful biases for organizing scenes into entities.

Slot-TTA combines test-time adaptation with a semi-supervised, slot-centric model. Its slots provide a structure for representing separate entities. For each new scene, the model is adapted through gradient descent using either reconstruction or cross-view synthesis objectives. These objectives let the model adjust using the observed scene rather than requiring a new set of test-time annotations.

The authors evaluate the approach on both images and three-dimensional point clouds. They report substantial out-of-distribution improvements over state-of-the-art supervised feed-forward detectors and alternative adaptation methods. The findings support combining an entity-oriented architecture with per-scene optimization, showing that the structure of the model matters alongside the self-supervised signal used to adapt it.
summary.tldr: Slot-TTA combines entity-oriented representations with per-scene test-time adaptation to improve decomposition of unfamiliar images and point clouds.

title: Test-time Adaptation with Slot-Centric Models

abstract: Parameter-space regularization in neural network optimization is a fundamental tool for improving generalization. However, standard parameter-space regularization methods make it challenging to encode explicit preferences about desired predictive functions into neural network training. In this work, we approach regularization in neural networks from a probabilistic perspective and show that by viewing parameter-space regularization as specifying an empirical prior distribution over the model parameters, we can derive a probabilistically well-motivated regularization technique that allows explicitly encoding information about desired predictive functions into neural network training. This method—which we refer to as function-space empirical Bayes (FS-EB)—includes both parameter- and function-space regularization, is mathematically simple, easy to implement, and incurs only minimal computational overhead compared to standard regularization techniques. We evaluate the utility of this regularization technique empirically and demonstrate that the proposed method leads to near-perfect semantic shift detection, highly-calibrated predictive uncertainty estimates, successful task adaption from pre-trained models, and improved generalization under covariate shift.
