paragraphs: Regularization helps neural networks generalize by expressing preferences during training. Standard methods usually act on model parameters, which makes it difficult to state directly how predictions should behave. This paper develops a probabilistic route to regularizing predictive functions, allowing desired behavior to enter training more explicitly than through parameter preferences alone.

The authors interpret parameter regularization as specifying an empirical prior over model parameters. From that starting point, they derive function-space empirical Bayes, or FS-EB. The method combines parameter-space and function-space regularization, so preferences can address both the model's numerical representation and the functions it produces. They describe the resulting approach as mathematically simple, straightforward to implement, and requiring little additional computation.

Empirical evaluations report nearly perfect semantic-shift detection, well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, successful adaptation of pretrained models to tasks, and better generalization under covariate shift. These findings show several ways that explicit preferences about predictive behavior can be useful. Their scope is the evaluated settings: the reported outcomes support the method's utility without establishing that every possible functional preference will improve every application.
summary.tldr: FS-EB combines parameter and function regularization to encode desired predictive behavior, with empirical benefits for uncertainty, adaptation, and distribution shifts.

title: Function-Space Regularization in Neural Networks: A Probabilistic Perspective

abstract: In order for agents in multi-agent systems (MAS) to be safe, they need to take into account the risks posed by the actions of other agents. However, the dominant paradigm in game theory (GT) assumes that agents are not affected by risk from other agents and only strive to maximise their expected utility. For example, in hybrid human-AI driving systems, it is necessary to limit large deviations in reward resulting from car crashes. Although there are equilibrium concepts in game theory that take into account risk aversion, they either assume that agents are risk-neutral with respect to the uncertainty caused by the actions of other agents, or they are not guaranteed to exist. We introduce a new GT-based Risk-Averse Equilibrium (RAE) that always produces a solution that minimises the potential variance in reward accounting for the strategy of other agents. Theoretically and empirically, we show RAE shares many properties with a Nash Equilibrium (NE), establishing convergence properties and generalising to risk-dominant NE in certain cases. To tackle large-scale problems, we extend RAE to the PSRO multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework. We empirically demonstrate the minimum reward variance benefits of RAE in matrix games with high-risk outcomes. Results on MARL experiments show RAE generalises to risk-dominant NE in a trust dilemma game and that it reduces instances of crashing by 7x in an autonomous driving setting versus the best performing baseline.

Maximizing expected reward can leave large fluctuations in outcomes insufficiently addressed, which matters when an unfavorable outcome is a collision. This paper develops an equilibrium concept that explicitly accounts for reward variability arising from other agents’ strategies.

summary.tldr: Risk-Averse Equilibrium accounts for reward variability caused by other agents and reduces crashes sevenfold in the evaluated driving setting.

title: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Managing Risk in Multi-Agent Systems

abstract: We present an adaptive approach for robust learning from corrupted training sets. We identify corrupted and non-corrupted samples with latent Bernoulli variables and thus formulate the learning problem as maximization of the likelihood where latent variables are marginalized. The resulting problem is solved via variational inference, using an efficient Expectation-Maximization based method. The proposed approach improves over the state-of-the-art by automatically inferring the corruption level, while adding minimal computational overhead. We demonstrate our robust learning method and its parameter-free nature on a wide variety of machine learning tasks including online learning and deep learning where it adapts to different levels of noise and maintains high prediction accuracy.

The proposed approach improves over the state-of-the-art by automatically inferring the corruption level, while adding minimal computational overhead. paragraphs: Learning from corrupted training data requires handling samples that may give misleading information. This paper proposes an adaptive method that represents each sample’s corruption status with a hidden binary variable. A Bernoulli variable can express the two possibilities, corrupted or uncorrupted, while allowing the model to remain uncertain about which possibility applies.

The authors formulate training as likelihood maximization with these hidden variables marginalized out. In plain language, the objective accounts for possible corruption assignments instead of requiring the assignments to be supplied beforehand. They solve the resulting problem through variational inference using an efficient method based on Expectation-Maximization. A central feature is that the method infers the corruption level automatically.

The reported evaluations span multiple learning tasks, including online learning and deep learning. The method adapts to different noise levels while maintaining high prediction accuracy, and the authors report improvements over prior leading approaches with minimal computational overhead. Its described parameter-free character matters here because adaptation to corruption does not depend on a manually supplied corruption level.
summary.tldr: Hidden binary corruption variables let a robust learning method infer noise levels automatically with minimal computational overhead.

title: Adaptive Robust Learning using Latent Bernoulli Variables

abstract: Handling the substantial communication burden in federated learning (FL) still remains a significant challenge. Although recent studies have attempted to compress the local gradients to address this issue, they typically perform compression only within the original parameter space, which may potentially limit the fundamental compression rate of the gradient. In this paper, instead of restricting our scope to a fixed traditional space, we consider an alternative space that provides an improved compressibility of the gradient. To this end, we utilize the structures of input activation and output gradient in designing our mapping function to a new space, which enables lossless gradient sparsification, i.e., mapping the gradient to our new space induces a greater number of near-zero elements without any loss of information. In light of this attribute, employing sparsification-based compressors in our new space allows for more aggressive compression with minimal information loss than the baselines. More surprisingly, our model even reaches higher accuracies than the full gradient uploading strategy in some cases, an extra benefit for utilizing the new space. We also theoretically confirm that our approach does not alter the existing, best known convergence rate of FL thanks to the orthogonal transformation properties of our mapping.

In light of this attribute, employing sparsification-based compressors in our new space allows for more aggressive compression with minimal information loss than the baselines. We also theoretically confirm that our approach does not alter the existing, best known convergence rate of FL thanks to the orthogonal transformation properties of our mapping.

paragraphs: Federated learning requires clients to communicate model updates, and those messages can become expensive. Gradient compression reduces that burden, but the paper questions whether the usual parameter coordinates are the best place to compress. Its central idea is to change the representation of a gradient before applying a compressor.

The proposed mapping uses the structure of input activations and output gradients to produce an alternative space with more near-zero elements. The transformation itself preserves information. This distinction matters: the lossless claim concerns the change of representation, while subsequently discarding small elements can still introduce information loss. A representation with more small entries makes more aggressive sparsification possible with minimal loss.

The authors report stronger compression than the baselines and, in some cases, higher accuracy than uploading full gradients. They also show theoretically that the mapping preserves the existing best-known federated-learning convergence rate through its orthogonal transformation properties. Together, these findings suggest that choosing the coordinates for compression can matter alongside choosing the compressor.
summary.tldr: An information-preserving change of gradient coordinates enables more aggressive communication compression in federated learning with minimal information loss.

title: Achieving Lossless Gradient Sparsification via Mapping to Alternative Space in Federated Learning

abstract: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are non-invasive diagnostic tools crucial for detecting cardiac arrhythmic diseases in clinical practice. While ECG Self-supervised Learning (eSSL) methods show promise in representation learning from unannotated ECG data, they often overlook the clinical knowledge that can be found in reports. This oversight and the requirement for annotated samples for downstream tasks limit eSSL’s versatility. In this work, we address these issues with the Multimodal ECG Representation Learning (MERL) framework. Through multimodal learning on ECG records and associated reports, MERL is capable of performing zero-shot ECG classification with text prompts, eliminating the need for training data in downstream tasks. At test time, we propose the Clinical Knowledge Enhanced Prompt Engineering (CKEPE) approach, which uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to exploit external expert-verified clinical knowledge databases, generating more descriptive prompts and reducing hallucinations in LLM-generated content to boost zero-shot classification. Based on MERL, we perform the first benchmark across six public ECG datasets, showing the superior performance of MERL compared against eSSL methods. Notably, MERL achieves an average AUC score of 75.2% in zero-shot classification (without training data), 3.2% higher than linear probed eSSL methods with 10% annotated training data, averaged across all six datasets.

It uses large language models with external, expert-verified clinical knowledge databases to produce more descriptive prompts. The approach is intended to reduce hallucinations in generated content and strengthen the text descriptions used for zero-shot ECG classification.

The absence of training data refers to the downstream classification tasks; MERL itself learns from paired records and reports. These results support combining multimodal pretraining with clinically informed test-time prompts to reduce downstream annotation requirements.
summary.tldr: MERL learns from ECG–report pairs and uses clinically enhanced text prompts to classify ECGs without downstream training data.

title: Zero-Shot ECG Classification with Multimodal Learning and Test-time Clinical Knowledge Enhancement

abstract: Simplicial neural network models are becoming popular for processing and analyzing higher-order graph data, but they suffer from high training complexity and dependence on task-specific labels. To address these challenges, we propose simplicial scattering networks (SSNs), a parameter-free model inspired by scattering transforms designed to extract task-agnostic features from simplicial complex data without labels in a principled manner. Specifically, we propose a simplicial scattering transform based on random walk matrices for various adjacencies underlying a simplicial complex. We then use the simplicial scattering transform to construct a deep filter bank network that captures high-frequency information at multiple scales. The proposed simplicial scattering transform possesses properties such as permutation invariance, robustness to perturbations, and expressivity. We theoretically prove that including higher-order information improves the robustness of SSNs to perturbations. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that SSNs outperform existing simplicial or graph neural models in many tasks like node classification, simplicial closure, graph classification, trajectory prediction, and simplex prediction while being computationally efficient.

paragraphs: Simplicial data represents higher-order relationships that go beyond ordinary graph connections. Neural models for this data can be costly to train and dependent on labels for a specific task. This paper introduces simplicial scattering networks, or SSNs, to extract task-independent representations without labels or learned parameters.

The method constructs scattering transforms from random-walk matrices associated with different adjacencies in a simplicial complex. These transforms form a deep bank of filters that captures high-frequency information across multiple scales. The design provides a structured way to extract features while avoiding the parameter-training process of a conventional neural representation model.

The authors establish permutation invariance, robustness to perturbations, and expressivity properties. They also prove that incorporating higher-order information improves robustness. Empirical evaluations report computational efficiency and stronger performance than existing simplicial or graph neural models across many tasks, including classification, trajectory prediction, and simplex prediction. These findings support fixed, mathematically structured feature extraction as a useful approach to higher-order data, with theoretical properties complementing the task evaluations.
summary.tldr: Simplicial scattering networks extract label-free, parameter-free higher-order features with theoretical robustness properties and strong empirical performance.

title: Unsupervised Parameter-free Simplicial Representation Learning with Scattering Transforms

abstract: Bilevel optimization has been recently applied to many machine learning tasks. However, their applications have been restricted to the supervised learning setting, where static objective functions with benign structures are considered. But bilevel problems such as incentive design, inverse reinforcement learning (RL), and RL from human feedback (RLHF) are often modeled as dynamic objective functions that go beyond the simple static objective structures, which pose significant challenges of using existing bilevel solutions. To tackle this new class of bilevel problems, we introduce the first principled algorithmic framework for solving bilevel RL problems through the lens of penalty formulation. We provide theoretical studies of the problem landscape and its penalty-based (policy) gradient algorithms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms via simulations in the Stackelberg game and RLHF.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization models situations where one optimization objective depends on the solution to another. Existing applications have largely focused on supervised learning with static objectives and favorable structure. Reinforcement learning introduces dynamic objectives, creating additional difficulties for problems such as incentive design, inverse reinforcement learning, and learning from human feedback.

The paper develops a framework for these bilevel reinforcement learning problems using penalty formulations. The central move is to express the nested optimization relationship through a penalized problem, creating a basis for gradient and policy-gradient algorithms. This gives the authors a common algorithmic approach to settings that extend beyond the static objectives considered by existing methods.

The contribution includes theoretical analysis of the optimization landscape and of the resulting penalty-based algorithms. Simulations in a Stackelberg game and reinforcement learning from human feedback demonstrate their effectiveness. These results connect the formulation to concrete settings involving interacting objectives, while the theoretical work provides a principled foundation for studying how such nested reinforcement learning problems can be solved.
summary.tldr: A penalty-based framework brings theoretical analysis and gradient algorithms to bilevel reinforcement learning, with demonstrations in games and RLHF.

title: Principled Penalty-based Methods for Bilevel Reinforcement Learning and RLHF

abstract: With the prevalence of pre-training-fine-tuning paradigm, how to efficiently adapt the pre-trained model to the downstream tasks has been an intriguing issue. $\textbf{P}$arameter-$\textbf{E}$fficient $\textbf{F}$ine-$\textbf{T}$uning(PEFT) methods have been proposed for low-cost adaptation. Although PEFT has demonstrated effectiveness and been widely applied, the underlying principles are still unclear. In this paper, we adopt the PAC-Bayesian generalization error bound, viewing pre-training as a shift of prior distribution which leads to a tighter bound for generalization error. We validate this shift from the perspectives of oscillations in the loss landscape and the quasi-sparsity in gradient distribution. Based on this, we propose a gradient-based sparse fine-tuning algorithm, named $\textbf{S}$parse $\textbf{I}$ncrement $\textbf{F}$ine-$\textbf{T}$uning(SIFT), and validate its effectiveness on a range of tasks including the GLUE Benchmark and Instruction-tuning. The code is accessible at https://github.com/song-wx/SIFT/.

Although PEFT has demonstrated effectiveness and been widely applied, the underlying principles are still unclear. We validate this shift from the perspectives of oscillations in the loss landscape and the quasi-sparsity in gradient distribution. The code is accessible at https://github.com/song-wx/SIFT/.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts pretrained models at lower cost, but its effectiveness calls for a theoretical explanation. This paper uses a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound to study that question. It interprets pretraining as a change in the prior distribution that yields a tighter bound on generalization error.

The authors examine this interpretation through two properties of the pretrained model: oscillations in the loss landscape and quasi-sparsity in the gradient distribution. Together, these analyses connect the proposed explanation of pretraining to the behavior of optimization during adaptation. The sparse structure observed in gradients motivates focusing fine-tuning changes on selected parameters.

Based on this reasoning, the paper introduces Sparse Increment Fine-Tuning, or SIFT, a gradient-based sparse fine-tuning algorithm. Evaluations on tasks including the GLUE benchmark and instruction tuning support its effectiveness. The work links a generalization-bound perspective to a concrete adaptation method: the theory motivates sparse updates, and the task evaluations assess whether that strategy works in practice. The abstract does not claim that one sparse update pattern suffices for every task.
summary.tldr: The paper motivates sparse fine-tuning through a PAC-Bayesian view of pretraining and introduces SIFT, validated on GLUE and instruction-tuning tasks.

title: Sparse is Enough in Fine-tuning Pre-trained Large Language Models

abstract: Dataset distillation has emerged as a strategy to overcome the hurdles associated with large datasets by learning a compact set of synthetic data that retains essential information from the original dataset. While distilled data can be used to train high performing models, little is understood about how the information is stored. In this study, we posit and answer three questions about the behavior, representativeness, and point-wise information content of distilled data. We reveal distilled data cannot serve as a substitute for real data during training outside the standard evaluation setting for dataset distillation. Additionally, the distillation process retains high task performance by compressing information related to the early training dynamics of real models. Finally, we provide an framework for interpreting distilled data and reveal that individual distilled data points contain meaningful semantic information. This investigation sheds light on the intricate nature of distilled data, providing a better understanding on how they can be effectively utilized.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation creates a small synthetic dataset that retains useful information from a larger real dataset. Models trained on these compact datasets can perform well, but that success leaves open what the synthetic examples actually encode. This paper investigates their behavior, representativeness, and the information carried by individual examples.

The study finds that distilled data cannot replace real training data outside the standard dataset-distillation evaluation setting. It also identifies a mechanism behind retained task performance: distillation compresses information associated with the early training dynamics of models trained on real data. This connects the usefulness of distilled examples to the learning process they reproduce.

The authors additionally provide an interpretation framework and show that individual distilled points contain meaningful semantic information. Together, the findings describe distilled data as carrying both training-related information and interpretable content. They clarify why strong performance in the standard evaluation setting does not establish general interchangeability with real data, while explaining some of the information that enables compact synthetic datasets to work.
summary.tldr: Distilled datasets encode early training dynamics and meaningful semantics, but do not generally substitute for real data outside standard distillation evaluation.

title: What is Dataset Distillation Learning?

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer remarkable capabilities, yet their high inference costs restrict wider adoption. While increasing parameter counts improves accuracy, it also broadens the gap between state-of-the-art capabilities and practical deployability. We present Puzzle, a hardware-aware framework that accelerates the inference of LLMs while preserving their capabilities. Using neural architecture search (NAS) at a large-scale, Puzzle optimizes models with tens of billions of parameters. Our approach utilizes blockwise local knowledge distillation (BLD) for parallel architecture exploration and employs mixed-integer programming for precise constraint optimization. We showcase our framework’s impact via Llama-3.1-Nemotron-51B-Instruct (Nemotron-51B) and Llama-3.3-Nemotron-49B, two publicly available models derived from Llama-70B-Instruct. Both models achieve a 2.17x inference throughput speedup, fitting on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU while retaining 98.4% of the original model’s benchmark accuracies. These are the most accurate models supporting single H100 GPU inference with large batch sizes, despite training on 45B tokens at most, far fewer than the 15T used to train Llama-70B. Lastly, we show that lightweight alignment on these derived models allows them to surpass the parent model in specific capabilities. Our work establishes that powerful LLM models can be optimized for efficient deployment with only negligible loss in quality, underscoring that inference performance, not parameter count alone, should guide model selection.

It applies neural architecture search to models with tens of billions of parameters. The central idea is to select an architecture according to deployment performance and constraints, rather than treating parameter count as the sole guide.

summary.tldr: Puzzle combines distillation and hardware-aware architecture search to deliver 2.17× throughput while retaining 98.4% of parent-model benchmark accuracies.

title: Puzzle: Distillation-Based NAS for Inference-Optimized LLMs

abstract: We revisit the problem of distribution learning within the framework of learning-augmented algorithms. In this setting, we explore the scenario where a probability distribution is provided as potentially inaccurate advice on the true, unknown distribution. Our objective is to develop learning algorithms whose sample complexity decreases as the quality of the advice improves, thereby surpassing standard learning lower bounds when the advice is sufficiently accurate. Specifically, we demonstrate that this outcome is achievable for the problem of learning a multivariate Gaussian distribution $N(\mu, \Sigma)$ in the PAC learning setting. Classically, in the advice-free setting, $\widetilde{\Theta}(d^2/\varepsilon^2)$ samples are sufficient and worst case necessary to learn $d$-dimensional Gaussians up to TV distance $\varepsilon$ with constant probability. When we are additionally given a parameter $\widetilde{\Sigma}$ as advice, we show that $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{2-\beta}/\varepsilon^2)$ samples suffices whenever $|| \widetilde{\Sigma}^{-1/2} \Sigma \widetilde{\Sigma}^{-1/2} - I_d ||_1 \leq \varepsilon d^{1-\beta}$ (where $||\cdot||_1$ denotes the entrywise $\ell_1$ norm) for any $\beta > 0$, yielding a polynomial improvement over the advice-free setting.

paragraphs: Learning a multivariate Gaussian distribution from samples requires estimating its structure accurately enough to approximate the full distribution. This paper asks how much data can be saved when the learner also receives potentially inaccurate advice. The goal is for better advice to translate into lower sample requirements.

The concrete result concerns advice about the covariance matrix. Without advice, learning a d-dimensional Gaussian to total variation error ε with constant success probability requires roughly d²/ε² samples in the worst case, ignoring logarithmic factors. The authors show that roughly d^(2−β)/ε² samples suffice under a specified accuracy condition on the supplied covariance estimate.

That condition measures the entrywise absolute error after transforming the true covariance using the advised covariance: the resulting matrix must lie within εd^(1−β) of the identity in entrywise ℓ₁ norm. For β greater than zero, the stated bound yields a polynomial improvement in dimension. The improvement is conditional on advice quality; it surpasses the advice-free requirement because the learner receives useful additional information.
summary.tldr: Sufficiently accurate covariance advice enables a polynomial reduction in the samples needed to learn a multivariate Gaussian.

title: Learning multivariate Gaussians with imperfect advice

abstract: Type inference for dynamic languages like Python is a persistent challenge in software engineering. While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in code understanding, their type inference capabilities remain underexplored. We introduce TypyBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs’ type inference across entire Python repositories. TypyBench features two novel metrics: TypeSim, which captures nuanced semantic relationships between predicted and ground truth types, and TypeCheck, which assesses type consistency across codebases. Our evaluation of various LLMs on a curated dataset of 50 high-quality Python repositories reveals that, although LLMs achieve decent TypeSim scores, they struggle with complex nested types and exhibit significant type consistency errors. These findings suggest that future research should shift focus from improving type similarity to addressing repository-level consistency. TypyBench provides a foundation for this new direction, offering insights into model performance across different type complexities and usage contexts. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/typybench/typybench

paragraphs: Inferring types in Python is challenging because programs can operate without explicit type annotations. This paper introduces TypyBench to evaluate how well language models infer types across entire repositories. The broader scope matters because an individually plausible type prediction must also fit with how values and functions are used throughout the codebase.

TypyBench introduces two complementary metrics. TypeSim measures semantic relationships between a predicted type and the reference type, recognizing more than exact textual agreement. TypeCheck assesses consistency across the repository. Together, these metrics separate the question of whether a prediction resembles the expected type from whether the collection of predictions works coherently across the program.

Evaluations on 50 curated Python repositories find that models achieve decent TypeSim scores but struggle with complex nested types and produce substantial consistency errors. The results suggest that better local similarity alone will not resolve repository-level inference problems. The benchmark supports a research focus on types that remain compatible across their different usage contexts.
summary.tldr: TypyBench finds that plausible Python type predictions can still be inconsistent across repositories, highlighting a gap in LLM type inference.

title: TypyBench: Evaluating LLM Type Inference for Untyped Python Repositories

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) create samples from a data distribution by starting from random noise and iteratively solving a reverse-time ordinary differential equation (ODE). Because each step in the iterative solution requires an expensive neural function evaluation (NFE), there has been significant interest in approximately solving these diffusion ODEs with only a few NFEs without modifying the underlying model. However, in the few NFE regime, we observe that tracking the true ODE evolution is fundamentally impossible using traditional ODE solvers. In this work, we propose a new method that learns a good solver for the DM, which we call Solving for the Solver (S4S). S4S directly optimizes a solver to obtain good generation quality by learning to match the output of a strong teacher solver. We evaluate S4S on six different pre-trained DMs, including pixel-space and latent-space DMs for both conditional and unconditional sampling. In all settings, S4S uniformly improves the sample quality relative to traditional ODE solvers. Moreover, our method is lightweight, data-free, and can be plugged in black-box on top of any discretization schedule or architecture to improve performance. Building on top of this, we also propose S4S-Alt, which optimizes both the solver and the discretization schedule. By exploiting the full design space of DM solvers, with 5 NFEs, we achieve an FID of 3.73 on CIFAR10 and 13.26 on MS-COCO, representing a $1.5\times$ improvement over previous training-free ODE methods.

With only a few evaluations, the authors find that traditional solvers cannot faithfully track the underlying trajectory. S4S addresses this by learning a solver whose objective is to produce good final samples by matching a strong teacher solver.

The approach optimizes the sampling procedure without modifying the underlying diffusion model. It is lightweight and data-free, and the authors describe it as compatible with arbitrary discretization schedules and architectures through black-box use. A further variant, S4S-Alt, jointly optimizes the solver and its discretization schedule, expanding which parts of the sampling process can adapt.

The authors characterize these results as a 1.5-fold improvement over previous training-free ODE methods.
summary.tldr: S4S learns a diffusion sampling solver from a stronger teacher to improve sample quality with very few neural-network evaluations.

title: S4S: Solving for a Fast Diffusion Model Solver

abstract: World models aim to learn action-controlled future prediction and have proven essential for the development of intelligent agents. However, most existing world models rely heavily on substantial action-labeled data and costly training, making it challenging to adapt to novel environments with heterogeneous actions through limited interactions. This limitation can hinder their applicability across broader domains. To overcome this limitation, we propose AdaWorld, an innovative world model learning approach that enables efficient adaptation. The key idea is to incorporate action information during the pretraining of world models. This is achieved by extracting latent actions from videos in a self-supervised manner, capturing the most critical transitions between frames. We then develop an autoregressive world model that conditions on these latent actions. This learning paradigm enables highly adaptable world models, facilitating efficient transfer and learning of new actions even with limited interactions and finetuning. Our comprehensive experiments across multiple environments demonstrate that AdaWorld achieves superior performance in both simulation quality and visual planning.

paragraphs: A world model predicts how an environment changes in response to actions. Adapting such a model becomes difficult when a new environment uses different actions and offers only limited opportunities for interaction. AdaWorld addresses this problem by incorporating action information during pretraining, without requiring explicit action labels for the videos used to learn that information.

The method extracts latent actions from videos through self-supervised learning. These learned representations capture important transitions between frames. An autoregressive world model then uses the latent actions to condition its predictions, learning how visual changes relate to this internal action representation. This gives subsequent adaptation a foundation that already connects action information with changes in the environment.

The authors report that this approach supports transfer and learning of new actions with limited interactions and finetuning. Across multiple environments, AdaWorld achieves superior simulation quality and visual planning performance in the reported experiments. The findings support learning action-related structure before adaptation as a way to make world models more reusable across environments with different action systems.
summary.tldr: AdaWorld learns latent actions from videos during pretraining to help world models adapt to new environments with limited interaction and finetuning.

title: AdaWorld: Learning Adaptable World Models with Latent Actions

abstract: Time series forecasting methods generally fall into two main categories: Channel Independent (CI) and Channel Dependent (CD) strategies. While CI overlooks important covariate relationships, CD captures all dependencies without distinction, introducing noise and reducing generalization. Recent advances in Channel Clustering (CC) aim to refine dependency modeling by grouping channels with similar characteristics and applying tailored modeling techniques. However, coarse-grained clustering struggles to capture complex, time-varying interactions effectively. To address these challenges, we propose TimeFilter, a GNN-based framework for adaptive and fine-grained dependency modeling. After constructing the graph from the input sequence, TimeFilter refines the learned spatial-temporal dependencies by filtering out irrelevant correlations while preserving the most critical ones in a patch-specific manner. Extensive experiments on 13 real-world datasets from diverse application domains demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of TimeFilter. The code is available at https://github.com/TROUBADOUR000/TimeFilter.

paragraphs: Forecasting multiple time-series channels requires deciding which relationships deserve attention. Modeling channels independently misses useful connections, while treating all dependencies alike can introduce noise. Grouping similar channels improves this choice, but coarse groups can fail to capture interactions that are complex or change over time.

TimeFilter uses a graph neural network to make dependency modeling more fine-grained and adaptive. It first constructs a graph from the input sequence, then refines the learned relationships across channels and time. Filtering takes place separately for individual patches, removing irrelevant correlations while preserving the connections considered most important for that patch.

This design lets the treatment of dependencies vary within a sequence instead of relying only on a fixed channel grouping. Experiments on 13 real-world datasets spanning diverse application domains report state-of-the-art forecasting performance. The findings support selective dependency modeling as a useful component of forecasting: the benefit comes from identifying relevant relationships at the local patch level, where broad channel-level decisions can be too coarse.
summary.tldr: TimeFilter improves forecasting by filtering channel and temporal relationships separately for each patch of a time series.

title: TimeFilter: Patch-Specific Spatial-Temporal Graph Filtration for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: The current Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) Learning paradigm suffers from an over-reliance on labeled data, so if we completely disregard labels, it leads to less symbol information, a larger solution space, and more shortcuts—issues that current Nesy systems cannot resolve. This paper introduces a novel learning paradigm, Verification Learning (VL), which addresses this challenge by transforming the label-based reasoning process in Nesy into a label-free verification process. VL achieves excellent learning results solely by relying on unlabeled data and a function that verifies whether the current predictions conform to the rules. We formalize this problem as a Constraint Optimization Problem (COP) and propose a Dynamic Combinatorial Sorting (DCS) algorithm that accelerates the solution by reducing verification attempts, effectively lowering computational costs and introduce a prior alignment method to address potential shortcuts. Our theoretical analysis points out which tasks in Nesy systems can be completed without labels and explains why rules can replace infinite labels for some tasks, while for others the rules have no effect. We validate the proposed framework through several fully unsupervised tasks including addition, sort, match, and chess, each showing significant performance and efficiency improvements.

paragraphs: Verification Learning asks when neuro-symbolic systems can learn without labeled examples. Removing labels leaves fewer clues about symbols, more possible solutions, and opportunities for shortcuts. The proposed approach replaces label-based reasoning with a verification function that checks whether current predictions satisfy rules, using that feedback together with unlabeled data.

The authors formulate learning as a constraint optimization problem. Their Dynamic Combinatorial Sorting algorithm reduces the number of verification attempts needed, lowering computational costs. A separate prior alignment method addresses potential shortcuts. These components tackle both the difficulty of searching through possible predictions and the risk that a rule-compatible solution may exploit an unintended shortcut.

The theoretical analysis distinguishes tasks for which rules can replace unlimited labels from tasks for which the rules provide no benefit. That distinction is central: label-free learning depends on what the rules can establish for the particular task. Experiments on fully unsupervised addition, sorting, matching, and chess tasks report significant improvements in performance and efficiency, supporting the framework in those tested settings.
summary.tldr: Verification Learning trains neuro-symbolic systems from unlabeled data and rule checks, while analyzing which tasks can benefit from replacing labels with rules.

title: Verification Learning: Make Unsupervised Neuro-Symbolic System Feasible

abstract: Drag-based editing allows precise object manipulation through point-based control, offering user convenience. However, current methods often suffer from a geometric inconsistency problem by focusing exclusively on matching user-defined points, neglecting the broader geometry and leading to artifacts or unstable edits. We propose FlowDrag, which leverages geometric information for more accurate and coherent transformations. Our approach constructs a 3D mesh from the image, using an energy function to guide mesh deformation based on user-defined drag points. The resulting mesh displacements are projected into 2D and incorporated into a UNet denoising process, enabling precise handle-to-target point alignment while preserving structural integrity. Additionally, existing drag-editing benchmarks provide no ground truth, making it difficult to assess how accurately the edits match the intended transformations. To address this, we present VFD (VidFrameDrag) benchmark dataset, which provides ground-truth frames using consecutive shots in a video dataset. FlowDrag outperforms existing drag-based editing methods on both VFD Bench and DragBench.

paragraphs: Dragging points in an image offers a convenient way to specify an edit, but matching those points alone can distort the surrounding object. FlowDrag addresses this geometric inconsistency by using a three-dimensional representation to guide the transformation. The intended point movement is considered together with the broader structure it affects.

The method constructs a 3D mesh from the image and deforms it using an energy function guided by the user’s drag points. It projects the mesh displacements back into two dimensions and incorporates them into a UNet denoising process. This connects precise movement from selected handles to target locations with a deformation of the object’s surrounding geometry.

The paper also introduces VidFrameDrag, a benchmark that uses consecutive video frames to provide ground-truth target images. Such references make it possible to assess whether edits match intended transformations, addressing the absence of ground truth in existing drag-editing benchmarks. FlowDrag outperforms existing methods on both this benchmark and DragBench, supporting the use of mesh-derived geometric guidance for coherent image manipulation.
summary.tldr: FlowDrag uses projected 3D mesh deformations to guide coherent drag-based image edits and introduces video-derived ground truth for evaluation.

title: FlowDrag: 3D-aware Drag-based Image Editing with Mesh-guided Deformation Vector Flow Fields

abstract: We investigate the logical reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and their scalability across complex deductive tasks. Using ZebraLogic, a newly developed benchmark dataset of logic grid puzzles derived from constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), we systematically evaluate LLM performance. ZebraLogic spans a broad range of search space complexities and incorporates diverse logical constraints, providing a controlled environment to assess reasoning abilities. Our results reveal a significant decline in accuracy as problem complexity increases—a phenomenon we term the “curse of complexity.” Notably, this limitation persists even with scaling model size and inference-time computation, suggesting fundamental constraints in current LLM reasoning capabilities. Additionally, we explore strategies such as Best-of-N sampling, backtracking mechanisms, and self-verification prompts to enhance logical reasoning performance. Our findings provide critical insights into the scaling behavior of LLMs, highlight their limitations, and outline potential directions for advancing their reasoning capabilities.

This creates a controlled setting for examining how a model’s ability to reach correct conclusions changes as the reasoning problem becomes more demanding.

The result suggests constraints in current models’ reasoning capabilities, while remaining an empirical finding about the models and scaling approaches studied.

The paper also explores Best-of-N sampling, backtracking, and self-verification prompts as possible ways to improve performance. Its stated contribution is a clearer picture of how reasoning scales across controlled levels of difficulty. The benchmark makes it possible to investigate whether additional resources and generation strategies address the increasing demands of complex deduction.
summary.tldr: ZebraLogic finds that language-model accuracy declines sharply on harder logic puzzles, even with larger models and more inference computation.

title: ZebraLogic: On the Scaling Limits of LLMs for Logical Reasoning

abstract: Hierarchical and overlapping clustering are two prevalent phenomena that often coexist in real-world system. While numerous studies have examined these two structures separately, characterizing and evaluating their hybrid forms remains an open challenge. To bridge this gap, we initiate the study of hierarchical overlapping clustering on graphs by introducing a new cost function and establishing its rationality through several intuitive properties. We further develop an approximation algorithm that achieves a constant approximation factor for its dual version. Our approach employs a recursive overlapping bipartition framework based on local search, enabling a highly scalable speed-up variant. Experimental results demonstrate that this speed-up algorithm outperforms all baseline methods significantly in both effectiveness (across synthetic and real datasets) and scalability.

paragraphs: Groups in a graph can be nested within larger groups, and a node can belong to more than one group. These hierarchical and overlapping patterns often occur together, but studying them separately leaves the combined structure difficult to evaluate. This paper develops an objective and an algorithm for clustering that captures both.

The authors introduce a cost function and justify it through several intuitive properties. They also develop an approximation algorithm with a constant-factor guarantee for the dual version of the problem. The algorithm recursively divides groups into two potentially overlapping parts, using local search to find those divisions. That framework also supports a faster variant intended for large graphs.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the accelerated algorithm significantly outperforms all evaluated baselines in effectiveness and scalability. The work therefore contributes both a way to judge hierarchical overlapping clusterings and a practical way to produce them. The theoretical approximation statement applies specifically to the dual formulation, while the scalability findings come from the experimental evaluation.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces an objective and scalable algorithm for graph clusters that are both nested and overlapping.

title: Hierarchical Overlapping Clustering on Graphs: Cost Function, Algorithm and Scalability

abstract: Modern machine learning pipelines are increasingly combining and mixing data from diverse and disparate sources, e.g., pre-training large language models. Yet, finding the optimal data mixture is a challenging and open problem. We formalize this data mixing problem as a bi-level objective: the best mixture is the one that would lead to the best model for a downstream objective. Unfortunately, this objective is generally intractable. In this paper, we make the observation that the bi-level data mixing objective becomes convex as our model class becomes larger. We develop and study a gradient-based approach for optimizing this convex objective, which we call MixMin, and test it on language modeling and chemistry tasks. MixMin was the only method that uniformly improved the data mixture in all our experiments. With MixMin, we improved the data mixture using less than 0.2% additional compute for a pythia-$410M$ model trained on $8.2B$ tokens, resulting between 1-5% relative improvement to negative log likelihood on PIQA, ARC Easy, SciQ, and OpenWebMath. Crucially, we found that MixMin mixtures for smaller models improved training of larger models, suggesting that MixMin mixtures may be scale-invariant. When mixing bioassay data to train an XGBoost model, we saw improvements to average precision scores of $0.03-0.15$.

paragraphs: Choosing how much training data to draw from each source can substantially affect a model’s downstream usefulness. MixMin formulates this choice as a nested optimization problem: a mixture is good when training on it produces a model that performs well on the downstream objective. Directly solving that problem is generally intractable.

summary.tldr: MixMin uses convex optimization to select training-data mixtures, improving language and chemistry results with low reported selection overhead.

title: MixMin: Finding Data Mixtures via Convex Minimization

abstract: Trajectory representation learning aims to transform raw trajectory data into compact and low-dimensional vectors that are suitable for downstream analysis. However, most existing methods adopt either a free-space view or a road-network view during the learning process, which limits their ability to capture the complex, multi-view spatiotemporal features inherent in trajectory data. Moreover, these approaches rely on task-specific model training, restricting their generalizability and effectiveness for diverse analysis tasks. To this end, we propose GTR, a general, multi-view, and dynamic Trajectory Representation framework built on a pre-train and fine-tune architecture. Specifically, GTR introduces a multi-view encoder that captures the intrinsic multi-view spatiotemporal features. Based on the pre-train and fine-tune architecture, we provide the spatio-temporal fusion pre-training with a spatio-temporal mixture of experts to dynamically combine spatial and temporal features, enabling seamless adaptation to diverse trajectory analysis tasks. Furthermore, we propose an online frozen-hot updating strategy to efficiently update the representation model, accommodating the dynamic nature of trajectory data. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that GTR consistently outperforms 15 state-of-the-art methods across 6 mainstream trajectory analysis tasks. All source code and data are available at https://github.com/ZJU-DAILY/GTR.

Existing methods often use either a free-space perspective or a road-network perspective, limiting the spatial and temporal information they capture. They also commonly train for individual tasks. Its multi-view encoder captures complementary features of trajectories. The pre-train-and-fine-tune structure then supports adapting these representations to different analysis tasks, rather than requiring each task to begin with an entirely separate learning process.

Experiments on two real-world datasets report consistent improvements over 15 state-of-the-art methods across six trajectory-analysis tasks. The results support the value of combining multiple views, dynamic feature fusion, and ongoing updating within a reusable representation framework.
summary.tldr: GTR learns reusable trajectory representations through multiple views, dynamic spatial-temporal fusion, and efficient online updating.

title: GTR: A General, Multi-View, and Dynamic Framework for Trajectory Representation Learning

abstract: High-resolution (HR) image perception remains a key challenge in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). To drive progress beyond the limits of heuristic methods, this paper advances HR perception capabilities of MLLMs by harnessing cutting-edge long-context techniques such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Towards this end, this paper presents the first study exploring the use of RAG to address HR perception challenges. Specifically, we propose Retrieval-Augmented Perception (RAP), a training-free framework that retrieves and fuses relevant image crops while preserving spatial context using the proposed Spatial-Awareness Layout. To accommodate different tasks, the proposed Retrieved-Exploration Search (RE-Search) dynamically selects the optimal number of crops based on model confidence and retrieval scores. Experimental results on HR benchmarks demonstrate the significant effectiveness of RAP, with LLaVA-v1.5-13B achieving a 43% improvement on $V^*$ Bench and 19% on HR-Bench. Code is available at https://github.com/DreamMr/RAP.

paragraphs: High-resolution images present multimodal language models with a large amount of visual information to process. Retrieval-Augmented Perception, or RAP, applies retrieval ideas to this challenge by selecting relevant image crops. The framework requires no training and combines the retrieved regions into information the model can use for its task.

Selecting a crop alone does not preserve its relationship to the full image. RAP therefore introduces a Spatial-Awareness Layout to retain spatial context when fusing crops. Its Retrieved-Exploration Search also adjusts how many regions to select, using model confidence and retrieval scores. This lets the amount of retrieved visual material respond to the task rather than remain fixed.

Experiments on high-resolution benchmarks report a 43% improvement on V* Bench and a 19% improvement on HR-Bench for LLaVA-v1.5-13B. These findings support retrieving relevant visual regions while preserving their layout as an effective way to improve perception in the evaluated setting. The method combines selection of image detail with control over how much detail is supplied.
summary.tldr: RAP improves high-resolution image perception by dynamically retrieving relevant crops and preserving their spatial context without training.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Perception: High-resolution Image Perception Meets Visual RAG

abstract: The entropic-regularized optimal transport (OT) has gained massive attention in machine learning due to its ability to provide scalable solutions for OT-based tasks. However, most of the existing algorithms, including the Sinkhorn algorithm and its extensions, suffer from relatively slow convergence in many cases. More recently, some second-order methods have been proposed based on the idea of Hessian sparsification. Despite their promising results, they have two major issues: first, there is limited theoretical understanding on the effect of sparsification; second, in cases where the transport plan is dense, Hessian sparsification does not perform well. In this paper, we propose a new quasi-Newton method to address these problems. First, we develop new theoretical analyses to understand the benefits of Hessian sparsification, which lays the foundation for highly flexible sparsification schemes. Then we introduce an additional low-rank term in the approximate Hessian to better handle the dense case. Finally, the convergence properties of the proposed algorithm are rigorously analyzed, and various numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate its improved performance in solving large-scale OT problems.

paragraphs: This paper develops an optimization method for entropy-regularized optimal transport. Although this formulation supports scalable transport-based applications, commonly used solvers can converge slowly. Methods that use second-order information offer another route, but approximating the Hessian by a sparse matrix has lacked sufficient theoretical explanation and can work poorly when the transport plan is dense.

The authors first analyze the benefits of Hessian sparsification, providing a foundation for more flexible choices of which entries to retain. They then augment the sparse approximation with a low-rank term. This additional component is designed to better represent the dense case while remaining within a quasi-Newton framework that uses an approximate Hessian.

The paper rigorously analyzes convergence and evaluates the algorithm on large-scale optimal transport problems. Numerical experiments demonstrate improved solver performance. Its contribution combines a better theoretical account of sparsification with an approximation that can capture more than sparse structure alone, directly addressing the dense-plan difficulty identified in earlier second-order approaches.
summary.tldr: A sparse-plus-low-rank Hessian approximation improves quasi-Newton optimization for entropy-regularized optimal transport, supported by convergence analysis and numerical experiments.

title: The Sparse-Plus-Low-Rank Quasi-Newton Method for Entropic-Regularized Optimal Transport

abstract: Supervised fine-tuning is a standard method for adapting pre-trained large language models (LLMs) to downstream tasks. Quantization has been recently studied as a post-training technique for efficient LLM deployment. To obtain quantized fine-tuned LLMs, conventional pipelines would first fine-tune the pre-trained models, followed by post-training quantization. This often yields suboptimal performance as it fails to leverage the synergy between fine-tuning and quantization. To effectively realize low-bit quantization of weights, activations and KV caches in LLMs, we propose an algorithm named Rotated Straight-Through-Estimator (RoSTE), which combines quantization-aware supervised fine-tuning (QA-SFT) with an adaptive rotation strategy that identifies an effective rotation configuration to reduce activation outliers. We provide theoretical insights on RoSTE by analyzing its prediction error when applied to an overparameterized least square quantized training problem. Our findings reveal that the prediction error is directly proportional to the quantization error of the converged weights, which can be effectively managed through an optimized rotation configuration. Experiments on Pythia, Qwen and Llama models of different sizes demonstrate the effectiveness of RoSTE. Compared to existing post-SFT quantization baselines, our method consistently achieves superior performances across various tasks and different LLM architectures. Our code is available at https://github.com/OptimAI-Lab/RoSTE.

paragraphs: A common deployment pipeline first fine-tunes a language model and then quantizes it to lower numerical precision. This separation can yield suboptimal results because task adaptation does not account for the later quantization. RoSTE combines quantization-aware supervised fine-tuning with an adaptive rotation strategy.

The method targets low-bit representations of weights, activations, and key-value caches. Its rotation configuration is chosen to reduce activation outliers, helping manage quantization error. The authors analyze prediction error in an overparameterized least-squares quantized training problem. In that setting, prediction error is directly proportional to the quantization error of the converged weights, providing theoretical motivation for optimizing the rotation.

Experiments use Pythia, Qwen, and Llama models of different sizes across multiple tasks. RoSTE consistently outperforms the evaluated methods that quantize after supervised fine-tuning. The findings support treating fine-tuning and quantization as a joint problem. The theoretical result explains the connection in a specific least-squares setting, while the language-model experiments establish the practical benefits across the tested architectures.
summary.tldr: RoSTE combines quantization-aware fine-tuning with adaptive rotations to improve low-bit language-model performance.

title: RoSTE: An Efficient Quantization-Aware Supervised Fine-Tuning Approach for Large Language Models

abstract: Identifying variables responsible for changes to a biological system enables applications in drug target discovery and cell engineering. Given a pair of observational and interventional datasets, the goal is to isolate the subset of observed variables that were the targets of the intervention. Directly applying causal discovery algorithms is challenging: the data may contain thousands of variables with as few as tens of samples per intervention, and biological systems do not adhere to classical causality assumptions. We propose a causality-inspired approach to address this practical setting. First, we infer noisy causal graphs from the observational and interventional data. Then, we learn to map the differences between these graphs, along with additional statistical features, to sets of variables that were intervened upon. Both modules are jointly trained in a supervised framework, on simulated and real data that reflect the nature of biological interventions. This approach consistently outperforms baselines for perturbation modeling on seven single-cell transcriptomics datasets. We also demonstrate significant improvements over current causal discovery methods for predicting soft and hard intervention targets across a variety of synthetic data.

We propose a causality-inspired approach to address this practical setting. First, we infer noisy causal graphs from the observational and interventional data. Then, we learn to map the differences between these graphs, along with additional statistical features, to sets of variables that were intervened upon. Both modules are jointly trained in a supervised framework, on simulated and real data that reflect the nature of biological interventions. This approach consistently outperforms baselines for perturbation modeling on seven single-cell transcriptomics datasets. We also demonstrate significant improvements over current causal discovery methods for predicting soft and hard intervention targets across a variety of synthetic data.

A second component examines differences between those graphs, together with additional statistical features, and predicts the set of intervention targets. Both components are trained jointly under supervision using simulated and real data that reflect biological interventions. The graphs therefore provide structured evidence within a learned prediction system.

It also improves on current causal discovery methods when predicting soft and hard intervention targets across synthetic datasets. These findings support learning how changes in inferred relationships correspond to intervention targets. The method's practical focus is especially relevant when small sample sizes and biological complexity make direct application of causal discovery difficult.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained system uses differences between inferred causal graphs to predict which biological variables an intervention targeted.

title: Identifying biological perturbation targets through causal differential networks

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown remarkable success across various scientific fields, yet their adoption in critical decision-making is often hindered by a lack of interpretability. Recently, intrinsic interpretable GNNs have been studied to provide insights into model predictions by identifying rationale substructures in graphs. However, existing methods face challenges when the underlying rationale subgraphs are complex and varied. In this work, we propose TopInG: Topologically Interpretable Graph Learning, a novel topological framework that leverages persistent homology to identify persistent rationale subgraphs. TopInG employs a rationale filtration learning approach to model an autoregressive generating process of rationale subgraphs, and introduces a self-adjusted topological constraint, termed topological discrepancy, to enforce a persistent topological distinction between rationale subgraphs and irrelevant counterparts. We provide theoretical guarantees that our loss function is uniquely optimized by the ground truth under specific conditions. Extensive experiments demonstrate TopInG’s effectiveness in tackling key challenges, such as handling variform rationale subgraphs, balancing predictive performance with interpretability, and mitigating spurious correlations. Results show that our approach improves upon state-of-the-art methods on both predictive accuracy and interpretation quality.

It also introduces a self-adjusting constraint called topological discrepancy, which encourages a persistent structural distinction between explanatory subgraphs and irrelevant ones. The findings support topology as a useful basis for learning graph explanations, with the theoretical identification result remaining conditional on the stated conditions.
summary.tldr: TopInG uses persistent topological structure to distinguish explanatory graph substructures, improving prediction and interpretation in reported experiments.

title: TopInG: Topologically Interpretable Graph Learning via Persistent Rationale Filtration

abstract: Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized Natural Language Processing by demonstrating exceptional performance across diverse tasks. This study investigates the impact of the parameter initialization scale on the training behavior and task preferences of LLMs. We discover that smaller initialization scales encourage models to favor reasoning tasks, whereas larger initialization scales lead to a preference for memorization tasks. We validate this reasoning bias via real datasets and meticulously designed anchor functions. Further analysis of initial training dynamics suggests that specific model components, particularly the embedding space and self-attention mechanisms, play pivotal roles in shaping these learning biases. We provide a theoretical framework from the perspective of model training dynamics to explain these phenomena. Additionally, experiments on real-world language tasks corroborate our theoretical insights. This work enhances our understanding of how initialization strategies influence LLM performance on reasoning tasks and offers valuable guidelines for training models.

The finding concerns a learning bias associated with initialization, rather than a guarantee that a particular scale produces reasoning.

To investigate the effect, the study combines real datasets with carefully designed anchor functions. These complementary settings support examining the observed task preference and its connection to early training behavior. The analysis identifies the embedding space and self-attention mechanisms as particularly important components in shaping that behavior.

The authors develop a theoretical account based on training dynamics and report supporting experiments on real-world language tasks. Together, the analysis and experiments suggest that initialization is a consequential choice for the kinds of capabilities training favors. The practical implication is that parameter scale at the start of training can help guide model development when reasoning performance is a priority.
summary.tldr: The study links smaller parameter initialization to a reasoning-oriented learning bias and larger initialization to a memorization-oriented bias.

title: An Analysis for Reasoning Bias of Language Models with Small Initialization

abstract: Mainstream strategies for finetuning pretrained multimodal models often degrade out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we develop a theoretical framework for multimodal contrastive finetuning, yielding closed-form solutions and a geometric decomposition for these strategies. This framework shows that self-distillation is more effective than other regularization approaches to retain the knowledge of the pretrained model. Our analysis reveals a largely overlooked limitation: standard Exponential Moving Average (EMA) teachers, widely used in robust finetuning, suffer from collapse. To solve this, we prove that a Weighted Moving Average (WMA) teacher maintains a persistent regularizing force over finite horizons and yields bias-free convergence in the task subspace while preserving orthogonal knowledge. These insights motivate TRACER (Trajectory-Robust Anchoring for Contrastive Encoder Regularization), which combines contrastive learning with WMA-guided multi-perspective distillation. Extensive experiments on CLIP finetuning demonstrate consistent OOD accuracy and calibration gains across three backbone architectures, and comprehensive ablations confirm that TRACER is both principled and robust to hyperparameter choices. Code is available at https://github.com/HesamAsad/TRACER.

title: TRACER: Persistent Regularization for Robust Multimodal Finetuning

abstract: Reinforcement learning algorithms such as GRPO have driven recent advances in large language model (LLM) reasoning. While scaling the number of rollouts stabilizes training, existing approaches suffer from limited exploration on challenging prompts and leave informative feedback signals underexploited, due to context-independent rollout allocation across prompts (e.g., generating 16 rollouts per prompt) and relying heavily on sparse rewards. This paper presents XRPO (eXplore–eXploit GRPO), a unified framework that recasts policy optimization through the principled lens of rollout exploration–exploitation. To enhance exploration, XRPO introduces a mathematically grounded rollout allocator that adaptively prioritizes prompts with higher potential for uncertainty reduction. It further addresses stagnation on zero-reward prompts through an in-context seeding strategy that injects curated exemplars, steering the model into more difficult reasoning trajectories. To strengthen exploitation, XRPO develops a group-relative, novelty-aware advantage sharpening mechanism that leverages sequence likelihoods to amplify low-probability yet correct responses, thereby extending the policy’s reach beyond sparse rewards. Experiments across diverse math and coding benchmarks on both reasoning and non-reasoning models demonstrate that XRPO outperforms existing advances (e.g., GRPO and GSPO) up to 4% pass@1 and 6% cons@32, while accelerating training convergence by up to 2.7x.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for language-model reasoning often generates the same number of candidate responses for every prompt and learns from sparse success signals. This can waste exploration on some prompts while leaving difficult ones without useful feedback. XRPO reorganizes GRPO around two connected questions: where to spend rollout effort and how to learn more from informative responses.

For exploration, an adaptive allocator prioritizes prompts with greater potential to reduce uncertainty. Curated examples are also supplied in context to help the model make progress on prompts whose rollouts otherwise receive zero reward. For exploitation, a group-relative, novelty-aware mechanism uses sequence likelihoods to strengthen learning from correct responses that the model currently considers unlikely.

Across mathematics and coding benchmarks, covering both reasoning and non-reasoning models, XRPO outperforms methods including GRPO and GSPO. The authors report gains of up to 4% in pass@1 and 6% in cons@32, with convergence accelerated by up to 2.7 times. These are reported maxima across the evaluations, supporting the value of coordinating rollout allocation with richer use of successful responses.
summary.tldr: XRPO adapts rollout allocation, seeds difficult prompts, and emphasizes unlikely correct responses to improve reasoning performance and training convergence.

title: XRPO: Pushing the Limits of GRPO with Targeted Exploration and Exploitation

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for zero-shot annotation and LLM-as-a-judge tasks, yet their reliability hinges on how model-internalized priors interact with user-provided instructions. We investigate three dimensions of this interaction: (1) how an LLM’s familiarity with data and task definitions relates to performance, (2) whether additional information in prompts can correct zero-shot errors (”decision stickiness”), and (3) model susceptibility to misaligned task definitions. We introduce Definition-Specific Familiarity (DSF), which measures alignment between a model’s elicited concept and the target definition. Across nine LLMs and five diverse toxicity datasets (spanning social media, gaming, news, and forums), DSF predicts model annotation performance after controlling for dataset identity (partial $r=+0.41$), and this association remains positive across all six prompting conditions tested. In contrast, three common text-memorization metrics show no positive association. We show that prompting has limited corrective power: only 34.8% of zero-shot errors are corrected by additional instructions or examples, with high-confidence errors especially persistent. Misaligned definitions systematically shift predictions without reducing reported confidence, making confidence unreliable for detecting definition–policy mismatch. Together, these findings establish definition alignment as a practical model-selection criterion and show that better prompting alone cannot substitute for validating model-policy fit.

These findings support checking whether a model's understanding fits the intended annotation policy when selecting it. In the studied settings, stronger prompting and confident answers do not substitute for validating that fit.
summary.tldr: Toxicity annotation depends on alignment with task definitions, while additional prompting often leaves confident mistakes uncorrected.

title: On the Limits of LLM Adaptability: Impact of Model-Internalized Priors on Annotation Task Performance

abstract: Image-to-point cloud registration is often challenged by viewpoint changes, cross-modal discrepancies, and repetitive textures, which induce scale ambiguity and consequently lead to erroneous correspondences. Recent detection-free methods alleviate this issue by leveraging multi-scale features and transformer-based interactions. However, they still suffer from attention drift across layers and intra-scale inconsistencies, hindering precise registration. Inspired by complex scene observation, we propose a “Focus–Sweep” paradigm and develop a Hierarchical Mamba Interaction Module within an SSM-based framework to enhance multi-level cross-modal feature association. In addition, we introduce a Dynamic Layer Allocation Strategy that adaptively determines the iteration depth to better exploit geometric constraints and improve matching robustness. Extensive experiments and ablations on two benchmarks, RGB-D Scenes V2 and 7-Scenes, demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Image-to-point cloud registration matches an image with a three-dimensional point cloud. Viewpoint changes, differences between the two data types, and repeated textures can create ambiguity about scale and produce incorrect matches. The paper targets remaining weaknesses in detection-free approaches that already use features at multiple scales and transformer interactions.

This module strengthens associations between image and point-cloud features at multiple levels. The design addresses attention drifting across layers and inconsistent associations within a scale, both of which the authors identify as obstacles to precise registration.

A Dynamic Layer Allocation Strategy additionally adapts the number of processing iterations to make better use of geometric constraints and improve matching robustness. Experiments and ablations on RGB-D Scenes V2 and 7-Scenes show state-of-the-art performance. The contribution combines improved cross-modal interaction with adaptive processing depth, treating both feature association and the amount of iterative refinement as important parts of obtaining reliable correspondences.
summary.tldr: FS-I2P combines hierarchical image–point cloud interactions with adaptive iteration depth to improve registration on two benchmarks.

title: FS-I2P: A Hierarchical Focus–Sweep Registration Network with Dynamically Allocated Depth

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models (MoE-LLMs) achieve strong performance but incur substantial memory overhead due to massive expert parameters. Mixed-precision quantization mitigates this cost by allocating expert-wise bit-widths based on their importance, approaching the accuracy-memory Pareto frontier and enabling extreme low-bit quantization. However, existing methods rely on layer-wise importance estimation and overlook router shifts induced by quantization, resulting in suboptimal allocation and routing. In this work, we propose Global Expert-level Mixed-precision Quantization (GEMQ) to overcome these limitations via (1) a global linear-programming formulation that captures model-wide expert importance based on quantization error analysis, and (2) efficient router fine-tuning to adapt routing to quantized experts. These components are integrated into a progressive quantization framework that iteratively refines importance estimation and allocation. Experiments demonstrate that GEMQ significantly reduces memory and accelerates inference with minimal accuracy degradation.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models store large collections of expert parameters, creating a substantial memory burden. Mixed-precision quantization reduces that burden by giving different experts different numerical bit widths. The challenge is deciding where precision matters most while accounting for the fact that quantization can change which experts the router should select.

GEMQ treats bit allocation as a model-wide problem. It uses quantization-error analysis to estimate expert importance and formulates allocation through linear programming. It also fine-tunes the router so that routing adapts to the quantized experts. This addresses both numerical changes within experts and the decisions that determine how those experts are used.

The two components operate progressively, with importance estimates and precision assignments refined over successive quantization stages. Experiments report substantial memory reduction and faster inference with minimal accuracy degradation. The findings support coordinating compression and routing across the whole model, because choosing precision using only layer-level importance can overlook interactions that matter after experts have been quantized.
summary.tldr: GEMQ jointly refines model-wide expert precision and routing to reduce MoE memory and inference costs with minimal reported accuracy loss.

title: GEMQ: Global Expert-Level Mixed-Precision Quantization for MoE LLMs

abstract: SAM3D enables scalable, open-world 3D reconstruction from complex scenes, yet its deployment is hindered by prohibitive inference latency. In this work, we conduct the first systematic investigation into its inference dynamics, revealing that generic acceleration strategies are brittle in this context. We demonstrate that these failures stem from neglecting the pipeline’s inherent multi-level heterogeneity: the kinematic distinctiveness between shape and layout, the intrinsic sparsity of texture refinement, and the spectral variance across geometries. To address this, we present Fast-SAM3D, a training-free framework that dynamically aligns computation with instantaneous generation complexity. Our approach integrates three heterogeneity-aware mechanisms: (1) Modality-Aware Step Caching to decouple structural evolution from sensitive layout updates; (2) Joint Spatiotemporal Token Carving to concentrate refinement on high-entropy regions; and (3) Spectral-Aware Token Aggregation to adapt decoding resolution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Fast-SAM3D delivers up to 2.67$\times$ end-to-end speedup with negligible fidelity loss, establishing a new Pareto frontier for efficient single-view 3D generation.
