paragraphs: SAM3D reconstructs three-dimensional content from images, but its inference latency makes deployment difficult. This paper investigates why generic acceleration methods are unreliable in that pipeline. It identifies different computational needs across shape and layout generation, sparse texture refinement, and geometries with different spectral characteristics.

Fast-SAM3D responds with three mechanisms that allocate computation according to current generation complexity. Modality-aware caching treats structural changes separately from sensitive layout updates. Joint spatial and temporal token selection concentrates refinement on high-entropy regions. Spectral-aware token aggregation changes decoding resolution to account for differences across geometries. These components target distinct sources of uneven computational demand.

The framework requires no additional training. Experiments report end-to-end speedups of up to 2.67 times with negligible loss of fidelity, improving the observed trade-off between reconstruction quality and runtime. The broader contribution is evidence that acceleration benefits from respecting the internal differences within a generation pipeline. Its reported speedup is an experimental maximum, and negligible fidelity loss does not imply perfectly identical reconstructions.
summary.tldr: Fast-SAM3D adapts caching, refinement, and decoding to different generation demands, achieving up to 2.67× speedup without additional training.

title: Fast-SAM3D: 3Dfy Anything in Images but Faster

abstract: Two-sided matching markets are pervasive in numerous real-world applications, ranging from labor markets to online advertising. A rich line of research has studied the matching bandit problem, where participants learn their preferences through iterative interactions. However, existing works assume a static environment with fixed participants and require synchronized learning, in which all participants start simultaneously and have access to a global clock. In reality, matching markets are inherently dynamic: participants may enter and leave at arbitrary time steps without any global signal, creating coordination challenges. To study the dynamic setting, we first investigate one-sided learning under uncoordinated player arrivals, where only the players need to learn their preferences. We propose the Way-SE algorithm, which achieves a regret of $O(\frac{K^2 \log T}{\Delta_{\min}^2})$, where $K$ is the number of arms, $T$ is the time horizon, and $\Delta_{min}$ is the minimum utility gap. This is done through a distributed exploration mechanism that coordinates exploration implicitly via just local clocks. More importantly, we extend our work to fully decentralized dynamic two-sided learning, where both sides need to learn their preferences, and players arrive or depart arbitrarily. We introduce Way-SE-2S, the first algorithm to achieve sublinear regret $O\left(\frac{K T^{1-1/K}(\log T)^{2/K}}{\Delta_{\min}^2}\right)$ in this challenging environment, without requiring global signals, restrictive preference structures, or observability of the results of competing agents. Our work provides the first theoretical guarantee for stable matching in fully decentralized and uncoordinated bandit markets.

paragraphs: Matching markets become difficult to learn in when participants arrive and leave independently. Existing bandit models often assume everyone starts together and shares a global clock, simplifying coordination unrealistically. This paper studies learning preferences with only local timing and limited visibility into other participants’ outcomes.

For one-sided learning with uncoordinated arrivals, Way-SE coordinates exploration implicitly and obtains logarithmic-in-horizon regret with additional dependence on the number of arms and minimum utility gap. The contribution is a way to learn toward stable matching despite missing synchronization. The exact rate depends strongly on market size and utility gaps, so sublinear regret alone does not imply uniformly rapid adaptation in every market.
summary.tldr: Way-SE algorithms provide regret guarantees for dynamic matching markets whose participants learn without a global clock.

title: Decentralized Bandits without Global Clock for Dynamic Matching Market

abstract: Neural networks for continual reinforcement learning (CRL) often suffer from plasticity loss, i.e., a progressive decline in their ability to learn new tasks arising from increased representational drift (churn) and Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) rank collapse. Current methods mitigating this problem involve algorithmic interventions such as regularization, resets, and optimization schedules. Here, we propose InterpLayers, a lightweight architectural solution that combines a fixed, parameter-free reference pathway with a learnable projection pathway using input-dependent interpolation weights. This structure makes InterpLayers orthogonal to existing algorithmic solutions. We show through theoretical analysis that InterpLayers upper-bound the output variability, bound churn, and prevent a collapse of the NTK rank through continual non-zero rank contribution from the interpolation mechanism. Across different distributional shifts, including permutation, windowing, and expansion, InterpLayers outperform similar gated architectures and achieve similar performance as current state-of-the-art methods without the need for optimization-level intervention or the introduction of sensitive hyperparameters. Ablation studies highlight that these improvements are sustained when InterpLayers are combined with existing algorithmic methods for preventing plasticity loss. These results position InterpLayers as a simple, complementary solution for maintaining plasticity in CRL.
originalAbstract: Neural networks for continual reinforcement learning (CRL) often suffer from plasticity loss, i.e., a progressive decline in their ability to learn new tasks arising from increased representational drift (churn) and Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) rank collapse. Current methods mitigating this problem involve algorithmic interventions such as regularization, resets, and optimization schedules. Here, we propose InterpLayers, a lightweight architectural solution that combines a fixed, parameter-free reference pathway with a learnable projection pathway using input-dependent interpolation weights. This structure makes InterpLayers orthogonal to existing algorithmic solutions. We show through theoretical analysis that InterpLayers upper-bound the output variability, bound churn, and prevent a collapse of the NTK rank through continual non-zero rank contribution from the interpolation mechanism. Across different distributional shifts, including permutation, windowing, and expansion, InterpLayers outperform similar gated architectures and achieve similar performance as current state-of-the-art methods without the need for optimization-level intervention or the introduction of sensitive hyperparameters. Ablation studies highlight that these improvements are sustained when InterpLayers are combined with existing algorithmic methods for preventing plasticity loss. These results position InterpLayers as a simple, complementary solution for maintaining plasticity in CRL.

Existing remedies often change optimization or training schedules; this work instead introduces a lightweight architectural component.

The theoretical analysis shows that this design bounds output variability and churn. It also prevents NTK rank collapse by maintaining a nonzero rank contribution from the interpolation mechanism.

Across distribution shifts involving permutation, windowing, and expansion, InterpLayers outperform comparable gated architectures and achieve performance similar to current leading methods without optimization-level interventions or sensitive new hyperparameters. Ablations show that the gains persist when combined with existing approaches to preserving plasticity. The architecture therefore offers a complementary way to maintain learning capacity: its stabilizing mechanism is built into the network and can operate alongside algorithmic treatments.
summary.tldr: InterpLayers preserve continual-learning plasticity by blending fixed and learned pathways, with theoretical stability guarantees and empirical benefits alongside existing methods.

title: Mitigating Plasticity Loss through Architectural Design in Continual Learning

abstract: We present SorryDB, a dynamically-updating benchmark of open Lean tasks drawn from 78 real world formalization projects on GitHub. Unlike existing static benchmarks, often composed of competition problems, hillclimbing the SorryDB benchmark will yield tools that are aligned to the community needs, more usable by mathematicians, and more capable of understanding complex dependencies. Moreover, by providing a continuously updated stream of tasks, SorryDB mitigates test-set contamination and offers a robust metric for an agent’s ability to contribute to novel formal mathematics projects. We evaluate a collection of approaches, including generalist large language models, agentic approaches, and specialized symbolic provers, over a selected snapshot of 1000 tasks from SorryDB. We show that current approaches are complementary: even though an agentic approach based on Gemini Flash is the most performant, it is not strictly better than other off-the-shelf large-language models, specialized provers, or even a curated list of tactics.

Its purpose is to connect benchmark progress with the work mathematicians and formalization communities actually need completed. Because the tasks come from ongoing projects, they also place emphasis on understanding the complex dependencies surrounding a theorem.

The benchmark updates continuously, providing a stream of new tasks rather than a permanently fixed collection. The authors argue that this reduces test-set contamination and gives a useful measure of an agent’s ability to contribute to new formal mathematics projects. They evaluate generalist language models, agentic methods, and specialized symbolic provers on a selected snapshot containing 1,000 tasks.

An agentic approach based on Gemini Flash performs best overall in that evaluation, but it does not strictly dominate the alternatives. The result indicates that aggregate leadership does not mean one approach covers everything the others can solve, making differences in solved tasks an important part of interpreting prover capability.
summary.tldr: SorryDB supplies continuously updated real-world Lean tasks and finds that current proving approaches have complementary strengths.

title: SorryDB: Can AI Provers Complete Real-World Lean Theorems?

abstract: Existing deep spatial–spectral fusion (SSF) methods typically learn the fusion mapping in the coordinate domain using convolutions and attentions, making it hard to scale across varying spatial resolutions and offering limited control over the frequency content of the reconstructions, which may further lead to severe spectral distortion. In this work, we propose Latent Spectral Operators (LSO), a SSF framework that learns fusion mappings between spectral functions through a structured operator parameterization. Specifically, LSO first applies a cross-attention projection, where learned latent tokens serve as spectral prompts, to compress high-dimensional observations into a compact latent representation, and then adopts a hierarchical, patch-based architecture to integrate rich multi-scale cues. Furthermore, to parameterize the latent fusion operator in a controllable manner, a Trigonometric Basis Solver is elaborated, which represents the mapping using a trigonometric basis expansion. This formulation naturally supports multi-frequency modeling, with a capacity-stability trade-off governed by the number of basis functions. Extensive experiments on the CAVE and Harvard benchmarks demonstrate that LSO achieves consistent state-of-the-art performance and exhibits strong transferability across different spatial scales.

paragraphs: Spatial–spectral fusion must integrate information while preserving the spectral content of the reconstruction. The paper argues that conventional coordinate-domain mappings offer limited control over frequency content and can struggle when spatial resolution changes. Latent Spectral Operators instead learns fusion as a mapping between spectral functions.

The framework first compresses high-dimensional observations through cross-attention, using learned latent tokens as spectral prompts. A hierarchical patch-based architecture then combines information across scales. Its Trigonometric Basis Solver expresses the latent fusion mapping through a trigonometric expansion, providing an explicit parameterization for modeling multiple frequencies.

The number of basis functions controls a stated trade-off between representational capacity and stability. Experiments on CAVE and Harvard report consistent state-of-the-art results and strong transfer across spatial scales. The method therefore connects the representation used for fusion with two practical concerns: controlling frequency behavior and handling changes in resolution. Its findings support structured latent operators as a useful alternative to learning the fusion mapping entirely through conventional coordinate-domain processing.
summary.tldr: Latent Spectral Operators combines compact spectral representations with trigonometric mappings to improve fusion and transfer across spatial scales.

title: Solving Spatial-Spectral Fusion with Latent Spectral Operators

abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown strong generalization, with some approaches seeking to explicitly generate linguistic reasoning traces or predict future observations prior to execution. However, explicit reasoning typically incurs non-negligible inference latency, which constrains the temporal resolution required for robotic manipulation. Moreover, such reasoning is confined to the linguistic space, imposing a representational bottleneck that struggles to faithfully capture ineffable physical attributes. To mitigate these limitations, we propose LaST$_0$, a framework that enables efficient reasoning before acting through a Latent Spatio-Temporal Chain-of-Thought (CoT), capturing fine-grained physical and robotic dynamics that are often difficult to verbalize. Specifically, we introduce a token-efficient latent CoT space that models future visual dynamics, 3D structural information, and robot proprioceptive states, and further extends these representations across time to enable temporally consistent implicit reasoning trajectories. Furthermore, LaST$_0$ adopts a dual-system architecture implemented via a Mixture-of-Transformers design, where a reasoning expert conducts low-frequency latent inference and an acting expert generates high-frequency actions conditioned on robotics-oriented latent representations. To facilitate coordination, LaST$_0$ is trained with heterogeneous operation frequencies, enabling adaptive switching during deployment. Across 10 real-world tasks spanning tabletop, mobile, and dexterous hand manipulation, LaST$_0$ improves mean success rates by 13%, 14% and 14% over prior SOTA VLA methods, respectively.

paragraphs: Robots need to reason about physical situations while producing actions quickly enough for manipulation. Explicit reasoning traces add inference delay, and language can struggle to express fine physical details. LaST₀ addresses these problems by reasoning in a compact latent space that represents information relevant to robotic control.

Its latent reasoning includes future visual dynamics, three-dimensional structure, and the robot’s own state. Extending these representations through time supports consistent implicit reasoning trajectories. A Mixture-of-Transformers architecture separates a reasoning expert, which operates less frequently, from an acting expert that generates frequent actions conditioned on the latent representations. These findings support separating the frequency of physical reasoning from the frequency of action generation while keeping the two coordinated.
summary.tldr: LaST₀ combines slower latent physical reasoning with faster action generation to improve real-world robotic manipulation.

title: LaST$_0$: Latent Spatio-Temporal Chain-of-Thought for Robotic Vision-Language-Action Model

abstract: Tabular foundation models based on pretrained prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) have shown strong generalization on diverse tabular tasks, but they are typically designed for non-strategic settings where data distributions are independent of deployed classifiers. In many real-world decision scenarios, however, individuals may strategically modify their features after deployment to obtain favorable outcomes, inducing a post-deployment distribution shift. This paper studies whether PFN-style tabular foundation models can generalize to such strategic tabular data. We show that strategic manipulation creates a fundamental mismatch between the non-strategic prior learned during pretraining and the post-manipulation strategic prior encountered at deployment, which leads to an irreducible structural prediction bias. To address this issue, we propose the Strategic Prior-data Fitted Network (SPN), an inference-time strategy-aware framework that adapts tabular foundation models to strategic environments without retraining or architectural modification. SPN constructs strategic in-context examples to approximate post-manipulation inputs and aligns PFN predictions with the induced strategic distribution via in-context learning, with theoretical guarantees on bias reduction. Experiments on real-world and synthetic tabular datasets show that SPN consistently improves robustness and predictive performance under strategic manipulation compared with both tabular foundation models and classical tabular methods.

paragraphs: Tabular foundation models based on prior-data fitted networks are usually pretrained for settings where deploying a classifier does not change the data distribution. It constructs strategic in-context examples that approximate the inputs expected after manipulation, then uses those examples to align predictions with the induced distribution. This requires neither retraining the foundation model nor changing its architecture, and the authors provide theoretical guarantees on bias reduction.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world tabular datasets report consistent improvements in robustness and predictive performance over tabular foundation models and classical tabular methods under strategic manipulation. The contribution is a way to adapt the context supplied to a pretrained predictor so that its assumptions better match behavior caused by deploying the predictor itself.
summary.tldr: SPN uses strategic in-context examples to reduce deployment-induced prediction bias in tabular foundation models without retraining.

title: When Tabular Foundation Models Meet Strategic Tabular Data: A Prior Alignment Approach

abstract: Real-world knowledge is often organized as hierarchies such as product taxonomies, medical ontologies, and label trees, yet learning hierarchical representations is challenging due to asymmetric structure and noisy semantics. We introduce Polaris, a polar hyperspherical embedding framework that separates semanticity from hierarchy using angular geometry and radius, enabling the learning of meaning and structure without interference. To map latent representation onto the sphere, we project it to the tangent space at the north pole, apply the exponential map, and learn unit-norm representations using spherical linear layers. Polaris then combines robust local constraints, global regularization that prevents geometric collapse, and uncertainty-aware asymmetric objectives that encourage directional containment. At inference time, Polaris uses structure-guided retrieval to efficiently narrow down candidate parents before final ranking. We evaluate Polaris on different settings of taxonomy expansion – spanning trees, multi-parent DAGs, and multimodal hierarchies, showing consistent improvements of up to $\sim$19 points in top-$K$ retrieval and up to $\sim$ 60% reduction in mean rank over fourteen strong baselines.

paragraphs: Hierarchies must represent both what concepts mean and how they relate directionally, such as which concept is a parent of another. Polaris separates these roles using angular geometry for semantics and radius for hierarchical structure. This addresses the difficulty of learning asymmetric relationships when semantic information is noisy.

The framework constructs spherical representations by projecting into a tangent space at the north pole and applying an exponential map. Spherical linear layers maintain unit-norm representations. Training combines local constraints, global regularization against geometric collapse, and uncertainty-aware asymmetric objectives that encourage directional containment. At inference, structure-guided retrieval narrows the candidate parents before the final ranking step.

The authors evaluate taxonomy expansion for trees, hierarchies with multiple parents, and multimodal hierarchies. Across these settings, they report consistent improvements over fourteen strong baselines, reaching approximately 19 points in top-K retrieval and approximately 60% reduction in mean rank. The results support explicitly separating semantic geometry from hierarchical position while using the hierarchy itself to guide retrieval.
summary.tldr: Polaris separates meaning and hierarchy in polar embeddings, improving reported parent retrieval across several taxonomy-expansion settings.

title: Polaris: Coupled Orbital Polar Embeddings for Hierarchical Concept Learning

abstract: Self-interpretation methods prompt language models to describe their own internal states, but remain unreliable due to hyperparameter sensitivity. We show that training lightweight adapters on interpretability artifacts, while keeping the LM entirely frozen, yields reliable self-interpretation across tasks and model families. A scalar affine adapter with just $d_\text{model}+1$ parameters suffices: trained adapters generate sparse autoencoder feature labels that outperform the training labels themselves (70% vs 50% generation scoring at 70B scale), identify topics with 94% recall@1 versus 1% for untrained baselines, and decode bridge entities in multi-hop reasoning that appear in neither prompt nor response, surfacing implicit reasoning without chain-of-thought. The learned bias vector alone accounts for 85% of improvement, and simpler adapters generalize better than more expressive alternatives. Controlling for model knowledge via prompted descriptions, we find self-interpretation gains outpace capability gains from 7B to 72B parameters. Our results demonstrate that self-interpretation improves with scale, without modifying the model being interpreted.

paragraphs: Asking a language model to explain its internal states can produce unreliable results that depend strongly on settings. This paper trains small adapters on existing interpretability artifacts, represented as vector-label pairs, while leaving the language model frozen. The aim is to make internal information easier for the model to describe without changing the model being examined.

A scalar affine adapter with only d_model + 1 parameters is sufficient for the reported results. At 70B scale, generated sparse-autoencoder feature labels score 70%, compared with 50% for the training labels. Topic identification reaches 94% recall@1 versus 1% for untrained baselines. The method also decodes intermediate entities in multi-hop reasoning that occur in neither the prompt nor the response.

The learned bias vector accounts for 85% of the improvement, and simpler adapters generalize better than more expressive alternatives. After controlling for model knowledge using prompted descriptions, interpretation gains grow faster than capability gains across models from 7B to 72B parameters. These findings support lightweight adaptation as a way to improve self-interpretation and expose otherwise unstated reasoning information in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Tiny adapters trained on interpretability artifacts improve frozen language models’ descriptions of their internal states across tasks and model families.

title: Learning Self-Interpretation from Interpretability Artifacts: Training Lightweight Adapters on Vector-Label Pairs

abstract: Normalization Equivariance (NE) is a structural prior that improves robustness to distribution shift in image-to-image tasks. A function $f$ is normalization equivariant iff $f(a y + b\mathbf{1}) = a f(y) + b\mathbf{1}$ for all $a>0$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}$. Existing NE methods constrain every internal layer to NE-compatible operations. These constraints add runtime cost and exclude standard transformer components such as softmax attention and LayerNorm. We introduce Wrapped Normalization Equivariance (WNE), a parameter-free wrapper that normalizes the input, applies any backbone, and denormalizes the output. We prove every NE function admits this factorization, so the wrapper exactly parameterizes the class of NE functions. On blind denoising, wrapping CNN and transformer architectures improves robustness under noise-level mismatch with no measurable GPU overhead, while architectural NE baselines are up to $1.6\times$ slower.

paragraphs: Normalization equivariance requires an image-processing function to respond predictably when its input is multiplied by a positive scale and shifted by a constant: the output must undergo the same transformation. Existing ways of enforcing this property constrain every internal layer. Those constraints add runtime cost and exclude standard transformer operations such as softmax attention and LayerNorm.

Wrapped Normalization Equivariance uses a parameter-free outer wrapper instead. It normalizes the input, runs a chosen backbone, and then denormalizes the output. The authors prove that every normalization-equivariant function can be expressed in this form. Consequently, the factorization exactly describes the desired function class while allowing the backbone to use ordinary architectural components.

In blind image denoising experiments, wrapping both convolutional and transformer architectures improves robustness when noise levels differ from those expected by the model. The wrapper has no measurable GPU overhead in the reported evaluation, whereas architectural equivariance baselines are up to 1.6 times slower. The result makes this structural robustness property accessible without imposing restrictions throughout the network.
summary.tldr: A parameter-free normalization wrapper enforces normalization equivariance for arbitrary backbones and improves denoising robustness without measurable GPU overhead.

title: Normalization Equivariance for Arbitrary Backbones, with Application to Image Denoising

abstract: Post-hoc controllability of fair machine learning models, the ability to control the trade-off between fairness and accuracy after training, is valuable for practical deployment. Existing post-processing methods provide such post-hoc controllability but often suffer from significant accuracy degradation, whereas in-processing methods achieve efficient trade-offs but require computationally expensive retraining for each change in trade-off ratio. To achieve both post-hoc controllability and efficient trade-offs, we propose a novel fair classification algorithm that learns effective feature representations to improve the trade-off efficiency of post-processing fair classifiers, by a gradient-based optimization approach. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves trade-off efficiency comparable to, or even surpassing, in-processing methods, without requiring any retraining.
originalAbstract: Post-hoc controllability of fair machine learning models, the ability to control the trade-off between fairness and accuracy after training, is valuable for practical deployment. Existing post-processing methods provide such post-hoc controllability but often suffer from significant accuracy degradation, whereas in-processing methods achieve efficient trade-offs but require computationally expensive retraining for each change in trade-off ratio. To achieve both post-hoc controllability and efficient trade-offs, we propose a novel fair classification algorithm that learns effective feature representations to improve the trade-off efficiency of post-processing fair classifiers, by a gradient-based optimization approach. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves trade-off efficiency comparable to, or even surpassing, in-processing methods, without requiring any retraining.

paragraphs: A deployed classifier may need different balances between fairness and accuracy as requirements change. Methods that adjust predictions after training offer this flexibility, but can lose substantial accuracy. Methods that incorporate fairness during training can produce better trade-offs, yet changing the desired balance typically requires expensive retraining. This paper aims to combine flexible adjustment with an efficient fairness-accuracy trade-off.

The proposed algorithm learns feature representations specifically to improve the behavior of post-processing fair classifiers. It uses gradient-based optimization to shape the information available to the later adjustment stage. The key design choice is therefore to prepare the representation during training so that changing the fairness-accuracy balance afterward can work more effectively.

Experiments on real-world datasets show trade-off efficiency comparable to, and sometimes better than, the in-processing methods considered. These adjustments do not require retraining the proposed model. The findings support a practical connection between representation learning and deployment flexibility: training can improve the options available to a later fairness adjustment, rather than committing the model to a single balance.
summary.tldr: Learning representations for post-processing lets classifiers adjust their fairness-accuracy balance after training while achieving competitive trade-off efficiency.

title: Fair Classification with Efficient and Post-hoc Controllable Fairness-Accuracy Trade-off

abstract: Long-tailed recognition fundamentally suffers from optimizer blindness where the optimization process mistakenly conflates the magnitude of gradient accumulation with the scarcity of semantic information. Existing strategies relying on static frequency-based priors fail to correct this bias and result in state blindness regarding supervision and micro-level blindness regarding parameter updates. To address these limitations, we propose the AES framework to establish a dynamic and state-aware correction system across the entire learning lifecycle. We specifically introduce Adaptive Residual Supervision loss to act as a real-time reality check for supervision completeness via precision shielding. We also propose Entropy-aware PCGrad to resolve parameter-level conflicts by quantifying task specificity through gradient entropy. Additionally, we devise Sample-level Conflict Arbitrated Fusion to serve as a dynamic inference arbiter that routes predictions based on instance difficulty. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-100-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018 demonstrate that our method consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance by effectively balancing head-class stability and tail-class discrimination. paragraphs: Long-tailed recognition asks a model to recognize classes with very different amounts of training data. The paper attributes an important difficulty to optimizer blindness: accumulated gradient magnitude can be confused with how much semantic information a class lacks. Corrections based on fixed class frequencies do not track the changing state of supervision or individual parameter updates.

AES addresses this problem at three stages. Adaptive Residual Supervision adjusts supervision through a mechanism called precision shielding, intended to assess its completeness during training. Entropy-aware PCGrad uses gradient entropy to quantify task specificity and resolve conflicts between parameter updates. At inference, Sample-level Conflict Arbitrated Fusion routes predictions according to the difficulty of each individual example.

Together, these components make correction depend on the model’s current state and the sample being processed. Experiments on CIFAR-100-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018 report state-of-the-art performance. The stated result is a better balance between maintaining reliable recognition of common classes and distinguishing rare classes, linking improvements to coordinated adjustments across supervision, optimization, and prediction.
summary.tldr: AES adjusts supervision, gradient conflict handling, and prediction routing dynamically to improve recognition of both common and rare classes.

title: AES: Curing Optimizer Blindness in Long-Tailed Recognition via State-Aware Correction

abstract: Neural population geometry shapes downstream computation. Recent empirical findings in neurobiology suggest that a hyperbolic structure underlies population activity in the hippocampus. Here we provide a theoretical framework for this phenomenon. First, we propose a plausible construction of hippocampal tuning curves that statistically induces hyperbolic geometry. Next, we establish a connection between neural decoding and associative memory by demonstrating that the Modern Hopfield Network update rule computes the minimum mean-squared-error (MMSE) estimator. Finally, we introduce a novel associative memory model defined in hyperbolic space that yields significantly larger capacity than leading models. Our results suggest that animals encode spatial information as a latent hyperbolic cognitive map, improving both memory capacity and decoding accuracy.

First, we propose a plausible construction of hippocampal tuning curves that statistically induces hyperbolic geometry. Next, we establish a connection between neural decoding and associative memory by demonstrating that the Modern Hopfield Network update rule computes the minimum mean-squared-error (MMSE) estimator. Finally, we introduce a novel associative memory model defined in hyperbolic space that yields significantly larger capacity than leading models. paragraphs: Patterns of activity across many neurons have a geometry, and that geometry can influence the computations supported by those patterns. Motivated by empirical suggestions of hyperbolic organization in hippocampal activity, this paper develops a theoretical account of how such organization could arise and why it might benefit memory and decoding.

The authors first construct plausible hippocampal tuning curves whose collective activity statistically induces hyperbolic geometry. They then connect neural decoding with associative memory by showing that the Modern Hopfield Network update rule computes a minimum mean-squared-error estimator. This links retrieving an associated memory with estimating information from a neural representation.

Building on that connection, the paper introduces an associative memory model defined in hyperbolic space and reports significantly greater capacity than leading models. The combined results suggest that a latent hyperbolic map could help animals encode spatial information with better memory capacity and decoding accuracy. This is a theoretical explanation supporting that possibility; the proposed construction and computational benefits do not themselves establish that animals necessarily use the suggested representation.
summary.tldr: A theoretical framework links hyperbolic hippocampal representations to neural decoding and an associative memory model with greater capacity.

title: Hyperbolic neural population geometry benefits computation

abstract: Neural operators perform well on structured domains, yet their behaviour on irregular geometries remains poorly understood. We show that this limitation is not merely an encoding issue, but a depth-wise failure mode inherent to deep operator architectures. We formalise the Geometric Forgetting Hypothesis: due to the Markovian structure of operator layers and their reliance on global mixing mechanisms, neural operators progressively lose access to domain geometry as depth increases. Using layer-wise geometric probing, we demonstrate that both spectral and attention-based operators systematically lose geometric fidelity. We show that this geometric forgetting degrades accuracy, stability, and generalisation. To counteract it, we introduce a lightweight geometry memory injection mechanism that restores geometric constraints at intermediate depths with minimal architectural overhead. This simple intervention consistently mitigates forgetting and exposes a geometric shortcut instability in transformer-based operators, revealing that geometric retention is a structural requirement rather than a design choice.

paragraphs: Neural operators work well on structured domains, but irregular geometry presents a less understood challenge. This paper argues that supplying a good geometric encoding at the input does not fully address the problem. Information about the domain’s shape can become progressively less accessible as it passes through deeper operator layers.

The authors formalize this behavior as the Geometric Forgetting Hypothesis, connecting it to the Markovian structure of operator layers and their use of global mixing. They probe geometry at successive layers and find declining geometric fidelity in both spectral and attention-based operators. Their analysis links this loss to worse accuracy, stability, and generalization, making retention through depth a central architectural concern.

To counter the loss, the paper introduces geometry memory injection, a lightweight mechanism that restores geometric constraints at intermediate layers. It consistently mitigates forgetting with little architectural overhead. The intervention also reveals a geometric-shortcut instability in transformer-based operators. Together, these findings motivate maintaining access to geometry throughout the model, beyond representing it well at the initial input.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that neural operators lose geometric information with depth and proposes intermediate geometry injections to mitigate that loss.

title: Do Neural Operators Forget Geometry? The Forgetting Hypothesis in Deep Operator Learning

abstract: Accurately localizing and segmenting small targets in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) infrared sequences remains a challenging task. Since targets are often indistinguishable from the background in individual frames, existing methods, even when equipped with advanced foundation model and powerful inter-frame association mechanisms, still fail to detect them. Motivated by the observation that targets tend to emerge gradually from the background over time and become distinguishable, we propose Temporal-Emerged Prompting for Segment Anything Model (TEP-SAM), a principled framework designed to explicitly exploit such temporal-emerged cues to modulate and prompt SAM. TEP-SAM operates by jointly modeling global motion patterns and local motion deviations to locate potential targets. It further enhances target region features by leveraging motion discrepancy, thereby generating temporal-emerged cues for SAM and enabling non-interactive segmentation. By bridging large-scale semantic pretraining with task-specific temporal modeling, TEP-SAM effectively adapts SAM to the challenging multiframe infrared small target detection task. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, particularly under severely low-SNR conditions and in complex dynamic background.

paragraphs: TEP-SAM addresses small targets that are difficult to distinguish from background noise in infrared video. A single frame may contain too little visible evidence for reliable detection, even when a strong segmentation model is available. The paper instead draws on the observation that a target can become distinguishable as its behavior unfolds over time.

The framework jointly models broad motion patterns and local departures from those patterns to locate possible targets. It then uses motion discrepancies to strengthen features in candidate target regions. The resulting temporal cues modulate and prompt the Segment Anything Model, allowing segmentation without interactive prompting by a person.

This links SAM’s large-scale semantic pretraining with motion information specific to infrared target detection. Experiments report effectiveness especially under very low signal-to-noise conditions and complex, changing backgrounds. The findings support explicitly constructing cues from how targets emerge over time, rather than expecting individual frames or general inter-frame association alone to provide sufficiently clear evidence for segmentation.
summary.tldr: TEP-SAM turns temporal motion differences into automatic prompts for segmenting faint, small infrared targets.

title: Temporal-Emerged Prompting for Segment Anything in Multiframe Infrared Small Target Detection

abstract: Fairness in machine learning prediction has attracted growing attention in recent years. In this article, we propose a causal–inference–based framework for fair prediction, defined through path-specific counterfactual interventions. Instead of imposing fairness via constraints on predictive objectives or model parameters, our approach specifies fairness directly at the level of counterfactual prediction semantics. Given a learned causal graph, we construct a predictive distribution for the outcome $Y$ using a structural causal model and generate counterfactual predictions by selectively intervening on causal paths emanating from sensitive attributes. By allowing or blocking the propagation of sensitive information along designated paths, possibly involving multiple sensitive sources, our framework induces a hierarchy of interpretable fairness notions, generalizing standard path-specific causal semantics. Our empirical experiments demonstrate how different fairness levels can be instantiated and compared in practice.

paragraphs: Fairness can depend on which routes of influence from a sensitive attribute are considered acceptable. This paper builds a framework that expresses those choices through counterfactual predictions. It defines fairness at the level of what a prediction means under selected interventions, making the treatment of sensitive information explicit.

Given a learned causal graph, the framework uses a structural causal model to construct a predictive distribution for the outcome. It then intervenes selectively on paths originating from sensitive attributes, allowing influence along some paths and blocking it along others. The construction can involve multiple sensitive sources and generalizes standard path-specific causal semantics.

Different choices of permitted and blocked paths create a hierarchy of interpretable fairness notions. Experiments demonstrate how these levels can be instantiated and compared in practice. The learned causal graph is an explicit starting point of the approach: the framework uses its structure to express which influences predictions retain. Its contribution is a common causal language for organizing and comparing different fairness requirements.
summary.tldr: The framework organizes fairness notions by selectively allowing or blocking sensitive-attribute influence along paths in a learned causal graph.

title: The Fairness Hierarchy: A viewpoint from causal inference

abstract: The rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has created an urgent demand for more reliable and robust evaluation protocols, however, existing static benchmarks are prone to data contamination and performance saturation, which can result in inflated or misleading evaluation results. To address these limitations, we first introduce a graph formulation to represent both static and dynamic visual question answering (VQA) samples. Building upon this formulation, we propose Knowledge-Enhanced Benchmark Evolution (KBE), a dynamic multimodal evaluation framework that first analyzes the original static benchmark, then expands it by integrating multimodal knowledge, transforming the static benchmark into a controllable, dynamic evolving version. Crucially, KBE can both reconstruct questions by Re-selecting visual information in the original image and expand existing questions with external textual knowledge. By explicitly controlling the degree of question exploration, KBE enables difficulty-controllable evaluation across a wide range of model capabilities. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that KBE effectively mitigates data contamination and benchmark saturation, while providing a more comprehensive and flexible assessment of MLLM performance.

paragraphs: A fixed visual question-answering benchmark can become less informative as models encounter its contents or approach its performance ceiling. This paper introduces Knowledge-Enhanced Benchmark Evolution, or KBE, to turn a static benchmark into an evolving evaluation. The aim is to reduce misleading scores while retaining control over what the resulting questions test.

KBE begins with a graph representation of visual question-answering samples and analyzes the original benchmark. It then creates variations in two ways: selecting different visual information from the same image and extending questions with external textual knowledge. Explicit control over how far questions are explored allows the framework to vary difficulty across a range of model capabilities.

The authors report that KBE mitigates both data contamination and benchmark saturation in their experiments. This supports evaluating models through controlled changes to existing questions instead of relying exclusively on a fixed collection. The findings establish a more flexible assessment approach, with difficulty and question content treated as adjustable parts of evaluation rather than permanent properties of the benchmark.
summary.tldr: KBE evolves visual question-answering benchmarks through controlled visual and knowledge-based changes to reduce contamination and saturation.

title: Dynamic Multimodal Evaluation via Knowledge-Enhanced Benchmark Evolution

abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a principled Bayesian framework for uncertainty estimation, but their computational complexity severely limits scalability to large datasets. We propose SIKA-GP, which accelerates GP inference using sparse inducing kernel approximations based on a dyadic ordered template basis, incurring only ${O}(\log M)$ complexity dependence on the number of inducing points. Our approach constructs compact and expressive kernel representations from sparsely activated bases, enabling efficient tensorized GPU computation and seamless integration with modern large-scale models. SIKA-GP can be naturally embedded into Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) with sparse activations, yielding significant speedups in both training and inference without sacrificing predictive performance. The method naturally extends to deep feature learning, addressing the scalability challenges introduced by deep architectures and high-dimensional feature representations. Empirical results on vision and transformer-based language benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently delivers fast and accurate GP models, providing a principled path toward scalable kernel learning.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer a Bayesian approach to prediction and uncertainty estimation, but their computational demands make large-scale use difficult. SIKA-GP addresses this bottleneck by approximating kernels with sparse inducing representations. The goal is to retain expressive kernel models while reducing the computation needed to use them.

The method builds on a dyadic ordered template basis, activating only a sparse set of basis elements. Its complexity dependence on the number of inducing points is logarithmic. Compact representations also support tensorized GPU computation and integration with large models, connecting the mathematical approximation to an implementation suited to modern hardware.

SIKA-GP can be embedded in Bayesian neural networks with sparse activations and extends to deep feature learning with high-dimensional representations. The paper reports substantial training and inference speedups without sacrificing predictive performance. Evaluations on vision and Transformer-based language benchmarks consistently produce fast, accurate Gaussian-process models. These findings support sparse kernel representations as a practical route for carrying Bayesian kernel methods into larger learned-feature systems.
summary.tldr: SIKA-GP uses sparse kernel bases with logarithmic dependence on inducing-point count to accelerate Gaussian-process models and Bayesian deep learning.

title: SIKA-GP: Accelerating Gaussian Process Inference with Sparse Inducing Kernel Approximations for Bayesian Deep Learning

abstract: Transformers excel in natural language processing and computer vision tasks. However, they still face challenges in generalizing to Out-of-Distribution (OOD) datasets, i.e. data whose distribution differs from that seen during training. OOD detection aims to distinguish outliers while preserving in-distribution (ID) data performance. This paper introduces the OOD detection Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) Theory for transformers, which establishes the conditions for data distribution and model configurations for the OOD detection learnability of transformers. It shows that outliers can be accurately represented and distinguished with sufficient data under conditions. The theoretical implications highlight the trade-off between theoretical principles and practical training paradigms. By examining this trade-off, we naturally derived the rationale for leveraging auxiliary outliers to enhance OOD detection. Our theory suggests that by penalizing the misclassification of outliers within the loss function and strategically generating soft synthetic outliers, one can robustly bolster the reliability of transformer networks. This approach yields a novel algorithm that ensures learnability and refines the decision boundaries between inliers and outliers. In practice, the algorithm consistently achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance across various data formats.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks a model to recognize inputs that differ from its training distribution while preserving performance on familiar data. This paper develops a Probably Approximately Correct learning theory for transformer-based detection. It identifies conditions on data distributions and model configurations under which outliers can be represented and distinguished accurately with sufficient data.

The authors use the relationship between those theoretical requirements and practical training to motivate auxiliary outliers. Their proposed algorithm penalizes outlier misclassification in the training loss and introduces strategically generated soft synthetic outliers. These additions are intended to refine the boundary between familiar inputs and outliers, translating the theory into a training procedure.

The resulting learnability claim is tied to the conditions established by the analysis; it does not assert that every transformer can distinguish arbitrary unfamiliar data. In experiments across different data formats, the algorithm consistently achieves reported state-of-the-art performance. The contribution connects a conditional account of when detection can be learned with an empirical method for improving transformer reliability.
summary.tldr: A conditional learning theory for transformer outlier detection motivates training with outlier penalties and soft synthetic outliers.

title: How Out-of-Distribution Detection Learning Theory Enhances Transformer: Learnability and Reliability

abstract: The Relevance Vector Machine (RVM) is a sparse approximate Bayesian kernel method. It provides full predictive distributions for test cases. However, the predictive uncertainties have the unintuitive property, that they get smaller the further you move away from the training cases. We give a thorough analysis. Inspired by the analogy to nondegenerate Gaussian Processes, we suggest augmentation to solve the problem. The purpose of the resulting model, RVM*, is primarily to corroborate the theoretical and experimental analysis. Although RVM* could be used in practical applications, it is no longer a truly sparse model. Experiments show that sparsity comes at the expense of worse predictive distributions.

However, the predictive uncertainties have the unintuitive property, that they get smaller the further you move away from the training cases. We give a thorough analysis. paragraphs: The Relevance Vector Machine is a sparse approximate Bayesian kernel method that produces predictive distributions, including uncertainty about its predictions. The paper investigates a counterintuitive behavior: its predictive uncertainty decreases as a test case moves farther from the training cases. The analysis therefore concerns the quality of uncertainty estimates, not merely the predicted values.

Inspired by a comparison with nondegenerate Gaussian processes, the authors propose augmenting the model to address this behavior. The resulting model, RVM*, primarily serves to support their theoretical and experimental analysis. It could be applied in practice, but the augmentation means it no longer retains the original model's true sparsity.

The experiments show a tradeoff in which sparsity comes with worse predictive distributions. This matters because a model's compactness and the reliability of its uncertainty estimates are distinct properties. RVM* helps expose that tension by changing the model in a way intended to repair its uncertainty behavior, while giving up the sparse representation that makes the original RVM attractive.
summary.tldr: Augmenting the Relevance Vector Machine addresses its shrinking uncertainty away from training data but sacrifices true sparsity.

title: Healing the relevance vector machine through augmentation
Learning hierarchical task networks by observation

abstract: Motivated by causal inference problems, we propose a novel method for regression that minimizes the statistical dependence between regressors and residuals. The key advantage of this approach to regression is that it does not assume a particular distribution of the noise, i.e., it is non-parametric with respect to the noise distribution. We argue that the proposed regression method is well suited to the task of causal inference in additive noise models. A practical disadvantage is that the resulting optimization problem is generally non-convex and can be difficult to solve. Nevertheless, we report good results on one of the tasks of the NIPS 2008 Causality Challenge, where the goal is to distinguish causes from effects in pairs of statistically dependent variables. In addition, we propose an algorithm for efficiently inferring causal models from observational data for more than two variables. The required number of regressions and independence tests is quadratic in the number of variables, which is a significant improvement over the simple method that tests all possible DAGs.

paragraphs: This paper proposes regression that minimizes statistical dependence between the input variables and the residuals left after prediction. The motivation comes from causal inference with additive noise models, where the relationship between inputs and unexplained variation matters. The method does not assume a particular noise distribution, making it nonparametric with respect to that distribution.

The authors argue that this objective suits causal inference, but identify a practical difficulty: optimization is generally nonconvex and can be hard to solve. Despite that obstacle, they report good results on a causality challenge task involving pairs of statistically dependent variables. The task is to distinguish which variable is the cause and which is the effect.

The paper also proposes an efficient algorithm for inferring causal models from observational data with more than two variables. Its required number of regressions and independence tests grows quadratically with the number of variables. This improves on the simple strategy of testing every possible directed acyclic graph, connecting the regression criterion with a more scalable causal-model search.
summary.tldr: Dependence-minimizing regression supports additive-noise causal inference without specifying a noise distribution, though its optimization is generally nonconvex.

title: Regression by dependence minimization and its application to causal inference in additive noise models

abstract: We study the problem of supervised linear dimensionality reduction, taking an information-theoretic viewpoint. The linear projection matrix is designed by maximizing the mutual information between the projected signal and the class label (based on a Shannon entropy measure). By harnessing a recent theoretical result on the gradient of mutual information, the above optimization problem can be solved directly using gradient descent, without requiring simplification of the objective function. Theoretical analysis and empirical comparison are made between the proposed method and two closely related methods (Linear Discriminant Analysis and Information Discriminant Analysis), and comparisons are also made with a method in which Renyi entropy is used to define the mutual information (in this case the gradient may be computed simply, under a special parameter setting). Relative to these alternative approaches, the proposed method achieves promising results on real datasets.

paragraphs: Supervised dimensionality reduction seeks a smaller representation that preserves information useful for identifying classes. This paper studies linear projections from an information-theoretic perspective. It chooses the projection by maximizing mutual information between the projected observations and their class labels, using Shannon entropy to define that information.

The central computational contribution is a way to optimize this objective directly. The authors use a theoretical result giving the gradient of mutual information, allowing gradient descent without simplifying the objective function. This matters because the quantity being optimized remains the stated measure of class-relevant information, rather than a simplified replacement introduced to make optimization easier.

The paper provides theoretical and empirical comparisons with Linear Discriminant Analysis and Information Discriminant Analysis. It also compares against a related approach based on Renyi entropy, whose gradient is simple under a particular parameter setting. Results on real datasets are described as promising relative to these alternatives. The contribution combines a principled projection objective with a direct optimization route and encouraging empirical evidence.
summary.tldr: The method learns linear projections by directly optimizing Shannon mutual information with class labels, producing promising results on real datasets.

title: Communications Inspired Linear Discriminant Analysis

abstract: We propose a non-parametric link prediction algorithm for a sequence of graph snapshots over time. The model predicts links based on the features of its endpoints, as well as those of the local neighborhood around the endpoints. This allows for different types of neighborhoods in a graph, each with its own dynamics (e.g, growing or shrinking communities). We prove the consistency of our estimator, and give a fast implementation based on locality-sensitive hashing. Experiments with simulated as well as five real-world dynamic graphs show that we outperform the state of the art, especially when sharp fluctuations or non-linearities are present.

The model predicts links based on the features of its endpoints, as well as those of the local neighborhood around the endpoints. This allows for different types of neighborhoods in a graph, each with its own dynamics (e.g, growing or shrinking communities). We prove the consistency of our estimator, and give a fast implementation based on locality-sensitive hashing. Experiments with simulated as well as five real-world dynamic graphs show that we outperform the state of the art, especially when sharp fluctuations or non-linearities are present.

paragraphs: A changing network can contain neighborhoods with different patterns of evolution, such as communities that grow while others shrink. This paper proposes a nonparametric method for predicting links from a sequence of graph snapshots. It uses information about both candidate endpoints and the local neighborhoods around them.

Including neighborhood features allows the prediction model to account for different local dynamics within the same graph. The authors prove consistency of their estimator and provide a fast implementation based on locality-sensitive hashing. The work therefore addresses both the statistical behavior of the prediction method and the computational task of applying it efficiently.

Experiments use simulated networks and five real-world dynamic graphs. The method outperforms the state of the art in those evaluations, with particular gains when changes involve sharp fluctuations or nonlinear patterns. These findings support modeling local network context when forecasting links. They also connect the method's flexibility to the situations where the reported empirical advantage is especially pronounced.
summary.tldr: A consistent nonparametric link predictor uses endpoint and neighborhood features to model local dynamics, with strong results on fluctuating networks.

title: Nonparametric Link Prediction in Dynamic Networks

abstract: We study the stability vis a vis adversarial noise of matrix factorization algorithm for matrix completion. In particular, our results include: (I) we bound the gap between the solution matrix of the factorization method and the ground truth in terms of root mean square error; (II) we treat the matrix factorization as a subspace fitting problem and analyze the difference between the solution subspace and the ground truth; (III) we analyze the prediction error of individual users based on the subspace stability. We apply these results to the problem of collaborative filtering under manipulator attack, which leads to useful insights and guidelines for collaborative filtering system design.
originalAbstract: We study the stability vis a vis adversarial noise of matrix factorization algorithm for matrix completion. In particular, our results include: (I) we bound the gap between the solution matrix of the factorization method and the ground truth in terms of root mean square error; (II) we treat the matrix factorization as a subspace fitting problem and analyze the difference between the solution subspace and the ground truth; (III) we analyze the prediction error of individual users based on the subspace stability. We apply these results to the problem of collaborative filtering under manipulator attack, which leads to useful insights and guidelines for collaborative filtering system design.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization is used to complete partially observed matrices, including those underlying collaborative filtering. This paper studies how the resulting solution changes under adversarial noise. Its focus is stability: how manipulation affects the recovered matrix, its underlying subspace, and predictions for individual users.

The analysis proceeds at those three levels. First, the authors bound the gap between the factorization solution and the ground truth using root mean square error. Next, they interpret factorization as a subspace fitting problem and analyze the difference between the fitted and true subspaces. Finally, they use subspace stability to study prediction errors for individual users.

This sequence connects overall reconstruction error to the internal structure learned by the model and then to user-level consequences. The authors apply the results to collaborative filtering under manipulator attacks and derive insights and design guidelines. The contribution is an analytical account of how adversarial disturbance relates to recommendation errors, providing a basis for reasoning about system design under manipulation.
summary.tldr: The paper links adversarial noise to matrix reconstruction, subspace stability, and individual-user prediction errors in collaborative filtering.

title: Stability of matrix factorization for collaborative filtering
